title: Custom CNN Model for Healthcare Industry IoT Attack Detection and Classification
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has affected almost every facet of existence. Smart healthcare is one of the primary sectors utilizing IoT platforms and remedies to a significant extent. IoT-based intelligent health services have greatly raised the value of the healthcare sector by utilizing wearable and mobile devices. As a result, a large amount of health data interchange is used to provide better, faster, and more accurate diagnosis. But smart healthcare systems are also very vulnerable to various malicious attacks and security flaws, such as manipulation, forgeries, and privacy breaches. In this study, we introduce a customized convolutional neural networks (CNN) model and concentrate on early detection of botnet assaults to enhance the security and reliability of the healthcare business. The efficacy and generalizability of the suggested models are confirmed by experiments conducted on Bot-IoT dataset.

title: Cyber Security for Remote Patient Monitoring System
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: The Internet of Things is an emerging topic of technical, social, and economic significance. Consumer products, durable goods, cars and trucks, industrial and utility components, sensors, and other everyday objects are being combined with Internet connectivity and powerful data analytic capabilities that promise to transform the way we work, live, and play. Projections for the impact of IoT on the Internet and economy are impressive, with some anticipating as many as 100 billion connected IoT devices and a global economic impact of more than $11 trillion by 2025. Internet of Things (IoT) devices is rapidly becoming ubiquitous while IoT services are becoming pervasive. Their success has not gone unnoticed and the number of threats and attacks against IoT devices and services are on the increase as well. Cyber-attacks are not new to IoT, but as IoT will be deeply interwoven in our lives and societies, it is becoming necessary to step up and take cyber defense seriously. Currently, most proposed IoT attacks are proof-of-concepts and have yet to generate any profit for attackers. This does not mean that attackers won’t target IoT devices in future, even if it is just to misuse the technology or have a persistent anchor in a home network. The use of weak passwords is a security issue that has repeatedly been seen in IoT devices. These devices often do not have a keyboard, so configuration has to be done remotely. Unfortunately, not all vendors force the user to change the devices’ default passwords and many have unnecessary restrictions which make the implementation of long, complex passwords impossible. The Open Web Application Security Project’s (OWASP) Lists Top Ten Internet of Things Vulnerabilities. This thesis has three main contributions. (i) It enables secure communication in the IoT using lightweight compressed yet standard compliant IPsec, DTLS, and IEEE 802.15.4 link layer security; and it discusses the pros and cons of each of these solutions. The proposed security solutions are implemented and evaluated in an IoT setup on real hardware. (ii) This thesis also presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of novel IDS for the IoT. (iii) Last but not least, it also provides mechanisms to protect data inside constrained nodes. This paper mainly focuses on Remote Patient Monitoring Systems. However, deploying new technologies in healthcare applications without considering security makes patient privacy vulnerable. Moreover, the physiological data of an individual are highly sensitive. Therefore, security is a paramount requirement of healthcare applications, especially in the case of patient privacy, if the patient has an embarrassing disease. Security is provided for data which is being fetched from the patients through wearable devices and transferred to the concerned doctors by using a public key encryption technique namely ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) is used.

title: Cyber-Situational Awarenss in Clinical Trials Using Wearable Device Technology
venue: Proceedings of the International Symposium on Human Factors and Ergonomics in Health Care
abstract: It is estimated 1 in 3 clinical trials utilize a wearable device to gather real-time participant data, including sleep habits, telemetry, and physical activity. While wearable technologies (including smart watches, USBs, and implantable devices) have been revolutionary in their ability to provide a higher precision and accuracy to data acquisition external to the research milieu, there is hesitancy among providers and participants alike given security concerns, perception of cyber-related threats, and meaning attributed to privacy issues. The purpose of this research is to define cyber-situational awareness (CSA) as it pertains to clinical trials, evaluate its current measurement, and describe best practices for research investigators and trial participants to enhance protections in the digital age. This paper reviews integrated elements of CSA within the process of informed consent when wearable devices are implemented for trial procedures. Evaluation of CSA as part of informed consent allows the research site to support the participant in knowledge gaps surrounding the technology while also providing feedback to the trial sponsor as to technology improvements to enhance usability and wearability of the device.

title: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities in Smartwatches as Health Devices using Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
venue: International Conference on Computing, Engineering and Design (ICCED)
abstract: Modern technology places a wealth of information at users' fingertips, including health monitoring capabilities through wearable devices such as smartwatches. Smartwatches offer various benefits for human health, such as monitoring heart rate, pulse rate, blood oxygen levels, physical activity reminders, stress levels, sleep analysis, daily step counts and function as digital medical records. This device plays an important role in detecting serious health conditions, such as atrial fibrillation and sleep disorders, by providing early warnings to users to seek medical care immediately. While smartwatches have empowered individuals to be proactive in maintaining health, they also present new challenges, concerns have arisen regarding potential cybersecurity threats related to user privacy and data security. This study aims to identify threats and vulnerabilities associated with the use of smartwatches and assess the risks arising from these vulnerabilities. An in-depth literature review of cyber attack threats and vulnerabilities in the use of smart watches. In addition, this study also proposes mitigation strategies that can be applied to reduce these risks, including improving security protocols and educating users about potential dangers. Thus, this study makes an important contribution to understanding the complexity of risks associated with smartwatch use and provides practical recommendations to mitigate possible negative impacts.

title: Cybersecurity and Privacy in AI-Enabled Wearable Textile Systems
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a pivotal advancement in textile systems, integrating intelligent sensing, wearable computing, IoT, and machine learning applications on smart fabrics for real-time monitoring of object behavior through predictive analytics. The primary areas of application identified in the investigation include healthcare, industrial safety, sports and fitness. Emerging domains represent; AI-enhanced wearable fabrics are perpetually evolving for ongoing patient surveillance and preventive health measures. The most significant security risk identified during this analysis is data breaches, closely followed by limited system access, adversarial AI assaults and denial of service attacks. Privacy-preserving technologies have emerged as a significant domain, with encryption along with blockchain, edge computing, and federated learning. This meta-analysis offers insights regarding contemporary research trends and obstacles in cybersecurity which will assist researchers in creating secure and sustainable AI-integrated wearable textile systems.

title: Cybersecurity, Foreign Investment, and the Evolving Meaning of Full Protection and Security
abstract: Foreign investors increasingly rely on digitally mediated assets and operations, like data centres, cloud services, and industrial control systems, that are situated within or controlled by host states. The law governing the obligations of host states to prevent and respond to cyber incidents affecting those investments remains uneven and fragmented. Current study examines whether, and in what manner, the classical investment law standard of full protection and security (FPS) can be interpreted to encompass a positive duty of cyber due diligence. Drawing on treaty practice, arbitral jurisprudence, and general public international law on state responsibility, it traces the conceptual and doctrinal routes through which cyber risks may be characterized as security risks to an investment and brought within the ambit of FPS. The research provides an ordered understanding of cyber due diligence, built around three core dimensions namely regulatory preparedness, operational readiness and remedial responsiveness. Regulatory preparedness is the existence of reasonably up-to-date legal frameworks on cybersecurity and breach notification; operational readiness is the institutional capacity and technical and organizational measures in critical infrastructure; and remedial responsiveness is the incident handling, cooperation with affected investors, and transparency in the aftermath of an attack. These dimensions are tested against hypothetical but realistic scenarios, including ransomware attacks on industrial facilities and systemic data exfiltration from state licensed data centers, to explore how arbitral tribunals approach questions of causation, attribution, and contributory fault in cyber related FPS claims. Recognizing a digital variant of FPS need not transform host states into insurers against all cyber harm. Properly framed as an obligation of conduct, cyber due diligence clarifies the standard of reasonableness in circumstances where regulatory indifference or institutional inaction can significantly magnify transboundary harm. The article concludes with drafting suggestions for next generation investment treaties that seek to integrate cyber due diligence into FPS and related clauses while preserving the regulatory autonomy required for evolving cybersecurity policy.

title: DETECTING POLICY-PREFERENCE CONTRADICTIONS IN PRIVACY POLICIES
abstract: Privacy policies are intended to inform users about how their data is collected and used, yet they remain lengthy, complex, and rarely read. While automated policy analysis tools have improved the extraction of data practices, they do not systematically detect contradictions between policy statements and individual user privacy expectations. Existing approaches either rely on manual analysis or prompt-based large language models (LLMs), which suffer from inconsistency, high latency, and dependence on proprietary APIs. To address these limitations, we introduce a preference-conditioned framework for detecting policy-preference contradictions, formulated as a multi-label classification task. We construct a dataset of 2,384 annotated policy segments from 1,464 real-world privacy policies across eight user-defined preferences, combining real data with validated synthetic augmentation to mitigate class imbalance. Manual validation shows an agreement rate of 87.69%. We fine-tune a DeBERTa-v3-base model that achieves a macro F1 score of 0.8950 and exact match accuracy of 0.8167, outperforming both a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression baseline and a zero-shot instruction-tuned LLM. These results demonstrate that supervised, preference-conditioned learning provides more reliable and consistent detection of policy–preference conflicts than both lexical methods and prompt-based inference. The resulting model is fast, reproducible, and locally deployable, making it suitable for real-time privacy analysis. Overall, this work introduces a new benchmark and establishes a practical framework for preference-aware privacy policy understanding

title: DIGITAL HEALTH, DATA SOVEREIGNTY AND THE SDGS: A FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE PRACTICES WITH MOBILE HEALTHCARE APPLICATIONS
first_author: Mr. Mayur Kanhaiyalal Solanki & Dr.(Mrs.)Varsha Ganatra
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In an era where mobile technology permeates every aspect of people’s lives, the question of who controls health data has become both urgent and essential. As of 2024, more than 100,000 health-related mobile apps are available in major app stores, and these applications generate large volumes of personal health data every day. In addition, cybersecurity threats have surged and the number of individuals impacted by healthcare data breaches nearly tripled from 14 million to 45 million between 2018 and 2021. Patients increasingly consider data privacy as a fundamental right and over ninety percent people believe that health app developers should be transparent, offer meaningful consent processes, and allow them to opt out of data usage or sharing. These trends expose a growing gap between the promise of mobile health and the realities of ethical and sustainable practice. Recognizing this, global health leaders and national regulators are emphasizing the need for stronger governance. In 2024, the G20 health ministers affirmed that trusted, secure, interoperable digital health systems supported by regulatory frameworks that respect national context are essential for equitable healthcare and resilience. At the UN World Data Forum, participants called for a global health data governance framework rooted in rights-based, equitable principles, in order to unlock the public value of health data while protecting individuals’ rights. Meanwhile, India’s Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission has significantly advanced sovereign digital health infrastructure and by early 2025, more than 739 million health IDs had been issued, linking approximately 490 million health records. The mission includes a Health Data Management Policy that embeds “privacy and security by design,” consent frameworks, user control rights, and interoperability as core elements. Nonetheless, draft legislation such as DISHA remains pending, highlighting persistent challenges in implementing robust health data protection in practice. Beyond policy, emerging technological models like the Decentralized Health Intelligence Network (DHIN) offer promising alternatives. DHIN combines federated learning, personal health records, and blockchain incentives to ensure individuals retain control over their health data, benefit financially from participation, and safeguard AI development with decentralized safeguards. Drawing on these dynamics, this paper proposes a comprehensive framework that aligns mobile health application design and deployment with three pillars: data sovereignty, ethical governance, and SDG-driven impact. It emphasizes clear role definitions (like data owner, data steward), codified consent and ownership rights, federated system architectures, and interoperability standards tailored to local contexts. It also explores how platforms can integrate mHealth apps into broader digital public infrastructure while preserving individual autonomy and privacy. This study grounds its analysis in real-world data, lived experience, and ethical principles. It demonstrates that privacy and sovereignty are not obstacles to innovation. On the contrary, they serve as foundational enablers that support and guide responsible technological advancement.Properly governed mobile healthcare applications can advance SDG 3 (health), SDG 5 (gender equality), SDG 9 (innovation and infrastructure), and SDG 16 (peace, justice and strong institutions). In summary, when built around user control and accountability, mobile health systems can deliver more trustworthy, sustainable, and inclusive health services empowering individuals while building healthier societies. This research explores how mobile healthcare applications can support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, not only by improving health outcomes under SDG 3 but also by reinforcing data sovereignty as a pillar of trust, equity, and sustainability.

title: DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN DIABETES MANAGEMENT: THE ROLE OF CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN ENDOCRINOLOGY
venue: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science
abstract: The ongoing development of digital technologies, when used appropriately in diabetes care, has a significant impact on the management of patients with diabetes. New technologies enable the monitoring and adjustment of treatment in patients without the need for face-to-face appointments. The aim of this review is to discuss the role of continuous glucose monitoring, artificial intelligence, wearables, mobile applications and telemedicine in the development of diabetes care. Their clinical, organisational and social significance has been analysed. This is a review article based on publications from major biomedical databases.Reviewed articles provide evidence that continuous glucose monitoring is more accurate for assessing blood glucose levels than traditional glucose or HbA1c measurements. Artificial intelligence can be used to predict fluctuations in blood glucose levels and improve the personalization of clinical decisions. It has been shown to be particularly effective when combined with automated insulin delivery systems. Mobile devices and apps, as well as telemedicine, can increase patients’ interest in their own health and, consequently, their involvement in the treatment process; however, their value depends on the quality of the collected data, interoperability, clinical usability, and the ability of healthcare professionals to understand the generated reports. The use of digital tools is associated with cyber threats regarding data privacy, as well as inequalities in access to healthcare and trust in technology among patients. Future research should cover long-term effectiveness, safety, equitable access, and the methods of implementing this technology into everyday patient care.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN PHYSICAL EDUCATION, EXERCISE SCIENCE, AND WELLNESS PROMOTION: EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES, RESEARCH, AND PRACTICE
abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping how movement, fitness, and health behaviour are taught, measured, and supported across schools, sport, clinical rehabilitation, and everyday life. This chapter synthesizes recent, peer-reviewed evidence on emerging technologies in physical education, exercise science, and wellness promotion, including wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics, virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), mobile applications and gamification, and telehealth or mobile-health (mHealth) platforms. Drawing on systematic reviews and empirical studies published between 2021 and 2026, the chapter outlines how these tools support personalized instruction, real-time biomechanical feedback, remote and hybrid exercise delivery, and behaviour-change interventions, and it discusses an illustrative applied case in which multimodal AI monitoring — combining wearable inertial sensors, electromyography, heart-rate variability, and computer-vision pose estimation — was used to compare yoga, traditional exercise, and an integrated yoga-plus-technology training condition among collegiate athletes. The chapter also documents persistent barriers such as the digital divide, inadequate practitioner training, data-privacy risk, and uneven evidence quality. Two summary tables and an illustrative figure are provided to compare technology domains, benefits, and implementation challenges. The chapter concludes that digital tools offer meaningful, evidence-supported potential to modernise physical education, exercise science, and wellness practice, but that this potential is conditional on equitable infrastructure, sound pedagogy, professional development, rigorous independent replication, and clear ethical governance of data.

title: DP-DL-ZT: a zero-trust-enhanced differential privacy framework with CNN-LSTM for cyber threat detection in IoT healthcare
Dancing Figures
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Dancing Figures is a group of STEAM learning activities that links trigonometric functions with music and dance. Students select or compose periodic functions, tune parameters (amplitude and frequency) in GeoGebra, and drive a MaLT2 “dancing” figure so its motion synchronizes with a chosen song.The prototype evolved across three versions: from simple sine/cosine control of movement, to trigonometric polynomials that better capture melody and energy, and finally to an embodied duet where one figure follows the function while a second figure is controlled live by the student’s hand via MaLT-Dance.The activity targets upper-secondary learners (11th–12th grade) and foregrounds concepts such as periodicity, rate of change, and coordination between analytic and embodied representations of change.Students work iteratively: they listen to a given song, choose a function in GeoGebra, port coefficients values into MaLT2 to animate a figure, and adjust until the movement aligns with musical criteria (rhythm, melody, intensity, etc.); in the embodied version (v3), one figure is function-driven, while the second one responds to horizontal hand motion.The technologies used are GeoGebra, MaLT2, and (optionally) MaLT2Dance, with example materials provided alongside the prototype. By pressing this link https://youtu.be/Jv3wlTECnRE, you accept that your browser will send information to YouTube to view the video. YouTube privacy policy Additional Information for Researchers Dancing Figures explores how students coordinate periodic functions with music/dance to create aesthetically-guided meaning for the mathematical concepts of periodic functions and covariation. Versions progress from simple trigonometric functions (sin/cos) to trigonometric polynomials (to capture melody/energy, not just tempo) and finally to embodied interaction with MaLT2Dance, where one figure follows a function and a second figure is controlled by the student’s hand.Theoretical lenses used for its design: Constructionist design with open, creative artefact-making (Papert & Harel, 1991) Embodied interaction/learning via MaLT2Dance (function ↔ movement coupling) (Co)variational reasoning around periodic change (Thompson & Carlson, 2017) Examples of potential research questions: How does embodied control change strategies for coordinating amplitude/frequency/phase? Do trigonometric polynomials promote talk about rate of change and melody shape more than single sinusoids? What kind of covariational reasoning do students develop while planning and performing a ‘hybrid’ mathematical-body choreography? title: Das Redes Vestíveis aos Sistemas Ciber-Humanos: Uma Perspectiva na Comunicação e Privacidade dos Dados
abstract: The Short Courses Book of 39th Brazilian Symposium on Computer Networks and Distributed Systems (SBRC 2021) contains the short courses selected for presentation in the online edition of the event, from August 16 to 20, 2021, in the city of Uberlândia/MG. The main objective of the SBRC Short Courses is to offer short-term training and updating on topics not typically covered in curricular structures and which are of great interest among academics and professionals. The Book has traditionally been used as high-quality study material by undergraduate and graduate students and professionals in the field. The Short Courses covers current topics of interest to the community, such as emerging software systems; mobility, security in information-centric networks; virtualization of network functions in the Internet of Things (IoT); wearable networks, and cyber-human systems; and federated learning applied to IoT. In the first chapter, entitled “Emergent Software Systems: Theory and Practice,” the authors present the concept of Emerging Software Systems. The Emerging Software approach aims to reduce the initial effort to create standalone solutions; it supports fully adaptable systems capable of autonomously learning about the system structure and its operating environment without any pre-defined knowledge. In the second chapter, “Revisitando as ICNs: Mobilidade, Segurança e Aplicações Distribuídas através das Redes de Dados Nomeados”, the authors present an introduction and review of the fundamentals of Information-Centric Networks (ICN) and then the Named Data Networking (NDN) architecture. The authors present the main issues related to mobility, security, and distributed applications through demonstrations and practical activities with previously configured environments. The third chapter, “Virtualização de Funções de Rede na IoT: Um Panorama do Gerenciamento de Desempenho x Segurança”, deals with the use of Network Function Virtualization (NFV) in IoT from the point of view of network management, performance, and security. The text presents issues and state-of-the-art related to the performance of NFV in the detection and mitigation of threats in specific IoT networks. The fourth chapter, “Das Redes Vestíveis aos Sistemas Ciber-Humanos: Uma Perspectiva na Comunicação e Privacidade dos Dados”, addresses the rapid evolution that has been taking place from the beginnings of wearable networks to cutting-edge research in nanonetworks. This rapid evolution underlies the construction of cyber-physical and cyber-human systems that have applications in several areas. The authors describe the need to explore the vulnerabilities and challenges that these networks have concerning data privacy and the resilience of their services and present a discussion, demonstrating these weaknesses through practical examples and a survey of the state of the art of academic proposals for privacy protection and resiliency of your services. In the fifth and final chapter, “Aprendizado Federado aplicado à Internet das Coisas”, the authors present the main foundations of Federated Learning (FL), covering the tools and steps necessary for the development of IoT applications and services. The concepts covered include an introduction to Machine Learning (centralized and distributed), the state-of-the-art in FL, an overview of current work, challenges, and future perspectives for advancing the field. The five chapters broadly address current community issues, making them practical work for researchers and professionals in computer networks and distributed systems.

title: Data Breaches and Trends in Internet of Health Things
abstract: Internet of Health Things (IoHT) is disrupting the healthcare delivery mechanism by closing the gap in healthcare delivery through interoperable wearable health trackers, remote monitoring systems, and smart medical devices. These innovations offer considerable benefits in patient care and operational efficiency. At the same time, however, these innovations are also creating critical vulnerabilities for data security. The following chapter goes in-depth into multidimensional IoHT risks-from device-level weaknesses up to network vulnerabilities and risks of data transmission and storage. It identifies various types of data breaches, including unauthorized accesses, ransomware, and man-in-the-middle attacks, and indicates how they might affect patient privacy, financial stability, and regulatory compliance. Some emergent technologies used in firming IoHT security include blockchain, AI-powered threat detection, and encryption techniques. Apart from this, regulatory frameworks also evolve with emerging threats: for example, HIPAA and GDPR. While the future of IoHT looks very bright, this path to strong data privacy and security requires cooperation among healthcare organizations, developers of technology, and regulators. The chapter has accentuated the point that proactive strategy formulation in security is a dire need in order to instill confidence in the systems of IoHT and assure their benefits without compromising patient safety and data privacy.

title: Data Integrity and Digital Health Systems as Drivers of Women’s Socio-Economic-Political Empowerment
venue: International Journal of Leading Research Publication.
abstract: The intersection of women's health and their socio-economic and political empowerment is a multifaceted domain where physiological well-being acts as a prerequisite for societal participation. Access to accurate health information and reliable healthcare infrastructure is fundamental to this empowerment, yet the data underpinning women's health is frequently characterized by measurement errors, sparsity, and privacy risks. This paper examines the role of health data integrity and emerging digital technologies in facilitating or hindering women's agency. We argue that while digital tools and longitudinal studies offer pathways to empowerment through better health management, they are currently compromised by algorithmic hallucinations, privacy vulnerabilities, and methodological biases. By synthesizing recent advancements in statistical calibration, FemTech privacy analysis, and Large Language Model (LLM) benchmarking, we propose a comprehensive framework for validating the information ecosystems that women rely upon. We conclude that socio-economic-political empowerment cannot be fully realized without first resolving the "validity crisis" in women's health data and digital interfaces.

title: Data Privacy and Security Challenges in Smart Health Wearable Devices
Data Privacy and Social Media in the United States: Federal Limits, State Innovation, and the Challenges of Technological Change
venue: The American Journal of Comparative Law
abstract: The United States is a notable outlier in the global landscape of data privacy law.1 While a majority of countries have adopted comprehensive privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) adopted by the European Union,2 the United States has struggled to establish a similar omnibus framework. Instead, U.S. data privacy law consists of a patchwork of sector-specific federal statutes, state laws, and agency regulation.3 The fragmented nature of the U.S. privacy regime can be attributed partly to the conception of personal data as a commodity in the U.S. data market. Viewed from this perspective, Americans are “consumers” who willingly trade away some of their privacy for access to free or low-cost online services.4 Lawmakers have traditionally favored minimal intervention in this exchange, perceiving regulation as a restraint on trade and an impediment to innovation that would ultimately benefit the consumer.5 Thus, U.S. data privacy regulation has evolved in an inconsistent, incremental, and reactive manner—triggered largely by specific instances of data misuse, rather than as a result of a cohesive, comprehensive, and forward-looking strategy.6 In recent years, mounting concerns over privacy violations have led U.S. lawmakers to reassess how best to balance technological innovation against risks to consumers. Social media platforms lie at the center of this legislative debate.7 Their manipulative design practices, algorithmic content moderation and amplification, extensive collection of personal data, reliance on targeted advertising, and outsized influence on millions of Americans have made social media platforms a particular focal point for legislators in the area of data privacy.8 At the same time, new privacy laws targeting social media have been met with legal challenges, highlighting the unique structural, statutory, and constitutional obstacles that complicate U.S. regulation in this area. This Report represents the national report for the United States on this topic, prepared in conjunction with the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law in 2026. The Report, which covers a number of the topics and subtopics received in the form of the general rapporteur’s questionnaire, surveys the law governing data privacy and social media in the United States, traces the framework’s development, and examines the countervailing forces that continue to shape and constrain regulatory reform in the face of continued and often rapid technological advances. The U.S. Constitution does not mention privacy. The Framers of the Constitution did not conceive of “privacy” as a standalone constitutional right in the way that modern law understands it, and the concept of privacy as a legal category did not exist in the late eighteenth century when the Constitution was established.9 The Constitution nevertheless contains provisions that safeguard privacy-like interests.10 The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Amendments set forth the rights of individuals to be free from unwarranted government intrusions into their home, person, property, and to some extent, information.11 The Fourth Amendment’s guarantee of the right of the people “to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures” is the constitutional right that provides the closest analogue to modern conceptions of information privacy rights.12 The Fourth Amendment was initially construed narrowly to restrict only physical searches and seizures of a person’s property by the government.13 This understanding began to shift significantly during the Warren Court era. In 1965, the Supreme Court recognized a “zone of privacy” in the area of marital relations based on the “penumbras” of several enumerated constitutional rights.14 Two years later, in Katz v. United States, the Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment protects a criminal defendant’s telephone conversations from unwarranted electronic interception, explaining that the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places, and that its guarantees do not turn on physical intrusion.15 Instead, the Court said, the Fourth Amendment protects that which a person “seeks to preserve as private.”16 Justice Harlan’s concurrence in Katz introduced the “reasonable expectation of privacy” test, which has allowed the scope of Fourth Amendment protections to evolve with technological and social change, along with society’s changing understandings of privacy.17 To take one notable example: drawing on the Katz framework more than five decades later, the Court in Carpenter v. United States18 held that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the “whole of their physical movements,” and therefore that historical cell-site location information is protected by the Fourth Amendment.19 But despite its shift to a more flexible and evolving approach to the Fourth Amendment, the Supreme Court has not extended Fourth Amendment protections to privacy violations by private actors or to informational privacy more broadly. In Katz, the Court emphasized that the Fourth Amendment “cannot be translated into a general constitutional ‘right to privacy’” and made clear that protection against private intrusions is a matter for legislation, not constitutional adjudication.20 More recently, in NASA v. Nelson,21 the Court declined to decide whether the Constitution provides a standalone right to “informational privacy,”22 describing the issue as unresolved. In his concurrence in Nelson, Justice Scalia underscored this point, arguing that no such constitutional right exists at all.23 The Court’s evolving view in the 1960s of privacy as a distinct legal interest—reflected in decisions like Katz and Griswold— emerged against an intellectual backdrop shaped in part by the earlier work of Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis.24 In their seminal 1890 Harvard Law Review article, The Right to Privacy, Warren and Brandeis warned that new technologies such as instantaneous photography and the expansion of the press posed unprecedented threats to personal privacy.25 Surveying existing common-law principles, they identified an implicit right to privacy that they believed should give rise to a cognizable cause of action.26 They famously characterized this interest as a “right to be let alone,” a formulation that soon entered constitutional discourse—most famously in Justice Brandeis’s dissent in Olmstead v. United States27— as a foundational principle of personal liberty and a precursor to later judicial recognition of privacy rights. This conception has profoundly influenced the modern American understanding of privacy across constitutional, statutory, and tort law.28 In 1960, William Prosser built on the Warren and Brandeis conception of privacy to identify four distinct privacy torts: (1) intrusion upon seclusion; (2) public disclosure of private facts; (3) false light; and (4) appropriation.29 These categories, later adopted in the Restatement (Second) of Torts,30 continue to provide the core common-law ­remedies for a wide range of privacy-related injuries, including surveillance, eavesdropping, disclosure of private or false information, and the unauthorized commercial use of an individual’s identity.31 These early common law privacy torts are also instructive insofar as they supply litigants with a potential basis for standing to sue for damages for intangible privacy harms in federal court. Article III of the Constitution limits federal judicial power to “cases” and “controversies,” where the plaintiff has an actual “stake” in the matter, i.e., standing to sue.32 To have standing, a plaintiff must have suffered a “concrete” and “particularized” injury that is traceable to the defendant and that can be remedied by the court.33 In Transunion v.
