title: EXPLAINABLE MACHINE LEARNING FOR SAFETY-CRITICAL IOT (E.G., HEALTHCARE WEARABLES)
abstract: Machine learning (ML) increasingly controls or informs decision-making in safety-critical Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications such as healthcare wearables (arrhythmia detection, fall detection, glucose monitoring). For safe real-world deployment we must not only build accurate models but also make them explainable, robust, auditable, and certifiable within constrained, real-time embedded environments. This paper surveys explainable ML (XAI) methods that are relevant to resource-constrained wearables, organizes them into an engineering taxonomy, analyzes threats (adversarial inputs, sensor faults, distribution shift), and proposes a layered architecture that combines (1) model selection with intrinsic interpretability, (2) post-hoc local and global explanation modules adapted to time-series sensor data, (3) on-device runtime monitors & fallbacks, and (4) privacy-preserving training (federated learning + secure aggregation + DP). We evaluate tradeoffs between fidelity, latency, and energy, propose evaluation metrics suitable for safety contexts, and discuss regulatory and clinical adoption pathways. Concrete recommendations and an annotated roadmap for future work are provided.

title: EXPLORING THE BENEFITS AND CHALLENGES OF SMART COMMUNITY ELDERLY CARE SERVICES
abstract: This literature review explores the potential benefits and implementation challenges of smart elderly care technologies. Findings show innovations like remote monitoring, wearables, and integrated care platforms can enhance safety, independence, and quality of life for seniors. However, barriers like unclear ROI, privacy risks, and user adoption issues exist. For successful adoption, it is critical to assess tradeoffs, optimize for elderly users, lead culture change sensitively, and take a gradual approach. Harnessing technology thoughtfully while addressing human complexities is key to unlocking the value of smart elderly care. Keywords: Elderly Care, Smart Technology, Remote Monitoring, Sensors, Wearables, Telehealth, Social Isolation

title: Early Detection of Adverse Cardiac Events Using Intelligent Wearable Sensing and Edge-based Deep Learning Models
venue: International Conference on Decision Aid Sciences and Applications (DASA)
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of mortality globally. Continuous, non-invasive monitoring presents a critical opportunity for the early detection of Adverse Cardiac Events (ACEs). This paper proposes a hierarchical edge-cloud architecture that leverages the ubiquity of wearable sensors, the analytical power of Deep Learning (DL), and the efficiency of Edge Computing for a proactive cardiac alert system. We design a two-tier framework: (1) A lightweight, 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) optimized via TinyML principles is deployed on an edge device (e.g., a smartphone) for real-time analysis of Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals and initial anomaly detection. (2) Upon detection of a high-risk pattern, relevant ECG segments are offloaded to a cloud-based server where a more complex Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) or Transformer-based model performs deep contextual analysis to confirm the threat and assess the risk level. This hybrid approach optimizes battery life, reduces response latency, and enhances patient privacy by minimizing raw data transmission. Experimental validation on the public MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database demonstrates high classification accuracy for critical arrhythmias and showcases the system’s potential to revolutionize proactive cardiac telemedicine.

title: Early Stroke and Panic Detection using AI in Neurology
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Neurological emergencies span a wide spectrum, from sudden vascular events such as ischemic stroke to acute psychiatric-neurological crises such as panic attacks. Both categories are time-sensitive and both currently rely heavily on manual clinical assessment, which limits the speed and consistency of detection. This paper presents a detailed review of six recent peer-reviewed sources (2024–2025) on artificial intelligence (AI) in neurology, and uses their combined findings to build a case for, and a design of, an integrated two-module early-detection framework: an imaging-based deep-learning pipeline for stroke triage, and a wearable-sensor-based sequence-modelling pipeline for panic/anxiety detection. The review covers foundational AI concepts (machine learning, deep learning, neural network architectures), the current clinical evidence base for stroke-imaging AI, the comparatively nascent evidence for physiological/behavioural AI in affective and psychiatric-neurological states, and the shared ethical, technical, and regulatory challenges — interpretability, bias, data privacy, and validation — that recur across every source reviewed. The paper then details a proposed system architecture, dataset and preprocessing requirements, candidate model architectures, an evaluation plan with specific metrics, expected outcomes, and a discussion of limitations and future work. The overall conclusion is that stroke-detection AI is a mature and clinically validated field that can serve as a design template for a still-emerging class of wearable, sensor-driven AI tools for detecting acute panic and anxiety states.

title: Edge Computing Enabled Hardware Architecture for Intelligent Cardiac Risk Detection
venue: International Journal Of Recent Trends In Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases require continuous and real-time monitoring to enable early detection and timely medical intervention. Traditional cardiac monitoring systems depend heavily on cloud-based processing, which introduces latency, increases privacy risks, and limits immediate emergency response. In addition, existing wearable and hospital-based solutions often lack accurate continuous monitoring and real-time intelligent decision-making. To address these challenges, this project proposes an edge computing enabled hardware architecture for intelligent cardiac risk detection. The system integrates wearable biomedical sensors such as ECG, heart rate, and SpO₂ with an embedded edge processing unit capable of local signal analysis and machine learning–based risk prediction. title: Edge Intelligence in Wearable Healthcare IoT: A Systematic Review
venue: International Journal of Engineering Development and Research
abstract: The rapid proliferation of wearable healthcare devices and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies is fundamentally reshaping modern healthcare toward continuous, real-time patient monitoring. Traditional cloud-centric architectures, however, introduce significant challenges including communication latency, bandwidth saturation, and patient data privacy risks. These limitations have catalysed the emergence of edge intelligence — a paradigm where artificial intelligence and data processing are performed proximate to the wearable device rather than in a remote cloud infrastructure. This systematic review synthesises research published between 2019 and 2026 on edge-enabled wearable healthcare IoT systems. The paper presents a comprehensive taxonomy of system architectures, sensing technologies, AI/ML techniques, and communication models employed in wearable health monitoring. A comparative analysis of 70+ peer-reviewed studies highlights the advantages of edge intelligence in latency reduction, privacy preservation, and energy efficiency. Survey trends, open research gaps, and unresolved challenges are critically examined, culminating in a structured future research roadmap for intelligent, patient-centric healthcare ecosystems.

title: Edge-oriented predictive modeling of elderly health conditions via compact temporal encoding
abstract: In elderly care systems, wearable devices and ambient sensors can continuously produce large amounts of health-related data. In practical elder care environments, health prediction is often affected by missing sensor readings, unstable transmission, and the limited computing capability of edge devices. Directly uploading raw physiological streams to the cloud is not always suitable, since it may introduce privacy risks and response delay. Motivated by this issue, this study develops a compact temporal encoding method for edge-side health prediction. Instead of matching raw physiological records, recent multivariate observations are converted into binary temporal descriptors. Similar historical states are then retrieved locally and used for missing-value recovery and short-term trend estimation. In this way, the proposed method can reduce communication cost and edge-side processing burden. Experiments on the PhysioNet BIDMC dataset show that EdgeHealthHash keeps prediction errors close to those of stronger temporal baselines, while requiring less runtime and communication than raw-vector matching and GRU-based prediction. These results indicate that the proposed framework is more suitable for lightweight edge-side monitoring than for replacing full clinical prediction models, especially when data transmission and response delay are major concerns.

title: Edge-to-Cloud Continual Learning for Privacy-Preserving Chronic Disease Management
abstract: Chronic disease management requires continuous monitoring and adaptive treatment strategies, yet traditional healthcare systems suffer from fragmented data collection and reactive interventions. This study presents an edge-to-cloud continual learning architecture that integrates wearable biosensor networks, longitudinal patient data, and privacy-preserving machine learning to enable personalized treatment recommendations. The system employs a three-tier computational model: edge devices perform low-latency real-time signal processing (135 ms), cloud servers provide secure storage and federated model aggregation, and continual learning algorithms adapt treatment plans as patient conditions evolve. The architecture implements iCaRL-based incremental learning with K=500 exemplar replay, combined with differential privacy (ε=2.1) and Paillier homomorphic encryption to protect patient confidentiality during model updates. A prospective clinical validation study enrolled N=132 patients (diabetes n=77, cardiac n=30, respiratory n=25) across three urban clinics over 12 weeks. The edge-to-cloud system achieved 92.6% treatment recommendation accuracy (95% CI: 90.1-95.1%), representing a 6% improvement over cloud-only baseline (86.8%) and 17.6% improvement over static models (75.0%). The hybrid architecture reduced end-to-end latency by 65.3% compared to cloud-only processing (255 ms vs. 735 ms), meeting the <2-second requirement for acute clinical alerts. Privacy evaluation demonstrated membership inference attack AUC of 0.50 (indicating formal privacy safety, threshold ≤0.55) while maintaining clinical accuracy. Backward transfer analysis showed 98.1% retention of prior knowledge after 100 learning rounds, with only 0.2% degradation, demonstrating effective mitigation of catastrophic forgetting. These results establish the feasibility of privacy-preserving, adaptive chronic disease management systems that combine edge intelligence with cloud-based population learning while maintaining patient confidentiality and clinical effectiveness.

title: Editorial
venue: JUCS - Journal of Universal Computer Science
abstract:
Dear Readers, 
 It is a great pleasure to announce the eighth J.UCS issue of 2026. As always, I would like to thank all the authors for their sound research and the editorial board and guest reviewers for the extremely valuable reviews and suggestions for improvement. These contributions together with the support of the community and the generous support of the KOALA initiative enable us to run our journal and maintain its quality. 
 I continuously like to expand our editorial board to cover all aspects and trends in computer science. If you are a tenured associate professor or above with a good publication record, please apply to join our editorial board. We are also interested in high-quality proposals for special issues on new topics and emerging trends.
 In this regular issue, I am very pleased to present 6 accepted papers by 26 authors from 8 countries: China, Indonesia, Irak, Iran, Spain, Türkiye, United Kingdom, USA. 
 In a collaboration with researchers from Spain and the UK, Guadalupe Ortiz, Javier Tena, Adrian Garcia-Bermejo, Alfonso Garcia-de-Prado, and Stephan Reiff-Marganiec address the lack of Complex Event Processing (CEP) solutions for resource-constrained microcontrollers (MCUs) by introducing MicroCEP, an open architecture with a lightweight CEP engine, a pattern language, runtime reconfiguration, and a deployment methodology for edge devices. The proposed approach enables real-time event correlation and autonomous decision-making on MCUs, and experimental results demonstrate its feasibility, low resource consumption, and effective collaboration across multiple edge devices. 
 Juana María Morcillo Martínez, José Luis López Ruiz, David Díaz Jiménez, María Mercedes Párraga Vico, and Macarena Espinilla Estévez from Spain present a mixed-methods study that analyzes the acceptance of non-invasive wearable technologies for elderly care through focus groups and surveys with future social and healthcare professionals, evaluating a privacy-oriented system that excludes cameras and microphones. The findings demonstrate that acceptance depends on discretion, transparency, person-centred design, and human support, while economic cost and the digital divide emerge as the main barriers, emphasising the need for participatory and ethical design in ageing-in-place technologies. 
 In a collaboration between researchers from the USA and China, Jiangke Wu, Xiaojun Chen, and Rongxing Shi address in their research the resource inefficiency and potential data discrepancies caused by passive post-failure compensation in traditional microservice Saga transactions. In this light, the paper introduces the Proactive Saga Failure Avoidance (PSFA) framework, which embeds an LSTM-based health prediction model into the Saga orchestrator to evaluate real-time service metrics and detect failures prior to transaction execution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the PSFA framework identifies failure precursors with 1.00 precision and 0.99 recall, successfully establishing a practical proactive fault-tolerance approach that shifts distributed transaction management from reactive compensation to pre-fault avoidance.
 In another collaborative research from Iran and Iraq, Nabeel Abdolrazagh Yaseen Alrashedi, Rasool Sadeghi, Wael Hussein Zayer Al-Lamy, Mehdi Hamidkhani, and Reihaneh Khorsand look into the problem of energy-efficient cooperative data offloading in heterogeneous cellular networks and propose a deep Q-network-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that enables mobile users to learn adaptive offloading strategies across cellular, Wi-Fi, and device-to-device communications. The proposed method significantly reduces energy consumption while also improving delay, throughput, and fairness, achieving up to 40% energy savings over random offloading and 16.6% over greedy offloading in the reported experiments.
 Zulkifli Zulkifli, Fitriana Fitriana, and Panji Bintoro from Indonesia present their study on a web-based system for predicting heart failure patient survival by integrating five machine learning algorithm Naive Bayes, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbor, Support Vector Machine, and Neural Network using clinical patient variables. The proposed system achieved its best reported performance with Naive Bayes and provides a practical multi-algorithm platform to support healthcare professionals in heart failure monitoring and survival prediction.
 And last but not least, Ela Kalifati, Kerem Küçük, Şevval Şolpan, Kazım Kıvanç Eren, and Mehmet Zeki Konyar from Türkiye propose in their article a device-level SMOTE-based class balancing approach. It compares KNN, SVM, Logistic Regression, and MLP on seven IoT devices from the ToN_IoT dataset, in order to address the class imbalance that causes machine learning models to overlook rare intrusion classes in IoT attack detection. Results show that SMOTE markedly improves minority-class recall and F1-score on severely imbalanced devices, with only marginal effects where the data are already balanced, demonstrating that selective oversampling with classical classifiers is an efficient path to robust multi-class IoT intrusion detection. 
 Enjoy Reading! 
 Cordially, 
 Christian Gütl, Editor-in-Chief

title: Editorial
abstract: In this first issue of Volume 33, we delve into the rich tapestry of linguistic diversity and academic discourse, showcasing a range of studies that shed light on various facets of language use, maintenance, and communication. The collection of articles in this issue offers valuable insights into the ever-evolving world of language. The first article in our lineup, Language Shift and Maintenance: A Case Study of the Telugu Community in Bagan Datoh, Perak (Malaysia), takes us to Bagan Datoh, Perak, where the Telugu language, despite being a minority language in Malaysia, continues to thrive in specific domains. This case study illuminates the dynamics of language choice among different generations and provides hope for the revitalization of Telugu among the younger generation. The second article, Metadiscourse Markers in Abstracts of Linguistics and Literature Research Articles from Scopus-Indexed Journals, shifts our focus to the world of academic writing, specifically the use of metadiscourse markers in abstracts. It highlights the crucial role these markers play in structuring and presenting research arguments. The comparative analysis between linguistics and literature abstracts provides valuable insights into disciplinary differences in the use of these markers. Our third article, An Exploratory Analysis of Linking Adverbials Used by Filipino, Pakistani, and Thai Writers of English, undertakes a contrastive interlanguage analysis, shedding light on how students from the Philippines, Pakistan, and Thailand use linking adverbials in their English academic writing. The importance of understanding the distinct production tendencies of various English varieties is emphasised in this article. Turning to a sensitive topic in the Malaysian context, the fourth article, Female Circumcision in Malaysia: Challenges and Lessons Learned in Using Focus Groups through an NGO-Academia Collaboration, explores female circumcision and the challenges faced in conducting research on this subject. It highlights the collaborative efforts between academia and a local NGO, offering valuable insights into data collection via focus group discussions. The fifth article, Prosodic Marking of New and Given Information in English and Mandarin by Chinese Speakers, ventures into the realm of prosody and its impact on language comprehension. Focusing on Chinese English as a Foreign Language learners, it investigates how Mandarin influences the prosodic marking of new and given information in English, shedding light on potential areas of misunderstanding. Our final article, Privacy Policy Pop-up: A Genre Analysis of Journal Websites’ HTTP Cookies, takes a dive into the world of online privacy and transparency. It analyses the communication of transparency through HTTP cookies on academic journal websites, uncovering the rhetorical strategies employed to inform users about data privacy. In this diverse collection of articles, we invite readers to explore the multifaceted world of language and academic discourse. Each study offers unique insights into the complexities of communication and the richness of linguistic diversity. We hope this issue serves as a valuable resource for scholars, researchers, and language enthusiasts alike, encouraging further exploration and understanding of these vital aspects of our academic and cultural landscape. title: Editorial: Talking fabrics – a new era in autonomous AI textile wearable (AITW) technology
venue: International Journal of Clothing Science and Technology
abstract: In a world where technology constantly transforms the boundaries of possibility, we find ourselves at the intersection of a quiet but powerful revolution: the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) with the fabrics that we wear as garments. This remarkable evolution in wearable technology is not simply a step forward but a giant leap into an era where our clothing becomes an extension of our own cognitive experience. In fact, it provides what AI needs to go from “chatting unaware of the user” to becoming more intelligent by understanding the user's physical and environmental conditions and hence providing “contextual understanding”, which is the next most important requirement in AI's quest to achieve large action models (LAM) for higher intelligence. The research presented here introduces this new frontier of “AI textiles (AIT).”The notion of intelligent textiles isn't new. Increasingly, fabrics are considered organic beings, capable of understanding and reacting to human conditions and environment (Stylios, 2020). What makes this work by Aliyana and Stylios exciting is its tangible manifestation of that vision. AI wearables (AITW) is a prime example of the realm of autonomous cognitive ability. An AIT is a system that listens, monitors and measures processes and converses with its wearer. Powered by self-harvested energy through triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) embedded in the textile, an AIT monitors biomechanical data (movement, temperature, breathing, heart rate, resistivity, touch, etc.), turns that data into contextual information so that the communication between the BOT and the user is moving to a higher level of AI than at present. By embedding AI in a fabric that responds to real-time data, AIT transcends the traditional role of wearables. It actively participates in all activities of its wearer, offering personalized feedback, from gait analysis through voice interaction and is responsive to the user's real-world needs. We can call these Autonomous Intelligent Agents (AIAs) or Autonomous Intelligent Copilots (AICs). They understand not just what the user says, but also the context, intent and situational background. They personalize responses and actions based on user history, preferences and real-time data. Make autonomous decisions and take proactive steps to help or alert the user and continuously learn and adapt, becoming more effective over time, rather than simply reacting to commands, as bots do at present. These autonomous agents will be the textile or the wearable garment itself, hence calling them AITAs or AITWAs, respectively.The evolution from passive question-answering AI like ChatGPT to advanced AAI represents a significant leap toward higher intelligence. This shift transforms AI from a reactive tool into an autonomous, proactive system capable of complex reasoning, decision-making and real-world action. Let us break down the reasons why and how this advancement occurs. This is a leap in intelligence because AIA surpasses models like ChatGPT in three critical dimensions: firstly, in autonomy and proactivity; unlike ChatGPT, which waits for user prompts, AIA independently initiates actions, sets goals and adapts strategies based on environmental data (e.g. user habits, sensor inputs, etc). An example might be an AIA monitoring a user's health metrics might proactively adjust room temperature or suggest rest without being asked. Secondly, in contextual depth and memory, ChatGPT resets context between interactions, while AIAs maintain long-term memory, retaining user preferences, historical data and environmental states to inform decisions. This enables nuanced personalization, such as refining recommendations based on past behaviour. Thirdly, in task execution and integration, AIAs integrate with external systems (APIs and IoT devices) to execute multi-step workflows like booking travel or controlling smart homes far beyond ChatGPT's text-based responses. They solve complex problems by analysing real-time data (e.g. optimizing logistics routes) (Constantino, 2025; Nahavandi et al., 2022).This advancement is achieved because AIA leverages four technical innovations to enable higher intelligence:Therefore, as we can see, AITs mark a paradigm shift by merging contextual awareness, autonomous decision-making and real-world action, transforming AI from a conversational partner into an intelligent collaborator. This is achieved through architectures that emulate human-like reasoning, continuous learning and seamless system integration, enabling agents to tackle dynamic, multifaceted challenges that passive models cannot. Table 1 shows a comparison between a chatbot like ChatGPT and AIT agents.Networked AITA/AITW agents' communication is where agents share contextual data from textile wearables about users during interactions, which could transform how humans connect by making conversations more informed, empathetic and efficient. This system would function like an advanced social layer over platforms (e.g. Facebook, X and Instagram), but with explicit user consent and real-time data exchange between AIAs, see Figure 1. Below, we analyse its potential to enhance interactions, its broader effects and key regulatory considerations.As we have discussed, textiles provide the ability of AIA to have continuous contextual enrichment and become AIA themselves as AITAs. AITAs could share non-sensitive, user-approved context (e.g. “Alex just returned from Japan” or “Sam prefers video calls over texts”) before or during conversations. This allows participants to tailor discussions to shared interests or recent events, fostering deeper engagement. Textiles worn by users can provide AI agents the ability of “proactive assistance”; agents might alert users to “potential sensitivities” (e.g. “avoid discussing travel: Maya's flight was cancelled today”) or suggest “conversation starters” based on mutual hobbies, reducing social friction and building rapport textiles will also provide “efficiency in networking”; for professional settings, agents could exchange role-specific backgrounds (e.g. “Taylor's expertise: IoT security”), enabling more focused and productive collaborations. In fact, these AI agents are the AITAs/AITGAs themselves.It is inevitable that there are incredibly positive effects with this new technical breakthrough but also negative effects, which will need mitigation. A welcome positive effect is the deeper personalization, in which conversations feel more relevant and empathetic, as agents provide real-time context about mood, preferences or milestones (South et al., 2025; IBM, 2024). But privacy could be eroded by oversharing without granular consent, exposing sensitive traits (e.g. health status) or enabling manipulation. Another welcome aspect is the build-up of stronger relationships, because shared context fosters trust and common ground, mimicking the intuition of close friendships, but at the same time, users may feel social pressure and might alter behaviour if aware they're being “analysed,” leading to inauthentic interactions, which may be a negative effect. The technology can have another positive effect in conflict reduction because agents could flag incompatible communication styles (e.g. “Jamal dislikes interruptions”) to prevent misunderstandings (South et al., 2025). However, this feature also risks amplifying bias if agents rely on incomplete data, reinforce stereotypes or inherit algorithmic biases that may influence user perceptions.As textile wearable garments can provide contextual-based data from the wearer to enable the AI agents to become more intelligent, personal and effective, as we have seen, several regulatory and ethical constraints must be put in place; for example, the wearer should have a “consent-first design” where the user must explicitly opt into data sharing per interaction, with options to limit context (e.g. “share my hobbies but not my location”). Regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act mandate this granular control. Then the question of “transparency”, in which agents should disclose when/why context is shared (e.g. “Based on your LinkedIn, I suggested your startup experience”) to maintain trust. And very importantly, the insurance of “human oversight”, in which high-stakes scenarios (e.g. conflict mediation) should require human review to override agent suggestions, aligns with GDPR's Article 2 “right to explanation” (European Union, 2016; UK Government, 2018). In consequence, AI agent/textile wearable networking could make human interactions more intuitive and meaningful by leveraging contextual data, turning superficial chats into enriched exchanges. However, this hinges on strict consent protocols, transparent data usage and bias mitigation to avoid privacy harms or social manipulation. While regulation (like the EU AI Act) is evolving to address these risks, the priority remains for user autonomy: ensuring agents enhance, not dictate, human connection (European Union, 2024).The future will involve textile wearables carrying AI-enabled devices with nano chips for local processing while leveraging larger cloud-based models, creating a hybrid architecture optimized for performance, privacy and efficiency. This approach aligns with the evolution of AIA (specifically edge AI agents), which combine autonomy, contextual awareness and distributed intelligence. In this case, AIGA became Edge AIGAs. These wearables are already autonomous in terms of energy and sensing by virtue of their yarns and fabric structures, and ideally, it will be their battery-free provision to be maintained so that their energy harvesting ability will be sufficient to make the AI nano chips for local processing work battery-free. Below is a breakdown of how this works:Let us discuss how this can work in a real end-use scenario.So, this is a real scenario which benefits from a textile enabling contextual understanding by sensing physiological and environmental data from the wearer and so lifting the intelligence of the agent to edge, which stays locally in the wearable textile system, facilitated by a nano chip in the textile and the cloud-based agent as seen in Table 2.There is an interesting and more sustainable AI industry in a future outlook based on the above considerations, such as 5 G/IoT Synergy, where there will be a faster edge-cloud synchronization for complex tasks (e.g. AR-assisted surgery) (MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Then, self-learning wearables (SLW) embedded with nano chips will locally retrain models using federated learning, reducing cloud dependence (Lyzr, 2024). This will make wearable textile garments truly autonomous edge agents on their own right, increasing the need for better implementation of ethical guardrails by easier-to-administer user-controlled consent layers (e.g. “Share heart data only for emergency alerts”) (MIT Computing, 2024; MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Therefore, carrying AI-enabled wearables with nano chips is essential for real-time responsiveness and privacy, while cloud-based models handle deeper intelligence. AI agents bridge these layers, creating a cohesive, efficient system where edge devices act as autonomous “first responders” and the cloud serves as a “strategic brain.” This architecture will dominate future tech and will change our lives forever. It is expected to replace Google, Facebook, Yahoo, X and Instagram. To achieve an advanced AIA capable of context awareness, personalization, decision-making and proactive assistance, the hardware and software must integrate edge-device efficiency with cloud-scale intelligence. Below is a summary of requirements based on current technological advancements:Edge textile wearables/IoT will need ultra-low-power processors, i.e., nano-chips like NeuroSense (consuming <100 µW) for real-time sensor data processing (e.g. motion), especially since their power (TENG) will have to be provided by the movement generated in the textile by the wearer (Aliyana et al., 2024). Sensing will be inherent to the textile-based wearable, and it will depend on the type of fibres the textile is made of. Finally, connectivity will be based on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), or 5G RedCap/NB-IoT will be employed to ensure minimal energy consumption during cloud communication (NeuroSense, 2024). In contrast, cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as NVIDIA H200 SXM, H100 SXM, TPUs and FPGAs, for training large AI models and executing complex inference tasks. In contrast, the cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as GPUs (NVIDIA H200 SXM and H1oo SXM, TPUs and FPGAs), for training large AI models and complex inference tasks. These chips consume hundreds of watts of power and require robust power delivery and thermal management systems. Scalable, high-throughput storage using NVMe SSDs will also be essential for rapid access to large datasets during training and retrieval. While edge devices focus on energy-efficient sensing and minimal computation, cloud systems are optimized for performance, throughput and large-scale model hosting, reinforcing the distributed nature of modern AI-powered wearables.Edge Software, which is based on the textile wearable agent, stays local within the nano chip-based system by means of tiny ML frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite or Edge Impulse, for deploying lightweight models on wearables (Latent AI, 2024). The need for a real-time OS, optimized for low-latency textile wearable sensing data processing and local decision-making. And importantly, federated learning enables on-device model updates without raw data leaving the device (Latent AI, 2024; Zilliz, 2024). Cloud software must perform AI orchestration so that platforms like SmythOS or Latent AI will be used to manage agent workflows, versioning and scaling (Milvus, 2024). MLOps tools will be used for continuous deployment, monitoring and updating of edge models (e.g. latent AI's telemetry) (Zilliz, 2024). And finally, facilitate APIs/services for cloud-based AI APIs (e.g., Azure Cognitive Services) for complex tasks like NLP. So, if we were to look at this hybrid architecture workflow, it would consist of the following layers:For this hybrid architecture workflow, we will need the following development requirements: hardware with ≥8 GB RAM, multi-core processors (Intel i5+/AMD Ryzen) and 20 GB + storage for testing wearable apps. And tools like SDKs for target platforms (Android/iOS), BLE debuggers and AI optimization suites. In essence, the future demands capable, durable and comfortable textile wearables; hardware that balances ultra-low-power edge processing with cloud-scale computation, coupled with software that enables seamless, privacy-preserving intelligence across this hybrid architecture (Nahavandi et al., 2022; Shajari et al., 2023; EEJournal, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024). And preferably everything is done without reliance on traditional batteries, drawing power directly from an array of TENG-integrated textiles. Based on this architecture workflow, a high-level sketch of system components and data flow is provided in Figure 2, with each key element described in the subsequent sections.Key components explained:Data flow sequence:This architecture balances low-latency edge processing with cloud-scale intelligence, enabling responsive, context-aware AI agents while maintaining data privacy and energy efficiency. The fabric is designed into a wearable vest and leggings, which, through a WebSocket, transmit the data to ChatGPT's LLM, where data are trained, and a meaningful conversation is then performed between the user and ChatGPT. Each footstep generated up to 0.35 μC of charge during high-intensity activity. With frequency responsiveness optimized between 2 and 8 Hz and signal stability maintained over 1,000 cycles, the architecture ensures robustness and repeatability. title: Editorial: Where does digital health leave people who use drugs?
abstract: Digital health is a term that has become increasingly important in public health, biomedicine and social studies of health and illness. WHO’s “Global Strategy on Digital Health” for 2020–2025 (WHO, 2021) and global experiences of the COVID-19 pandemic brought on the growing adoption of digitally-mediated interventions and the various forms of digital health tools aimed at improving health and transforming treatment modalities. Studies conducted during and after the COVID-19 pandemic noted that the pandemic exacerbated the health inequities for previously disadvantaged groups and identified serious limitations to the adaptation of digital tools for drug services, including the limited acceptance and technical resources (Perri et al., 2021; Sultan, 2021).The promise of tech-assisted and internet-based technologies is to alleviate barriers in reaching marginalized communities including people who use drugs, people who live with disabilities and chronic infectious diseases and those who reside in remote rural areas. Yet, definitions of digital health and what it is designed to achieve, in which circumstances and for whose benefit, vary greatly. Critical public health scholars note that many digital health services are designed to boost personal responsibility and self-care practices, thereby upholding neoliberal economy and promoting the idea of an “empowered health consumer” (Lupton, 2014) – narratives which do not adequately respond to the needs and circumstances of many frequent drug users. Whether digital health is an unambiguously useful development, and how it can reinforce certain forms of exclusion and inequities, is of particular importance to consider in drug policy, drug treatment, harm reduction and other drug services. Against this background, the increased uptake of digitalization in health raises important questions of access, inclusion and privacy.In response to growing calls to adopt digital health, numerous apps and other digital tools have been developed to assist traditional service options, and to offer immediate crisis interventions. In Scotland, for example, a centralized app developed as part of the Digital Lifelines Program has shown promise in lowering barriers to accessing vital overdose prevention and related harm reduction services, including by providing digital devices such as smartphones, tablets and laptops to people who are likely to experience problems from drug use (Strachan et al., 2024). In another study from Russia, in the absence of such a centralized app, doctors used the Telegram messaging app to refer patients who use drugs to relevant emergency care and other medical services (Davitadze et al., 2024). However, there are several critical questions about access to digital health. Digital divide in the form of digital literacy such as the ability to use WHO-initiated eHealth, mHealth and telemedicine, as well as access to internet, and other technological infrastructure have been widely debated (Lupton, 2014). Here evidence suggest that collaborative design and implementation that is centered around user perspective is key to establishing trust especially in governmental digital health programs (Marent et al., 2018). Yet, specific guidelines to address structural conditions for these barriers, power imbalances in service design and delivery, as well as integration of lived experience for more nuanced care remain a marginal discussion in the literature. Against this background, there is still a significant gap in how drug policies could respond to the digitalization of health services on a larger scale.Global agendas addressing health inequities poorly define marginalized and vulnerable groups, often covering their participation under broad terms such as “health inclusion” (Tweed et al., 2021). While this could include people who use drugs and live with chronic infectious diseases, are in older age, experience homelessness, violence, belong to sexual or ethnic minorities, these groups are not always specified. In addition, most interventions and studies focus on overdose prevention and mortality, while more nuanced services targeting specific groups or different drug use patterns, such as recreational drug use among youth, or drug education are still underdeveloped (Loverock et al., 2023). There is an urgent need for services that thoughtfully address this intersectionality.Accessible, inclusive and transferable development of digital health also requires addressing the question of stigma and discrimination in health services. Reproduction of stigmatization and structural inequities through digital services and large electronic databases owned by tech industries are some of the concerns raised by drug scholars and activists (Lenton et al., 2025). These must be taken into consideration when developing digital health services that have traditionally prevented people from accessing drug services in the first place. Moreover, rapid development and decentralization of digital drug markets intensified the need to develop digital harm reduction responses and online health promotion strategies for wider audiences (van der Sanden et al., 2023). Studies show that in the absence of reliable digital health platforms and fragmented resources, many users refer to open-source Internet for medical advice, peer knowledge exchange and digital assessment of symptoms. These strategies are also adopted by some recreational drug users especially through peer-to-peer platforms (Boothroyd and Lewis, 2016; Rhumorbarbe et al., 2019). However, recent discussions note the role of private tech companies that capitalize on this digital data economy, and emphasize the need to understand how to navigate information control and algorithmic moderation of vital health promotion content (Gomes and Sultan, 2024).Most studies reporting on the new digital health programs focus primarily on the outcomes of testing, usability and reach (Labrique et al., 2020). However, the growth of digital data economy also sparked concerns around data sharing, data protection and data bias. For example, pharmaceutical market studies showed that the acceleration of digital health brought on new dynamics between government-supported digitalization efforts and the privatization of health data by big pharmaceutical companies (Gross and Geiger, 2023). In Europe, consumer applications became easier to implement, especially in the face of EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, and other confidentiality and data management guidelines in trading with countries outside of the EU. Ireland and Germany, for example, have struggled to reconcile collaborations between tech industry and local governments to improve access to digital health (Gross and Geiger, 2023). Drawing parallels to drug policy here requires further investigations on data protection in the development of national digital programs designed to assist with drug use related health problems. Care is needed to accommodate the sensitivity required in both reaching users digitally as well as maintaining long-term engagement while ensuring balance between extreme surveillance and the reverse effect, data marginalization (Gilman and Green, 2018).Transdisciplinary engagement with digital health foregrounds advocacy and user-driven design that mobilizes affected communities and thereby shapes the political outcomes of global health agendas (Davis, 2025). A particular emphasis here is on participation and human rights which in this case aid to strengthen the argument for developing community-centered approach. International guidelines for the implementation of digital health under the umbrella terms of inclusion, democratization of health and health justice do not directly translate into practical execution. In calling for transdisciplinarity at Drugs, Habits and Social Policy, we place a stronger emphasis on offering an equal platform to insights from professional practice alongside research and policy outputs. By widening the scope of studies, the journal aims to increase the field’s engagement with interdisciplinary research and a range of stakeholders. As editors, our mission here is to support this engagement, and widen the borders of social, medical and policy studies of drug use to allow better integration of different forms of knowledge and expertise of broader range of stakeholders. The limited reach of digital health interventions and services to marginalized communities and population groups without health-care privileges remains an important gap in research and practice. Here the question of health inequities becomes pertinent as the societal transitions toward digitalized health care further stretches the gaps between different social strata.One of the questions that arise in this discourse, is how to leverage digital technologies to enhance the quality of life for people who use drugs and redefine how health care is provided for underserved groups. Linking debates between digital health interventions and digital drug services, the most pressing questions now are: how efficiently can the local services adapt to the global guidelines, who is left out in the rapid digitalization of health interventions, what do privacy and data protection guidelines mean for the implementation of emergency drug services, what kind of technological advancements are inevitable for the near future and what does it mean for drug and social policy reforms in the long term? Among other questions, research is needed to uncover how rapid datafication of health can affect already disadvantaged groups who may be further isolated due to data marginalization, not possess required credentials to access health services or refrain from sharing sensitive personal information due to stigmatization. Further research needs to investigate implications of global digital health frameworks and their implementation in non-Western countries, especially, in comparison to techno-scientific advancements in liberal democracies and address the questions of data colonialism that arise in this relationship.

title: Editorial: mHealth and smartphone apps in patient follow-up
abstract: Yu et al. conducted a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials focusing on the technological functionality and system architecture of mobile health interventions for diabetes management. 41 out of 3911 identified studies published prior to August 2024 were selected for the analysis which confirmed that mobile health applications are beneficial in managing diabetes.Qin et al. introduced an intelligent question-answering system designed to deliver personalized medical information to diabetic patients. The system demonstrated the effectiveness in integrating large language models with knowledge graphs to provide more accurate and contextually relevant medical guidance, addressing the limitations of traditional healthcare systems in handling complex medical queries.Li et al. conducted a systematic literature review that explored the impact of telemedicine in chronic patients from diverse socioeconomic contexts. A total of 35 out of 10755 identified studies published prior to November 2024 were selected for analysis. Four themes that can improve future telemedicine for patients with chronic diseases were synthesized: reminders and supervisors, access to knowledge, transition in medical treatment mode, and emotional support platform. Heidari et al. developed an mHealth solution to support a lifestyle modification intervention among pregnant Iranian women with hypertension based on self-determination theory. The developed solution was evaluated on 60 Iranian women (of which 30 were in the control group) in a study running from 2021-2023. The intervention demonstrated improvements in lifestyle factors and selfdetermination constructs. Kyriazakos et al. conducted a systematic literature review focusing on clinical outcomes of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and mHealth applications in the areas of remote patient monitoring (RPM) and digital therapeutics (DTx). 28 out of 629 identified studies published prior to April 2024 were selected. The review demonstrated the significant potential in revolutionizing chronic disease management through RPM and DTx exemplified by solutions like Healthentia.Rating Scale (MARS). The authors identified 40 online Indian pharmacy apps in Google Play Store and App Store of which 13 were chosen and evaluated using MARS. The MARS evaluation demonstrated significant positive associations across the four quality scales. The mean rating of the 13 apps fell between the range of 3.11 to 4.32 on a 5-point scale.Hosseinnia et al. conducted a systematic literature review focusing on applications for the management of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) that have been evaluated in various types of trials. A total of 14 out of 281 identified studies published prior to May 2024 were included. The applications targeted different facets of ADHD, including symptom monitoring, medication adherence, cognitive training, specific functioning, and behavior management. Sun et al. explored how doctors' social media behavior affects patient adherence and treatment outcome. The study showed that doctors posting professional knowledge content on social media positively impacted patient adherence and treatment effectiveness. In contrast, doctors sharing personal life-related content on social media were associated with lower patient adherence and poorer treatment outcome.The study by Qui and Zhou assessed the quality of heatstroke videos on TikTok. 90 out of the top 100 heatstroke-related videos were examined focusing on their characteristics, quality, and the content they conveyed. The study showed that the quality of information provided in heatstrokerelated videos on TikTok is generally inadequate and requires significant improvement. In addition, such content should be subject to government review to ensure its accuracy and reliability.Fei et al. analyzed the continuance intention of digital health resources. The study used crosssectional surveys and structural equation modeling analysis to explore factors influencing user willingness to continue using digital health resources. In summary, the keys to solving the problem of low continuance intention are improving the quality and service level of digital health resources and promoting users' value co-creation behavior.Meng and Guo examined the factors influencing users' intention to continue using mobile medical apps within the framework of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology model. Through a combination of questionnaire surveys and interviews, the study finds that doctor-patient trust, performance expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions significantly impact users' intention to utilize mobile medical apps.Zong et al. explored the relationship between information overload and overuse of medical services in mHealth applications using the health belief model. Data was collected from 1,494 respondents using a structured questionnaire. The study found that information overload significantly affected users' perceived severity, susceptibility, treatment benefits, barriers, selfefficacy, and action cues, and subsequently affected overuse of health care services.Liu at al. conducted a systematic literature review focusing on the efficacy of telemedicine intervention in self-management of patients with type 2 diabetes. 17 out of 4171 identified studies published prior to December 2023 were selected for the analysis. The review confirmed that telemedicine interventions may assist patients with type 2 diabetes in enhancing their selfmanagement and improving their blood glucose levels.Ortiz et al. performed a usability evaluation of the educational website "I understand my diabetes" ("Entiendo mi diabetes") for Mexican patients with type 2 diabetes attending primary care clinics. A cross-sectional study was done in 110 patients with type 2 diabetes from two family medicine clinics. The study found that the educational website had an adequate usability evaluation by patients, and they also considered it very useful for diabetes care.Han and Li studied the use of Online Follow-Up Services (OFUS) as a supplement to ordinary hospital care available through online health communities (OHC). A dataset including 3672 doctors in in a leading OHC in China was analyzed using the elaboration likelihood model. The results show that both doctors' knowledge contributions and patient feedback positively influence patients' effective use of OFUS.Babatunde et al. reported on the development and evaluation of an educational and monitoring mobile application for pregnant women in Nigeria. A method of user-centered design was employed involving pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Oyo State, Nigeria. The study demonstrated that mHealth applications have the potential to increase access to prenatal information and services in Nigeria and may reduce maternal and childhood mortality. Zhao et al. explored the potential of a computer vision-based method to perform sit-to-stand test for home-based self-assessment of physical condition in advanced knee osteoarthritis (KOA) patients. 104 KOA patients were enrolled in the study to evaluate their physical function and joint stiffness. The study demonstrated the potential for low-cost and user-friendly self-assessment of KOA patients with varying stiffness levels and functional limitations utilizing smartphones. Kasputytė et al. analyzed the association between the behavior of cancer patients, measured using passively and continuously generated data streams from smartphone sensors, and perceived fear of COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination status. 202 cancer patients were included in the study, which showed that the COVID-19 pandemic continues to have an impact on the behavior of cancer patients even after the termination of the global pandemic.While the included studies demonstrate important and relevant application areas of mobile health technology in patient follow-up, they also demonstrate some limitations that need to be addressed in future studies. Overall, it is important to focus on aspects that mature the technology and demonstrate its full potential and effects on patient care and various other important perspectives to facilitate future large-scale implementation and user adaptation. This includes but is not limited to:  Ensure proper user involvement strategies during development (i.e., using a codesign method) as well as rigorous usability testing and evaluation to enhance user acceptance and usability using appropriate scientific methods.  Demonstrate various effects and investigate different aspects of the developed technology, i.e., using a health technology assessment method that through a multidisciplinary process summarizes information about the medical, social, economic, ethical, and legal (i.e., GDPR and MDR in the European Union) issues in a systematic, transparent, unbiased, and robust manner to uncover strengths and limitations of the developed technology (i.e., [6]).We hope to see an increased focus to bring mobile health technology into real clinical practice to fully unlock its potential to improve future health outcomes and quality of life.

title: Een systematische review van bestaande positieve psychologische apps gericht op zelfcompassie en/of compassie
abstract: Background: Self-compassion consists out of three elements: mindfulness, common humanity and kindness. Having compassion for oneself is really no different than having compassion for others. Exercises focused on selfcompassion and/or compassion, are increasingly offered online as eMental health apps. However, there is no view on the quality of these apps, it is unclear whether the apps actually promote self-compassion and/or compassion. Objective: This study aimed to explore the availability and quality of current positive psychology apps providing self-compassion and/or compassion. Quality was assessed through scientific evidence, usability and persuasive technology. Methods: A systematic review framework was applied to the search and assessment of apps available in the Apple App store. Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, there are nine apps included in the evaluation. This evaluation is done based on a decision-tree for scientific evidence, the System Usability Scale and the Persuasive System Design model. Results: Three out of nine apps refer directly to scientifc evidence, 3/9 refer to a scientific support. The remaining 3/9 did not point out or refer to any scientific study. In addition, 3/9 are user-friendly, 3/9 apps are less user-friendly and the remaining 3/9 apps are not user-friendly at all. Finally, there is a partial use of persuasive technology. On average, 8.44 times persuasive elements are plied. Primary Task Support is most commonly used, subsequent System Credibility Support and Dialogue Support. Principles of the Social Support is used the least. Conclusion: The first steps were taken to evaluate the quality of apps focused on self-compassion and/or compassion. This study concludes that the quality of apps, focused on self-compassion and/or compassion, were limited when it came to the level of scientific evidence, usability and persuasive technology. It is recommended to give users more insight in the quality and availability of these apps. For example, this can be achieved by having researchers and other professionals (such as clinical psychologists), review the apps on the website. Furthermore, the advice is to also implement the other two elements of selfcompassion – common humanity and kindness – in the apps. For further research offers de Mobile App Rating Scale (MARS) a new opportunity to measure the subjective and objective quality of health apps. Keywords: Positive psychology, wellbeing, self-compassion and compassion eMental health, systematic review.

Effective German and English Language mHealth Apps for Self-management of Bronchial Asthma in Children and Adolescents: Comparison Study (Preprint)
abstract:
BACKGROUND
 Mobile health (mHealth) apps hold great potential for asthma self-management. Data on the suitability of asthma apps intended for children are insufficient, and the availability of German language apps is still inadequate compared with English language apps.
 
 
 OBJECTIVE
 This study aims to identify functional asthma apps for children in German and to compare them with English language apps. In line with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, the Google Play Store and Apple App Store are systematically searched to preselect the most efficient apps, which are then compared according to a self-compiled criteria catalog.
 
 
 METHODS
 Both app stores were screened for the term asthma. Following a PRISMA preselection process, the apps that met the inclusion criteria (ie, available free of charge, German or English language, and suitable for children) were rated by 3 independent persons following a criteria catalog consisting of 9 categories, some conceived for this purpose (availability, child-friendly, learning factor, and range of functions) and some adopted from existing validated catalogs (functionality and design, ease of use, potential for improving asthma self-management, fun factor and incentives, and information management and medical accuracy). The highest rated apps in German and English were compared.
 
 
 RESULTS
 A total of 403 apps were identified on the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store. Finally, 24 apps that met the inclusion criteria were analyzed. In the first step of the quality assessment, only 4 available German language asthma apps were compared with 20 English language asthma apps. The 4 German language apps were then compared with the 4 highest rated English language apps. All selected apps, independent of the language, were comparable in the following categories: availability, functionality and design, ease of use, and information management and medical accuracy. The English language apps scored significantly higher in the following categories: potential for improving self-management, child-friendly, fun factor, learning factor, and range of function. English language apps (mean total points 34.164, SD 1.09) performed significantly better than German language asthma apps (mean total points 22.91, SD 2.898; P=.003). The best rated English language app was Kiss my asthma (36/42 points), whereas the best rated German language app Kata achieved only 27.33 points.
 
 
 CONCLUSIONS
 The recommended English language apps are Kiss my asthma, AsthmaXcel, AsthmaAustralia, and Ask Me, AsthMe!, whereas the only recommended German language app is Kata. The use of apps plays an increasingly important role in patients’ lives and in the medical field, making mHealth a staple in the future of asthma treatment plans. Although validated recommendations on rating mHealth apps have been published, it remains a challenging task for physicians and patients to choose a suitable app for each case, especially in non–English-speaking countries.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Versus Oral Carbidopa/Levodopa in Advanced Parkinson’s Disease Patients: Design of a Phase 3, Randomized, Double-Blind, Double-Dummy, Active Controlled 12-Week Trial (2251)
abstract: Objective: Efficacy and Safety of Foslevodopa/Foscarbidopa Versus Oral Carbidopa/Levodopa in Advanced Parkinson’s Disease Patients: Design of a Phase 3, Randomized, Double-Blind, Double-Dummy, Active Controlled 12-Week Trial Background: As PD progresses, oral drug regimens may become insufficient for symptom control. Foslevodopa/foscarbidopa, formally known as ABBV-951, is a new soluble formulation of carbidopa and levodopa prodrugs being developed for the treatment of advanced PD delivered as a CSCI via a portable external pump. Design/Methods: This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group, active-controlled, multicenter study includes patients (≥30 years) whose motor symptoms are no longer adequately controlled by their current therapy and experience a minimum daily average of 2.5h of “Off” time per day (with a minimum of 2.0h each day). The study is comprised of a screening period, and an oral CD/LD stabilization period, followed by randomization into the 12-week double-blind treatment period. Patients will receive either 24-hour/day CSCI of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa plus oral placebo or 24-hour/day CSCI of placebo solution plus oral CD/LD. Assessments include the change from baseline to Week 12 in “On” and “Off” times from PD Diaries, MDS-UPDRS scores, quality of life, sleep symptoms, and PD symptoms measured using a wearable device. Local and systemic safety and tolerability will be assessed using the Infusion Site Evaluation Scale and adverse event monitoring. Results: This study will enroll approximately 130 advanced PD patients from an estimated 80 sites in the United States and Australia ( clinicaltrials.gov ID: NCT04380142) Conclusions: This study will provide important data on the safety and efficacy of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa, a potentially new advanced treatment option, delivered 24-hour/day via CSCI versus oral CD/LD in advanced PD patients. title: Efficacy on Non-motor and Motor symptoms and Quality of Life using a multidisciplinary telemedicine program in high-risk fall patients with Parkinson’s disease. (S32.003)
abstract: Objective: This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of a multidisciplinary telemedicine (TM) program to improve lifestyles, the burden of motor and non-motor symptoms (NMS), and quality of life (QoL) in fall patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and high risk of fall. Background: Falls in PD are very frequent, with devastating consequences, worse QoL, increasing comorbidity, and social isolation. Telerehabilitation has shown promising effects on motor symptoms, but the effectiveness of a multidisciplinary TM intervention in addition to standard clinical care on NMS, QoL and lifestyle remains unclear Design/Methods: Longitudinal, randomized study. PD Patients with high risk of falling and restricted access to multidisciplinary care were included (NCT04694443). A multidisciplinary TM program plus standard care was allocated to the study group for 4 months and compared to controls (in-office visits, standard care). TM included occupational therapy, nutrition, and PD clinical management. After discontinuing TM, both groups were compared at 8 months. Gait and PD motor severity were assessed using wearable sensors, MDS-UPDRS, Mini-Best and Freezing of gait questionnaire (FOGQ); quality of life (EuroHis-QoL8) and NMS (NMSS), Apathy Severity (LARS) and Depression/Anxiety Scale (BDI-II). Clinical information at baseline vs. 4 and 8-months visits were compared using parametric/non-parametric tests as needed. Results: 51 PD patients, 48.6 % males, median Hoehn Yhar stage 2 (1;3), mean age 68.6 ± 9.7 years were included. At 4 months, compared to controls, patients on TM had an improvement in the MDS-UPDRS II (p=0.01), Mini-Best (p<0.0001) FOGQ (p=0.01); EuroHis-QoL8 (p=0.004); LARS (p<0.0001) and BDI-II scores (p=0.004). After discontinuing TM at 8 months, FOG (p=0.01), and Mini-Best (p=0.001) scores were better in the TM group compared to controls. Conclusions: A multidisciplinary TM intervention alongside with standard care improves gait, QoL and NMS in PD patients with a high risk of falling. title: Efficient Data Management for Secure Healthcare Using Lightweight Blockchain and Enhancement of Internet of Things: A Review and Analysis
venue: 2026 International Conference on Innovations in Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Development (ICIETSD)
abstract: The swift increase in progress of wearable technologies improvement and Internet of Things (IoT) systems both have led to the intermediate steady accumulation of large volumes of highly sensitive healthcare information. The information is crucial to making good clinical decisions and proactive medical diagnoses. Nevertheless, the conventional centralized data storage platforms are severely restricted, such as exposure to privacy, security threats, lack of scalability, and enhanced susceptibility to cyberattacks. In order to deal with these issues, decentralized health care systems using lightweight blockchain systems have come up as an attractive option of secure data management.This paper will carefully review and critique blockchain-based IoT systems that have been built to be used in healthcare. Unlike the current survey, there is specific focus on the lightweight models of blockchain which are considered in the light of energy efficiency, security strategies, scalability and interoperability when used in the resource constrained IoT space. Although the decentralized nature of blockchain technology, is mutable, and offers reliable data exchange, the research findings reveal that there are still significant research gaps; thus, unresolved issues to the implementation of the technology practically. Moreover, the paper provides future research objectives and design considerations that can be made to create effective, secure, and interoperable healthcare data storage infrastructures by integrating IoT and lightweight blockchain technologies.

title: Eine Analyse von motivationalen und volitionalen Techniken zur Steigerung körperlicher Aktivität in Fitness-Apps
abstract: Diese Arbeit soll nachfolgenden Forschern und Forscherinnen eine verlässliche Datengrundlage bieten, damit die motivationale Wirkung von mobilen Fitness- und Gesundheits-Apps auch in der Praxis getestet werden kann. Weiterhin soll sie App-Entwicklern und -Entwicklerinnen Empfehlungen geben, wie Apps unter Einbeziehung von Verhaltensänderungstechniken (BCTs) gestaltet werden könnten. Dazu wurden in einer Studie nach einem exakten Ausschlussverfahren 19 von 200 Apps aus dem iOS App Store selektiert und auf enthaltene Verhaltensänderungstechniken untersucht. Unter der Rubrik „Gesundheit und Fitness“ wurde die Kategorie „umsatzstärkste“ ausgewählt, um ein repräsentatives Bild der Downloads aller User und Userinnen zu erhalten. Für die Bewertung der mobilen Anwendungen wurde die Taxonomie von Hagger, Keatley und Chan. (2014) „CALO-RE Taxonomy of Behavior Change Techniques“ herangezogen. Jeder, in einer App vorhandenen Technik, wurde ein Punkt vergeben, um sowohl die Apps als auch die Häufigkeit der vorkommenden BCT, schlussendlich vergleichen zu können. Ziel ist es zu ermitteln, in welchem Ausmaß Verhaltensänderungstechniken in den ausgewählten Apps inkludiert sind und wie sie umgesetzt werden können. Die analysierten Apps inkludieren im Durchschnitt 14,89 Verhaltensänderungstechniken, wobei das Maximum bei 24 BCTs und das Minimum bei 7 BCTs liegt. Von den 19 Apps enthalten sechs Applikationen 50% oder mehr der möglichen Verhaltensänderungstechniken. Bei der Auswertung konnte außerdem festgestellt werden, dass einige Verhaltensänderungstechniken deutlich häufiger in den Apps inkludiert waren als andere. Die Tendenz der App-Entwickler und Entwicklerinnen geht dabei vermehrt in die Richtung der Aufnahme von Techniken, die der Intentionsbildung, Dokumentation, Demonstration des Zielverhaltens sowie den sozialen Einflüssen dienen. Ebenfalls relevante Komponenten, wie beispielsweise die Rückfallprävention und das Barrierenmanagement, werden dabei kaum berücksichtigt. Jedoch kann man davon ausgehen, dass eine dauerhafte Aufrechterhaltung der Verhaltensänderung ohne die Bereitstellung adäquater Strategien zur Lösung kritischer Situationen nur selten möglich ist. Im Gegensatz dazu beinhaltet der Großteil der Apps jedoch Techniken, die zur Steigerung körperlicher Aktivität förderlich angesehen werden, sodass das Zielverhalten zumindest temporär umgesetzt werden kann.

Eliciting Design Guidelines for Privacy Notifications in mHealth Environments
abstract: The possibilities of employing mobile health (mhealth) devices for the purpose of self-quantification and fitness tracking are increasing; yet few users of online mhealth services possess proven knowledge of how their personal data are processed once the data have been disclosed. Ex post transparency-enhancing tools (TETs) can provide such insight and guide users in making informed decisions with respect to intervening with the processing of their personal data. At present, however, there are no suitable guidelines that aid designers of TETs in implementing privacy notifications that reflect their recipients' needs in terms of what they want to be notified about and the level of guidance required to audit their data effectively. Based on an analysis of gaps related to TETs, the findings of a study on privacy notification preferences, and the findings on notifications and privacy notices discussed in the literature, this paper proposes a set of guidelines for the human-centred design of privacy notifications that facilitate ex post transparency.

title: Elliptic Curve Enhanced Neural Encryption Models for Privacy Preservation in Smart Healthcare
venue: International Journal on Advanced Computer Engineering and Communication Technology
abstract: The rapid digitization of healthcare systems has led to the widespread adoption of smart healthcare technologies, including wearable devices, remote patient monitoring systems, and IoT-enabled medical infrastructures. However, the sensitive nature of medical data raises critical concerns regarding privacy, security, and unauthorized access. Traditional encryption methods often struggle to balance computational efficiency and strong cryptographic security in resource-constrained healthcare environments. This study proposes an Elliptic Curve Enhanced Neural Encryption Model (ECENEM) for privacy preservation in smart healthcare systems. The proposed framework integrates Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) for lightweight and secure key generation with deep neural networks for adaptive encryption pattern learning and anomaly-resistant secure communication. The model enhances privacy protection by combining mathematical cryptographic strength with AI-driven dynamic encryption behavior. Performance is evaluated using encryption strength, computational overhead, latency, and security resistance against common attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves higher security efficiency with lower computational cost compared to conventional encryption techniques.

title: Emanating Technologies in Modern Era of Clinical Trials
Emergentology
abstract: Figure: COVID-19FigureAs I write this: My home in San Francisco has the worst air quality in the world, and has had air quality index values over 350 for multiple days in a row. We recently experienced a California heat wave where my home was above 95°F. San Francisco doesn't have air conditioning. Wildfires are destroying the West Coast. I just saw a firenado from a firefighter's video on the front lines of the fires. COVID-19 continues to kill at a rate of 1213 people per day and 47,643 new cases per day in the United States. Mega locusts are molting across California. OK, fine, I made up that last one, but it's not unimaginable in 2020! The entire year doesn't even feel like a wash; it feels like 30 steps backward. So, I thought, what good will there be from 2020? COVID-19 has been mostly god-awful, but is there a silver lining? Hygiene and Masking I cannot be happier that masking has been commonplace in much (but unfortunately not all) of the United States, as has handwashing, not touching your face, and the American populace having much more awareness of infectious disease. Americans seem to be lacking in these areas (ask any man what hygiene is like in a public restroom), and I'm very happy to see masking becoming more accepted. I feel so comfortable in a surgical mask for all 12 hours of my shifts that it now feels weird that I didn't use to wear one routinely when a patient had infectious symptoms. I feel like a total bozo that at least some of my URIs and four-week-long coughs might have been prevented with a simple mask. Our colleagues on the other side of the world are supplying the evidence: Australia has been having one of its lightest flu seasons ever with less than a third of influenza-like illness during their normal flu season in July. (Australian Department of Health. Sept. 26, 2020; https://bit.ly/3i2FJpD.) Let's pray that we see similar gains. Can you imagine what it would be like to have only a third of the usual flu visits from December through March? Wouldn't that be spectacular? Less flu, croup, RSV? Fewer snotty, viral febrile kids? Telemedicine Telemedicine has been a long time coming, and COVID-19 lit a fire under our collective physician behinds. Some specialties, like psychiatry, for example, are particularly great fits for telemedicine, and have really flourished during COVID-19, and importantly so, with so much more anxiety, depression, and angst in the world. Other specialties scoffed at the idea of telemedicine for care, saying how critical the physical exam was. It does seem, however, that many of these specialties ignored or downplayed all the times the physical exam wasn't really needed, and it was just easier for them (and more financially viable) to insist that the patient come to the office. Thankfully, Medicare and the Department of Health and Human Services fairly quickly updated their regulations to support more telemedicine care (video and telephone), and other insurers followed suit. You can refill medications, manage chronic diseases, and review imaging or lab results without a patient coming in for a visit! Who knew? Even after COVID-19 ends, telemedicine has been so helpful to patients and physicians that Medicare will have to pry it from our cold, disconnected hands. “Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets” is a quote often applied to health care, and I think rightly so. If anything, I'd argue that the telemedicine regulatory changes don't go far enough. We are still locked in a system that requires a certain amount of physical exam to bill for care, when much of “care” (not specific to emergency medicine) is cerebral, not physical. We have also had few to no updates to HIPAA privacy rules to simplify communication, especially in the time of COVID. (Are you using technology the same way you did in 1996?) Sure, you can technically use FaceTime due to a COVID-era CMS good faith policy and technically you have always had the ability to text patients if you asked for their explicit consent, but what medical group or hospital is going to support this workflow when it's on temporary status and when there are so many medicolegal and privacy loopholes that open someone up to lawsuit risks in our country? I'd love to shoot a quick text to a patient to see how he is managing his broken ankle on my day off instead of connecting to my hospital VPN, logging in three times, finding the chart, opening a message, typing the message, and sending it so that the patient can then get an email that a doctor sent him a message, making him log in to the patient portal, read the message, and reply to the message, which I may not see until later because I'm logged off from the EHR for the rest of the day. In today's world, that's not happening. Telemedicine has many patient-sided benefits as well, which we in EM may be less familiar with: Not having to take off from work to see the doctor or use sick leave Not having to drive, commute, and find parking Not having to sit in a waiting room with other potentially sick patients Being able to discuss your personal private medical issues in your own clothes and in your own environment where you might feel more comfortable But it's not a panacea, of course. For every patient who may be more comfortable discussing things in person, there is probably one with intimate partner violence who is trapped in her home with her partner. No-Visitor Policies Like many hospitals, we have had a near-zero visitor policy in place for more than six months now (exceptions for pediatric, labor and delivery, and end-of-life patients), and while it has made some of emergency medicine easier, I know it has been harder for some of my patients. I'll admit it has been really nice to have more space in our tiny ED, and it has been easier not to have to explain things to each family member every time a new one arrives. But it's hard for my patients not to have their loved ones' support at the bedside when I break bad news, and I know the anxiety must be incredibly high when someone has to say goodbye to a parent, child, or partner at the door to the ED. COVID-19 and 2020 generally have certainly been more bad than good, but once the pandemic ends (I'm thinking 2022), let's not throw the baby out with the bath water, and let's keep some of the good changes COVID-19 has forced upon us.
