title: Emotion-Aware Edge Computing Framework for Next-Gen Human-Machine Collaboration
venue: International Conference on Mobile Computing and Sustainable Informatics (ICMCSI)
abstract: Emotion-aware computing is emerging as a critical enabler of naturalistic human-machine collaboration. With the growing demand for intelligent interfaces across edge environments such as smart homes, healthcare, and wearable devices, traditional cloud-dependent emotion recognition models suffer from high latency, privacy risks, and poor adaptability. The present research introduces an original Emotion-Aware Edge Computing Framework which combines multimodal sensing, Bi-GRU + emotion inference that uses attention and real-time adaptive interaction logic that executes directly on low-power edge computers such as Raspberry Pi 4. Lightweight sensors are used to capture facial expression, Tone and physiological (GSR and heart rate) signals and are preprocessed by normalization, landmark tracking, MFCC extraction, and statistical analysis. Mixed integration methods which involve early and late convergence are used to improve recognition performance. Optimized Bi-GRU model is implemented through TensorRT and quantization with the average accuracy of 90.1, and the inference latency has been lowered to approximately 61.5 ms, and its energy consumption has been less than $1.5 ~\mathrm{J} /$ inference. Its usability and responsiveness are confirmed by the user interaction studies with a high level of satisfaction (mean 9.0/10). The suggested framework realizes strong and privacy-conscious emotion detecting at the edge, transforming the meaning of affective human-machine interaction. Future directions involve the addition of more categories of emotions, cross cultural generalization, and federated learning to constantly refine the model without affecting privacy.

title: EmotionPass: Unobtrusive Emotion-based User Authentication on Glasses
abstract: Wearable devices are increasingly prevalent, necessitating reliable user authentication to mitigate privacy risks. Glasses, as a prominent category of wearable devices, have traditionally employed methods such as iris recognition, depth cameras, and electrooculography (EOG) for authentication purposes. However, these solutions are usually only applicable for bulky VR/XR goggles and are often impractical for emerging lightweight smart glasses due to the need for additional hardware modules. Thanks to their compact size, low cost, and privacy-preserving capabilities by capturing muscle movements, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) offer a promising alternative for user authentication. This study introduces EmotionPass, a novel system embedding IMU sensors in a pair of lightweight glasses for passive user authentication via facial expressions. Utilizing a Knowledge-Aware Network (KAN) and Supervised Contrastive Learning, our system extracts distinctive features from IMU signals. Experiments with 23 participants performing seven facial expressions demonstrated a high average accuracy of $99.22 \%$ and an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 0.0154 in user attack scenarios. We compared various baseline algorithms and proved the reliability and stability of our algorithm. The system maintained $92.51 \%$ accuracy for unseen expressions, with long-term usability confirmed. EmotionPass thus offers a non-invasive, cost-effective, and efficient solution for continuous user authentication in wearable settings.

title: Enabling Daily Tracking of Individual’s Cognitive State With Eyewear
abstract: Research studies show that sleep deprivation causes severe fatigue, impairs attention and decision making, and affects our emotional interpretation of events, which makes it a big threat to public safety, and mental and physical well-being. Hence, it would be most desired if we could continuously measure one’s drowsiness and fatigue level, their emotion while making decisions, and assess their sleep quality in order to provide personalized feedback or actionable behavioral suggestions to modulate sleep pattern and alertness levels with the aim of enhancing performance, well-being, and quality of life. While there have been decades of studies on wearable devices, we still lack good instruments to measure an individual’s cognitive state in natural settings. In this thesis, we propose novel eyewear solutions in order to track various cognitive states, with the focus of being low-power, unobtrusive, and robust to confounders present in everyday scenarios. We propose the following contributions: i) design and implementation of a system, iLid, that is able to extract key features of fatigue and drowsiness at low power and high frame rate from a wearable eye tracker in natural settings, ii) design of a privacy-sensitive system, W!NCE, for detecting various facial expressions and pain instances, by leveraging only three small dry electrodes on the nose-bridge of a normal looking pair of glasses, and iii) design of a comfortable, unobtrusive, and accurate sleep monitoring system, PhyMask that can be worn continuously during long duration of wear without impacting sleep. We introduce novel fabric-based sensing elements to measure various physiological signals such as brain activity, eye movement patterns, heart rate, and breathing rate as well as head posture and body motions during sleep.

title: Energy-Optimized Wireless Security for Sustainable Critical National Infrastructure: Zero-Trust Over Starlink with Kinesiology-Enhanced Operator Resilience

abstract: Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) demands resilient, energy-efficient, and secure communication solutions to counter escalating cyber-physical threats while satisfying sustainability requirements. This paper proposes an integrated energy-optimized security framework that combines Starlink Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite connectivity with Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA). A kinesiology-enhanced human resilience layer is incorporated, utilizing wearable sensors to monitor operator posture, muscle tension, and heart rate variability (HRV). Machine learning models analyze these biofeedback signals in real time to detect fatigue and stress, thereby reducing human-error-induced vulnerabilities. Energy optimization is realized through adaptive encryption (preferring ChaCha20 over AES-256), traffic-aware prioritization, duty-cycled terminal operation, and selective activation. Power measurements of Starlink terminals indicate baseline consumption of 20-40 W (Mini) to 110}-150 W (Flat High Performance). The proposed techniques achieve 40-70% reduction in average power, lowering daily energy usage from 2.9-3.6 kWh to 0.7-1.7 kWh per terminal. This significantly decreases solar array, battery, and off-grid infrastructure requirements. The framework demonstrates improved latency, availability, and security in remote and disrupted environments, with strong applicability to border security, emergency response, and utility operations in challenging terrains such as Croatia. Regulatory, dependency, and privacy challenges are also addressed.

title: Enhancing Construction Safety: The Role of AI and Robotics in Risk Mitigation
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics in construction safety monitoring has the potential to revolutionize the industry by significantly reducing workplace accidents and enhancing overall site safety. This study explores the current applications, benefits, and challenges of AI and robotics in construction safety. Utilizing real-time data from sensors, cameras, and wearable devices, AI-powered systems can assess safety threats, predict accidents, and optimize resource allocation. Robotics technology complements these efforts by automating hazardous tasks and augmenting human capabilities. Through a comprehensive literature review and an anonymous online survey of construction professionals, this research provides valuable insights into the practical realities and stakeholder perspectives on these technologies. Ethical considerations, data privacy, algorithm accuracy, and labor upskilling are also examined to ensure a holistic discussion. The findings highlight the importance of strategic implementation and stakeholder collaboration in leveraging AI and robotics to advance construction safety. This study contributes to the ongoing discourse on technological innovation in construction, advocating for a safer and more efficient industry.

title: Enhancing Cyber security in Medical IoT Devices Using AI-Based Data Analytics Approaches
abstract: The recent surge in interconnected Medical Internet of Things (MIoT) gadgets has revolutionized the healthcare delivery process, yet it has brought about sophisticated cybersecurity problems. The wearable input sensors and implantable medical devices are MIoT systems that generate and transmit sensitive health information, and are susceptible to malware, ransomware, and data interception attacks. The traditional rule-based security controls cannot adequately deal with the dynamic threats, which will take advantage of the heterogeneity and limited computing capabilities of MIoT devices. The current paper discusses the opportunities of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based data analytics to improve MIoT cybersecurity. It is possible to detect, categorize, and mitigate cyber threats within seconds, as AI models based on machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and anomaly detection algorithms can recognize them. The paper has reviewed available literature about AI based intrusion detection, analyzed performance indicators like detection rate, false positive rate, and latency, and outlined a conceptual architecture of predictive analytics and federated learning to guarantee privacy in defense. The results reveal that AI analytics would play an important role in the resilience, trust, and transparency of MIoT systems. The article ends with a discussion of the future research direction such as explainable AI (XAI), edge computing integration, and regulatory compliance as key strategies to provide a safe healthcare environment.

title: Enhancing Data Security, Sustainability, and Robotics Integration in IoT‐Enabled Healthcare Systems
abstract: IoT technologies have made significant impact on the healthcare industry through pervasive monitoring and data acquisition through wearables, sensors, and remote monitoring devices. Thus, it is necessary to develop mechanisms that are secure in a way of handling the data and energy-efficient in the context of limited power supply of IoT devices which are integrated with robotic tools. These challenges can be addressed by developing secure and energy-aware solutions specifically for IoT-enhanced health care systems. It presents features a detailed understanding of the current threats in IoT and robotic systems and relevant enhancements of encryption, authentication and privacy-preserving schemes suitable for implementation without limiting energy consumption. Moreover, the chapter looks at techniques ranging from the blockchain solutions, internet learning techniques, lightweight encryption, and robotics operational energy efficient security solutions. title: Enhancing Emotional Intelligence in Industrial Systems Using IoT
abstract: The manufacturing sector is a vital component of the global economy. It acts as a significant driver of economic growth, technological innovation, and in providing employment. The manufacturing industries are contributing approximately 16% to the global gross domestic product (GDP). This reflects its vital role in economic development. The sector covers a varied range of activities that includes processing the raw materials, goods production, and product assembly, spanning industries like automotive, electronics, textiles, and food processing. Although at present manufacturing industries are experiencing very fast technological advancements and transformations worldwide, there is an increasing emphasis on improving operational efficiency to increase yield and to reduce costs. At global level, the manufacturing industries are being shaped by trends like technological advancements, human capital, and workforce dynamics. This has given rise to the requirement for greater coordination between humans and technological factors. The assimilation of Internet of Things (IoT) with artificial intelligence (AI) has now brought about a transformation in industrial systems by integrating emotional intelligence (EI) into human machine interactions. This has facilitated for data monitoring in real time, enhance prediction capabilities, and enhance automation that leads to increase in the yield, safety, and workers well-being in industrial environments and ultimately leading to increased operational efficiency. Studies reveal that IoT-enabled systems play a vital role in monitoring emotions of the workers and improve decision making capabilities. This chapter provides an insight on how IoT-driven emotional intelligence enriches industrial systems by providing capabilities like real-time emotion sensing, adaptive automation, and AI-driven analytics. Physiological and behavioral data of the employees are collected using various wearable sensors, biometric devices, and environmental monitoring systems and the data is then used to assess stress on the employees. The fatigue level and their emotional states are also assessed using the collected data. Emotion aware industrial robots and AI-driven control systems can also be used for the purpose to increase safety in workplace, reduce fatigue related risks, and improve employee engagement. Applications in manufacturing, logistics, and smart factories reveals how emotionally intelligent IoT fosters a responsive and human centric industrial ecosystem. Nonetheless, challenges like data privacy, risks of cyber security, and few ethical concerns that arise due to IoT-driven emotional intelligence in industrial systems has to be addressed in order to ensure responsible deployment. The infrastructural shortfalls and skill gaps also exhibits potential for development through targeted investments in technology and human capital development. Overall this chapter explores the role of emotion in industrial settings, the concept of emotional intelligence, and how IoT-driven technologies can enhance emotional intelligence within industrial systems in order to develop an adaptive, effective, and well-organized workplace.

title: Enhancing IoT Smart Door Lock Security Using Chameleon Swarm Algorithm, SHA-256, and ECC
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, spanning from smart home appliances to wearable technology, has significantly heightened concerns regarding security and privacy across various sectors. As cyber threats become increasingly sophisticated and frequent, the urgency for robust, adaptable security frameworks within IoT infrastructures is more critical than ever. This study introduces a cutting-edge security framework tailored for IoT-based smart door locks, which employs a novel integration of the Chameleon Swarm Algorithm (CSA), Secure Hash Algorithm SHA-256, and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). We conducted comprehensive performance evaluations in a Microsoft Visual Studio 2012 environment, where our proposed framework was benchmarked against conventional hybrid methods based on Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Firefly Algorithm such as - SHA-256-ECC-GA and SHA-256-ECC-FA. These evaluations demonstrated that our framework significantly enhances security performance, achieving up to 15.17% faster encoding times at 100 iterations and markedly quicker decoding times at 150 iterations compared to the benchmark techniques. The improvements confirm the framework’s effectiveness in not only bolstering IoT device security but also in its potential for scalability and adaptability across diverse IoT applications. Furthermore, the integration of advanced algorithms like CSA, SHA-256, and ECC effectively addresses critical vulnerabilities, particularly in smart door locks, thereby paving the way for safer, more secure IoT environments. This study exemplifies how innovative cryptographic techniques can be strategically applied to meet the evolving security demands of the IoT landscape.

title: Enhancing Perception System Robustness Against Attacks and Natural Perturbations
venue: KTH Publication Database DiVA (KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
abstract: Deep learning has led to major progress in computer vision, but modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are still highly vulnerable to input perturbations, which limits their robustness in safety-critical applications. This challenge becomes even more critical in real-world industrial environments, such as autonomous machinery operating on construction sites, where visual data is influenced by unpredictable weather conditions, variable lighting, and physical wear and degradation. In addition, data scarcity, privacy constraints, and domain shift prevent the direct application of conventional large-scale training pipelines. This thesis addresses these challenges by proposing a comprehensive, multi-level framework that strengthens model-level robustness against adversarial attacks, enhances data-level robustness to natural environmental perturbations, and improves adaptive learning under distributed and data-constrained conditions, enabling reliable deployment of visual perception models in complex, safety-critical environments. The first contribution focuses on the robustness of model-level attacks against adversarial attacks. A meta-heuristic search method is proposed to automatically discover activation functions that increase resistance to adversarial perturbations without requiring adversarial training. A hybrid search strategy further improves convergence efficiency, yielding Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that outperform standard architectures under adversarial attacks while maintaining competitive clean-data accuracy. The second contribution introduces ConstScene, a large-scale semantic segmentation dataset representing real and synthetic construction-site imagery under diverse weather and sensor degradation conditions. Experiments reveal significant performance drops when models trained on clean data are exposed to perturbed inputs, demonstrating the need for environment-specific robustness benchmarks. The third contribution introduces an integrated framework that combines Federated Learning (FL) for decentralized collaborative training with Few-Shot Learning (FSL) for sample-efficient domain adaptation, supported by server-side Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO). The proposed approach enables effective model adaptation across distributed construction sites without sharing raw data, significantly improving robustness across heterogeneous client datasets. In general, this thesis proposes three contributions to enhance robustness in perception systems: model-level robustness against adversarial attacks, introducing the ConstScene dataset for benchmarking performance under real-world degradations and data-level robustness against natural perturbations, and an integrated framework enabling decentralized, sample-efficient model adaptation across heterogeneous environments.

title: Enhancing authentication in wearable devices: BLE-AES-CCM implementation
abstract: Bluetooth low energy (BLE) technology has gained widespread adoption in various applications but concerns about user privacy and tracking have emerged. In this research article, we propose a privacy-enhancing algorithm specifically designed for BLE to address these concerns. Our algorithm ensures user anonymity and protects sensitive information during BLE communication. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through experiments and comparisons with existing techniques, demonstrating its ability to mitigate privacy risks and safeguard user data. The increasing prevalence of wearable devices in various domains has raised concerns about data security and privacy. BLE technology is commonly used for communication in wearable devices due to its low power consumption. However, the inherent vulnerabilities of BLE in terms of data security necessitate the integration of robust encryption algorithms. In this study, we propose the integration of BLE with advanced encryption standard-counter with CBC-MAC (AES-CCM) as an effective solution to enhance data security in wearable devices. The proposed algorithm leverages the low energy consumption capabilities of BLE while providing a strong encryption mechanism through AES-CCM. By combining these technologies, data confidentiality, integrity, and privacy are effectively ensured during communication between wearable devices. AES-CCM offers encryption and authentication in a single operation, reducing computational overhead and enhancing the efficiency of secure data transmission. To evaluate the proposed algorithm, we conducted performance evaluations and efficiency analyses. The results demonstrated that the integration of BLE with AES-CCM strikes a balance between data security and low power consumption, making it a suitable choice for wearable devices. The algorithm showcased improved privacy protection, reduced vulnerability to attacks, and efficient energy utilization.

title: Ep. 2805: The Subprocessor Notification Nobody Reads
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: You've seen them — those emails about "subprocessor list updates" that land with all the enthusiasm of a terms-of-service popup. Nobody reads them, nobody acts on them, and even if you tried to investigate, the company won't tell you anything useful. So what's the point? In this episode, we dig into GDPR Article 28, the actual function of subprocessor notifications, and why these seemingly useless emails might serve a hidden purpose — not for you, but for the watchdogs who know how to pull the thread. Show Notes Every email user has seen them: subprocessor notification updates that land in your inbox with all the enthusiasm of a terms-of-service popup. A study from the University of Michigan found that over 90% of people never read privacy policies or terms of service — and subprocessor notifications are even further down the attention hierarchy. They're the basement of the basement. Under GDPR Article 28, a subprocessor is what you get when a data processor subcontracts work to another company. If you use a project management app hosted on AWS, and AWS brings in a specialized analytics firm, that firm is the subprocessor. The regulation requires controllers to notify users when subprocessors change — but the notification typically gives you nothing but a company name and a vague service description. The actual contracts between controllers, processors, and subprocessors are almost always confidential. The real function of these notifications isn't for individual users. It's for competitors, privacy activists, regulators, and journalists — people with the time and expertise to scrutinize the public record. When Schrems II invalidated the Privacy Shield framework, subprocessor lists suddenly forced companies to examine their data supply chains for the first time. The notification requirement creates a discoverable record that enables collective action, even if the individual email is functionally meaningless. title: Ep. 305: Is Your Typing Style More Secure Than Your Password?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: As we move further into 2026, the friction of traditional two-factor authentication is reaching a breaking point for many users. In this episode of My Weird Prompts, Herman and Corn dive deep into the world of passkeys, hardware tokens, and the emerging "fourth factor" of security: behavioral biometrics. They discuss whether we are headed toward a more secure world or one where our every move is monitored for the sake of convenience. From heartbeat signatures to Zero Trust architecture, learn how the tech industry plans to kill the password once and for all while keeping the hackers at bay. Show Notes In the latest episode of *My Weird Prompts*, hosts Herman and Corn Poppleberry sit down in their Jerusalem living room to tackle a growing modern frustration: authentication fatigue. With the digital landscape of early 2026 becoming increasingly complex, the duo explores the transition from traditional passwords to a future defined by "invisible" security measures. The discussion, sparked by a prompt from their housemate Daniel, delves into the mechanics of passkeys, the evolution of multi-factor authentication (MFA), and the controversial rise of behavioral biometrics. ### The Death of the Password Herman begins by clarifying the current state of passkeys, which have moved from a niche tech feature to a mainstream security standard. Unlike traditional passwords, which are strings of characters stored on a server, passkeys utilize public-key cryptography. Herman explains that when a user creates a passkey, their device generates a unique pair of keys: a public one shared with the website and a private one that never leaves the user's hardware. The brilliance of this system, according to Herman, is that it collapses the traditional two-step authentication process into a single gesture. By using a biometric scan—like Face ID or a fingerprint—to unlock the device, the user is simultaneously proving "something they have" (the device) and "something they are" (the biometric). This effectively satisfies multi-factor requirements without the need for cumbersome SMS codes or secondary authenticator apps, providing a direct remedy for the "2FA fatigue" Daniel described. ### Beyond the Third Factor: Behavioral Biometrics The conversation takes a futuristic turn as Corn asks whether high-security environments will simply "move the goalposts" as passkeys become the baseline. Herman confirms that we are already seeing the emergence of a "fourth factor": behavioral biometrics. This goes beyond what a user knows, has, or is, and focuses instead on how a user *behaves*. Herman describes a world where systems monitor the cadence of a user's keystrokes, the specific way they move a mouse, or even the angle at which they hold their phone. These patterns are unique to individuals and can serve as a continuous, invisible layer of security. If a user is logged in but their typing rhythm suddenly changes—perhaps indicating a different person has taken over the keyboard—the system can trigger a "step-up" authentication challenge. While this offers a seamless user experience, Corn raises valid concerns regarding privacy and the "Big Brother" nature of constant behavioral monitoring. ### The Hardware Standard and the AI Arms Race Despite the convenience of software-based passkeys, Herman insists that physical hardware keys, such as YubiKeys, remain the gold standard for high-stakes environments like government and finance. The primary advantage of these devices is isolation; because they are single-purpose tools not connected to a general-purpose operating system, their attack surface is significantly smaller than that of a smartphone or laptop. The hosts also revisit the topic of voice and facial recognition in the age of generative AI. With deepfakes becoming more sophisticated, Herman explains that the industry is fighting back with "liveness detection." This technology looks for subtle human physical cues that AI struggles to replicate in real-time, such as the acoustics of a room or the specific breath patterns associated with speech. It is a perpetual arms race between synthetic spoofs and AI-driven detection. ### The Future: Heartbeats and Zero Trust Perhaps the most intriguing concept discussed is the use of "continuous authentication" via wearables. Herman highlights research into using unique EKG signatures—the electrical rhythm of a person's heart—as a biometric factor. In this scenario, a smartwatch could constantly authenticate a user to their workstation. As long as the watch detects the owner's specific heartbeat, the devices stay unlocked. If the watch is removed, the "trust" is instantly severed. This leads to the broader philosophy of "Zero Trust" architecture. Herman explains that the industry is moving away from the "trust, but verify" model toward a "never trust, always verify" approach. In a Zero Trust world, security is dynamic. If a user logs in from a known location on a trusted device during normal hours, the friction is low. However, if that same user attempts to access sensitive data from an unusual IP address at 3:00 AM, the system will automatically demand additional factors. ### Conclusion: The Balance of Security and Friction As the episode wraps up, Herman and Corn reflect on the human element of security. They conclude that for any security system to be effective, it must avoid "security bypass behavior"—the tendency for users to find dangerous workarounds when a system becomes too annoying. The goal for the future of authentication is not to add more gates, but to make the gates smarter and more invisible, ensuring that the highest levels of protection don't come at the cost of the user's sanity. title: Ep. 798: Beyond the Button: How AI Learns From Your Feedback
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: When you click "thumbs down" on an AI response, it often feels like pushing a crosswalk button that isn't connected to anything. But behind that simple interface lies a massive, systematic pipeline designed to align artificial intelligence with human values. This episode explores the transition from manual human annotation to the sophisticated world of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We break down how your individual ratings calibrate "Reward Models"—digital judges that train the AI's core logic—and look at the cutting-edge shift toward personalized "digital backpacks" that allow models to learn your specific preferences without changing the base code for everyone else. Beyond the mechanics, we tackle the critical challenge of privacy in the age of agentic workflows. From automated PII scrubbing to the mathematical genius of differential privacy, discover how developers extract collective wisdom from billions of conversations without exposing your personal secrets. We also touch on the growing threat of data poisoning and how the industry separates genuine signal from the noise of a global user base. Show Notes For many users, the "thumbs up" and "thumbs down" icons at the bottom of an AI chat interface feel like placebos—digital fidget toys designed to give us a sense of agency without actually changing the machine. However, these buttons are the entry point for a massive, automated system known as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). This process is the primary engine for "alignment," the method by which developers ensure AI models are helpful, safe, and accurate. ### The Judge and the Student The feedback loop does not involve a human developer reviewing every individual rating. Instead, the process is tiered. It begins with professional annotators who rank responses to create a "gold standard" dataset. This data is used to train a Reward Model—a separate, smaller AI that acts as a judge. When a user provides feedback, that data point helps calibrate this Reward Model. The main language model then "practices" in a simulated environment, generating millions of responses that the Reward Model grades. Over time, the main model learns to prioritize outputs that receive the highest marks. ### The Shift to Personalized AI Historically, AI models were static; their "weights" or digital brains were frozen after training. If you told a model to stop using bullet points, it might comply for one session but forget your preference by the next. By 2026, the industry has moved toward "Low-Rank Adaptation" (LoRA), or personalized adapters. Think of this as a "digital backpack" that the base model wears specifically for you. This allows the AI to evolve based on your unique writing style and feedback without requiring an expensive update to the global model used by everyone else. ### The Privacy Shield Turning millions of private conversations into training data presents a significant privacy risk. To combat this, developers use sophisticated pipelines to scrub Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Beyond simple redaction, the industry has adopted "Differential Privacy." This mathematical framework adds statistical noise to datasets, allowing companies to identify broad patterns—such as "users prefer concise answers"—without ever being able to trace a specific piece of information back to an individual user. It provides the "aggregate truth" while maintaining a mathematical shield around the person. ### Guarding Against Poison As AI becomes more influential, the threat of "data poisoning" grows. This occurs when bad actors or trolls attempt to intentionally provide negative or biased feedback to degrade a model's performance. To maintain integrity, the training loops must be highly selective, using secondary models to filter for quality and consistency. This ensures that the AI learns from genuine human preferences rather than coordinated attempts to sabotage the system. The result is a model that is constantly being refined by the crowd, yet protected from the noise of the firehose. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/ai-feedback-loop-privacy

title: Estudio prospectivo del IoMT
venue: RECERCAT (Consorci de Serveis Universitaris de Catalunya)
abstract: The arrival of the Internet of Things (IoT) and its numerous applications is revolutionizing all the sectors in which it is being integrated. This project focuses on the application of the Internet of Things in the field of medicine, the so-called Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), starting by analyzing its evolution from the first telemetry systems to the current telemedicine. This project also studies some wearable devices applied to medicine that have already been implanted in our society. Besides, it examines its architecture and its applications. In addition to this, emerging technologies such as radio frequency identification (RFID) or the use of Big Data in the analysis of data in medicine are also analyzed. We will see how they are used, what types there are and some of their different applications. In order to apply all these technological systems correctly in the medical field, certain global and regional standards and protocols must be followed, which are also examined in this paper. Due to the massive increase of collected data and devices connected to the networks, this project studies the possible threats faced by patients, the security measures applied nowadays and the different security and privacy certifications in the medical field established both in the European Union and the United States. Finally, the main challenges that the IoMT will face in the future are listed and evaluated. As a conclusion, the difficulties that the IoMT technologies will have in order to be truly integrated in hospitals and in our healthcare system are analyzed, as well as why their use is not yet fully implemented.

title: Ethical Concerns Associated with Wearable Gadgets and Mental Well-being Software
abstract: This research paper examines the ethical, privacy, and security challenges associated with wearable gadgets and mental well-being software in modern digital healthcare systems. With the rapid adoption of fitness trackers, smartwatches, and mental health applications, large volumes of sensitive physiological and psychological data—such as heart rate, sleep patterns, stress levels, and mood states—are continuously collected and processed.The study highlights major security vulnerabilities present in wearable and mental wellness applications, including improper authentication and authorization, code injection, weak certificate validation, missing encryption of sensitive data, and insecure password recovery mechanisms. These weaknesses pose serious risks such as unauthorized data access, identity theft, discrimination, and psychological harm to users.Furthermore, the paper emphasizes the importance of integrating privacy and security measures during the early stages of software development rather than treating them as post-deployment fixes. Ethical principles such as autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice are discussed as foundational elements for responsible application design. The research also explores the role of regulatory frameworks and security models such as GDPR, HIPAA, and the Zero Trust model in safeguarding user data.The findings suggest that adopting privacy-by-design approaches, strong encryption practices, proper access control, and ethical governance can significantly reduce risks and enhance user trust. This study contributes to the growing discourse on secure and ethical digital health systems and provides practical insights for developers, researchers, and policymakers involved in wearable and mental health technologies.

title: Ethical Considerations and Challenges
Ethical Considerations in Mental Health Data Collection and Analysis
abstract: Wearable technology has changed the field of mental health by making it possible to collect data continuously and without being noticed. This data gives researchers useful information about people's mental health. Wearable technology in mental health, on the other hand, brings up a lot of social and legal questions about privacy, data gathering, and research. This essay looks at the moral and legal issues connected to mental health data in smart technology, focused on the values of liberty, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. People should be able to make their own choices about their health because autonomy is a basic moral value. People must be able to decide for themselves if they want to be a part of data collection and how that data is used when it comes to personal technology. This makes me wonder about informed consent, because people might not fully understand what it means to share their mental health information. Because of the principles of beneficence and non-maleficence, mental health smart technology should help people and cause them as little harm as possible. People who wear technology might be able to improve their mental health by showing early signs of mental health problems, but this also makes people worry about data protection and vulnerabilities. If mental health data is misused, then it could lead to shame and abuse against people who have mental health problems. For justice to be served, the pros and cons of smart technology for mental health should be evenly shared among all people. This makes me wonder about access to smart technology, because some people might not be able to afford or understand how to use these gadgets. Concerns have also been raised about the use of mental health data for business reasons, like focused ads, which could make inequality even worse.

title: Ethical Digital Marketing Theory
first_author: Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D, DBA
abstract: The rapid transformation of digital ecosystems has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of marketing practice, organizational communication, and consumer engagement. Over the past decade, the convergence of algorithmic targeting, big data analytics, artificial intelligence, and social media platforms has enabled unprecedented levels of personalization and behavioral influence. Marketing is no longer confined to persuasive messaging; it now operates within complex infrastructures capable of predicting preferences, shaping attention, and subtly guiding decision-making processes. In this evolving environment, ethical considerations can no longer be treated as supplementary concerns they must be integrated into the theoretical core of digital marketing itself. Since 2018, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) has conducted sustained interdisciplinary research examining the ethical tensions embedded within contemporary digital marketing systems. Through longitudinal observation, conceptual synthesis, and critical engagement with emerging practices, this research has identified a fundamental theoretical gap: while digital marketing strategies have advanced technologically, ethical frameworks have often lagged behind or remained fragmented. Existing models tend to emphasize performance metrics, conversion rates, engagement analytics, and optimization algorithms, yet they insufficiently address the moral architecture underlying these mechanisms. Ethical Digital Marketing Theory (EDMT) emerges as a response to this gap. It proposes that ethical reasoning must be structurally integrated into digital marketing strategy, platform design, data governance, and consumer interaction. Rather than perceiving ethics as a constraint on innovation, EDMT reframes ethical integrity as a strategic asset and a foundation for sustainable trust. The theory advances a human-centered paradigm in which profitability, transparency, autonomy, and social responsibility are viewed not as competing goals but as interdependent principles. The central premise of this work is that digital marketing operates within socio-technical systems that shape both economic outcomes and human experience. Algorithms curate visibility; predictive models anticipate consumer behavior; data infrastructures track user interactions in real time. These systems influence perception, preference formation, and even emotional response. As such, digital marketing strategies possess transformative power that extends beyond commercial transactions. They participate in constructing informational environments, cultural narratives, and behavioral norms. Research conducted by YER since 2018 has consistently highlighted three recurring ethical tensions: 1. Data Exploitation versus Data Stewardship The capacity to collect, analyze, and monetize user data presents significant opportunities for targeted communication. However, it also raises questions concerning privacy, consent, and informational asymmetry. EDMT argues that organizations must transition from exploitative data extraction toward responsible data stewardship, emphasizing transparency and accountability. 2. Behavioral Influence versus Consumer Autonomy Advanced targeting techniques can subtly guide consumer decisions through nudging mechanisms and emotional triggers. While influence is inherent to marketing, ethical boundaries become blurred when persuasive design compromises informed choice. EDMT underscores the importance of preserving consumer autonomy within digitally mediated persuasion. 3. Short-Term Engagement versus Long-Term Trust Engagement-driven metrics often reward sensationalism or emotional intensity. Yet strategies that maximize immediate visibility may erode credibility over time. Ethical Digital Marketing Theory proposes that long-term relational trust constitutes the most sustainable form of competitive advantage. The novelty of EDMT lies in integrating these tensions into a coherent theoretical architecture. Rather than addressing ethical dilemmas as isolated case studies, the theory conceptualizes them as systemic features of digital ecosystems. It bridges normative ethical philosophy, marketing strategy, behavioral science, and information governance into a unified analytical framework. This integrative orientation aligns with international scholarly standards and contributes to advancing marketing theory beyond instrumental rationality. A distinguishing feature of this approach is its humanistic authority. Ethical Digital Marketing Theory does not depict consumers as passive targets nor organizations as inherently predatory entities. Instead, it acknowledges a dynamic interplay between corporate strategy, technological infrastructure, regulatory environment, and consumer agency. Ethical responsibility is distributed yet interconnected. Marketers design campaigns; platforms configure algorithms; regulators establish boundaries; consumers interpret and respond. Sustainable digital ecosystems depend upon mutual accountability among these actors. Furthermore, EDMT positions ethics not merely as compliance with legal frameworks but as a proactive commitment to dignity, fairness, and transparency. Regulatory requirements often represent minimum standards. Ethical excellence requires surpassing compliance by cultivating cultures of integrity within organizations and embedding ethical reflection into technological innovation. Since initiating this research journey in 2018, YER has emphasized that digital transformation presents not only economic opportunities but also moral crossroads. The same technologies that enable hyper-personalization can either empower consumers through relevant information or manipulate them through opaque persuasion. The direction chosen depends on theoretical clarity and institutional commitment. This book introduces Ethical Digital Marketing Theory as both analytical framework and normative guide. It seeks to equip scholars, practitioners, policymakers, and organizational leaders with conceptual tools to navigate ethical complexity in digitally mediated markets. By articulating a structured approach to ethical integration, EDMT aspires to redefine success in digital marketing not solely as conversion efficiency, but as the harmonious alignment of innovation, responsibility, and human respect. In an era characterized by algorithmic acceleration and data ubiquity, ethical reflection must keep pace with technological capability. It affirms that sustainable progress arises when innovation is guided by principled insight and when commercial ambition is anchored in ethical responsibility. The contemporary digital marketplace is characterized by extraordinary innovation. Artificial intelligence personalizes advertisements in milliseconds; predictive analytics anticipates consumer desires before they are consciously articulated; behavioral tracking mechanisms map patterns of attention with granular precision. These developments have transformed marketing from a persuasive communication discipline into a data-intensive strategic science. Yet amid this rapid evolution, one foundational question persists: how should marketing operate ethically within digitally mediated environments that possess unprecedented power to shape perception, preference, and behavior? title: Ethical Fairness in Ubiquitous Health Sensing without Known Attributes
abstract: In ubiquitous and mobile health systems, computational models infer human states from wearable, behavioral, and physiological sensing data. In these settings, high accuracy alone is insufficient; models must act ethically and equitably across diverse people, contexts, and devices. However, fairness methods that rely on demographic or heterogeneous attributes during training are difficult to enforce because such attributes are often unavailable, privacy-sensitive, regulated, or undesirable to collect. Conventional parity-based fairness can also violate ethical principles by trading off subgroup performance. To address this challenge, we present Flare, Fisher-guided LAtent-subgroup learning with do-no-harm REgularization, a demographic- and heterogeneous-attribute-agnostic framework that aligns human-centered fairness with ethical principles for ubiquitous and mobile sensing. Flare leverages optimization geometry, particularly Fisher Information, to regularize curvature and uncover latent disparities in model behavior without demographic or heterogeneous attributes. By integrating representation, loss, and curvature signals, it identifies hidden performance strata and refines them through collaborative but do-no-harm optimization, enhancing subgroup performance while preserving ethical balance. We also introduce BHE (Beneficence-Harm Avoidance-Equity), a metric suite that operationalizes ethical fairness beyond statistical parity. Across mobile physiological, behavioral, and clinical sensing datasets, including EDA, OhioT1DM, IHS, and Percept-R, Flare improves ethical fairness over state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation, interpretability, and loss-landscape analyses show that these gains arise from flatter optimization geometry, simpler decision rules, and do-no-harm latent-subgroup adaptation. Runtime analysis supports the practicality of Flare for resource-constrained sensing deployments.

title: Ethical Issues in the Use of Smartphone Apps for HIV Prevention among Men who Have Sex with Men in Malaysia: A Qualitative Study (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND The use of smartphone apps can improve the HIV prevention cascade for key populations, such as men who have sex with men (MSM). In Malaysia, where stigma and discrimination toward MSM are high, mHealth app-based strategies have the potential to open new frontiers for HIV prevention efforts. However, little guidance is available to inform researchers about ethical concerns unique to the development and implementation of app-based HIV prevention programs. OBJECTIVE This paper aims to fill this gap by characterizing the attitudes and concerns of Malaysian MSM regarding HIV prevention mobile apps, particularly on ethical aspects surrounding their use. METHODS We conducted online focus group discussions (FGDs) with 23 MSM between August and September 2021. Using in-depth semi-structured interviews, participants were asked about the risks and ethical issues they perceived to be associated with using mobile apps for HIV prevention. Each session was digitally recorded and transcribed. Transcripts were inductively coded using Dedoose software and analyzed to identify and interpret emerging themes. RESULTS Although participants had a high willingness to use app-based strategies for HIV prevention efforts, they raised several ethical concerns related to their use. Prominent concerns raised by participants included privacy and confidentiality concerns, including fear of third-party access to personal health information (e.g., friends or family, government agencies), issues around personal health data storage and management, equity and equitable access, informed consent, and regulation. CONCLUSIONS Study findings highlighted the role of ethical concerns related to the use of app-based HIV prevention programs. Given the ever-growing nature of such technological platforms that are intermixed with a complex ethical-legal landscape, mHealth platforms must be safe and secure to minimize unintended harms, safeguard user privacy and confidentiality, and obtain public trust and uptake. title: Ethical Natural Language Processing for Suicide Risk Support: A Framework with Real-World Evidence, Legal Constraints, and Deployment Safeguards
abstract: Author: Khan Tahsin Abrar, Independent Researcher, Bangladesh Email: khan.tahsin.abrar.kta@gmail.com Abstract Natural language processing (NLP) and transformer-based models have shown strong performance for identifying suicide-related language in social media and clinical contexts, but ethical, legal, and methodological constraints limit their responsible use. This paper synthesizes validated findings on linguistic markers and model performance, highlights known limitations in generalization and fairness, and consolidates current regulatory positions that restrict emotion inference and algorithmic discrimination risks in non-clinical contexts. Grounded in the Belmont principles, Respect for Persons, Beneficence, and Justice, this work proposes a deployment framework limited to consent-based, clinician-supervised, assistive use for suicide-risk support, with explicit exclusions for hiring, border/immigration, and educational decision-making. The framework details governance (IRB considerations when applicable), data collection with informed consent, privacy by design, fairness evaluation with subgroup reporting, external validation, calibration, and human-in-the-loop escalation protocols. The paper aligns reporting to SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI guidance for AI interventions, emphasizing transparency on algorithm versions, inputs/outputs, error analysis, and human–AI interaction. A case study illustrates an ethically compliant counseling-center integration. The conclusion offers a practical path for responsible NLP use in suicide prevention that maximizes benefit and minimizes harm without resorting to covert profiling or prohibited emotion analytics.Keywords: natural language processing; suicide prevention; ethics; Belmont Report; fairness; SPIRIT-AI; CONSORT-AI; privacy-by-designIntroduction Suicide remains a global public health challenge, motivating the exploration of NLP methods to identify suicide ideation in digital text for early support and clinical referral. Multiple studies report high discrimination from transformer-based architectures on labeled social media datasets, with reported accuracies sometimes exceeding 95–98% on specific tasks and datasets (Lin et al., 2024; Levkovich et al., 2024; IEEE studies in 2024). However, reported metrics vary widely by dataset, label definitions, and task framing, and findings frequently depend on platform-specific data, which limits generalization (Lin et al., 2024; Levkovich et al., 2024).Concurrently, legal and regulatory guidance has tightened around emotion inference and algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes contexts: the European Union AI Act prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and educational settings except under narrow exceptions; the UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has warned that biometric emotion analysis is immature and discriminatory; and the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has cautioned that AI used in hiring can cause unlawful disparate impact (EU AI Act; ICO; EEOC guidance). These developments rule out many proposed “covert” profiling uses and underscore an ethical focus on transparent, consent-based, clinician-supervised support.This paper integrates technical evidence on suicide-risk NLP, ethical and legal constraints, and rigorous deployment practices into a cohesive framework for responsible use, explicitly excluding covert profiling, deception detection, and non-clinical high-stakes decisions. It offers a practical blueprint for assistive, consented, clinically overseen deployment aligned with AI reporting standards.2. Evidence on Linguistic Markers and Model Performance 2.1 Linguistic correlates of suicide risk Empirical studies consistently associate suicide-risk language with increased use of first-person singular pronouns and negative affect, along with markers such as authenticity, clout, and negation (Homan et al., 2022; Lao et al., 2022). Earlier corpus analyses of suicide notes and literary corpora using LIWC and related methods observed elevated first-person singular usage among suicidal authors versus controls, supporting the interpretability of these markers as features but not as standalone diagnostic signals (Homan et al., 2022; Lao et al., 2022).2.2 Transformer performance and dataset effects Recent evaluations report high performance of BERT-family models on suicide-related classification tasks in social media:Lin et al. (2024) reported mean accuracy near 98% for a RoBERTa-CNN approach on a SuicideWatch dataset, highlighting strong sensitivity to data quality pre-processing steps (PMID: 40039081).IEEE 2024 studies have reported accuracies in the 97–99% range for transformer variants on curated Twitter/Reddit datasets for suicide ideation classification (IEEE Xplore items in 2024; see Suicide Detection in Tweets Using LSTM and Transformers, 2024).Systematic reviews synthesize variability across datasets and tasks, noting high F1 scores in some contexts but also reductions when confronting ambiguity and domain shifts (Levkovich et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024 in review tables).These results demonstrate feasibility in benchmarked settings but also show that performance depends on dataset curation, label scope (for example, ideation vs. intent vs. crisis), and platform or language domain (Levkovich et al., 2024). External validation on independent cohorts, calibration testing, and subgroup fairness evaluation remain necessary before clinical claims.2.3 Validated clinical screeners for context and integration For triangulation with clinical practice, validated screeners such as PHQ‑9 and GAD‑7 have widely replicated sensitivity and specificity around commonly used thresholds, PHQ‑9 ≥ 10 for depression and GAD‑7 ≥ 10 for anxiety, often achieving sensitivity/specificity above 80% (Wright‑Berryman et al., 2023, summarizing Kroenke and Spitzer validations). Recent LMIC validation (Cambodia) found strong correlations of PHQ‑9 and GAD‑7 with criterion instruments (HSCL‑25 and HTQ), reinforcing their utility as clinical references in diverse contexts (Steinman et al., 2025). NLP tools should be positioned as adjunctive aids, not replacements for validated clinical instruments.3. Limits of Trait Inference and Discredited Voice Stress Analytics Attempts to infer stable traits like age or generation from text are error-prone and topic-sensitive, with substantial misclassification documented in sociolinguistic studies, undermining reliability for individual-level inference (Coppersmith et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2014/2017 streams summarized in Why Gender and Age Prediction from Tweets is Hard). Voice-stress and micro-tremor deception detection has repeatedly failed rigorous validation, including field tests showing near-chance detection rates, and is not a scientifically reliable basis for high-stakes assessment (NIJ, 2008; legal/forensic reviews). These findings reinforce the prohibition on covert profiling, deception detection, or “mind reading” claims.Legal and Regulatory ConstraintsEU AI Act Article 5 prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and education settings with narrow exceptions tied to safety/medical contexts and strict safeguards.UK ICO has publicly warned that biometric emotion analysis is immature, discriminatory, and often pseudo-scientific, urging organizations to avoid deployment absent robust evidence.U.S. EEOC guidance on AI in hiring stresses Title VII liability for disparate impact and the need for validation, auditing, and fairness documentation. Collectively, these norms exclude covert profiling and high-stakes non-clinical applications (employment, education, border/immigration, insurance). Consent-based, clinician-supervised, assistive use in health contexts remains the ethically defensible scope.Ethical Framework Grounded in Belmont Respect for Persons requires explicit informed consent, clear disclosures about purposes, risks, retention, and opt-out/withdrawal rights, plus extra protections for vulnerable populations. Beneficence requires demonstrable benefit, false-positive harm mitigation, crisis-response protocols, and continuous monitoring. Justice requires equitable data representation, subgroup performance reporting, and deployment designs that do not exacerbate disparities. Methods and Governance for Responsible Deployment 6.1 Scope and prohibitions Permitted: voluntary screening with explicit consent; clinician decision support in mental health care; crisis hotline augmentation; IRB-approved research with full disclosures. Prohibited: hiring/employment screening; admissions/performance decisions in education; border/immigration triage; insurance underwriting; covert surveillance; deception detection or biometric “emotion analysis” in regulated settings.6.2 Data collection, consent, and privacy-by-designConsent: task-specific, plain-language disclosures on purpose, data uses, retention/deletion, and withdrawal rights.De-identification: remove direct/indirect identifiers; manage stylometric re-identification risks; consider differential privacy, k-anonymity, or secure computation where applicable.Governance: role-based access controls; data minimization; segregation of research and operational environments; audit logging.6.3 Model development and validationValidation: use temporal and demographic-aware splits; perform external validation on independent cohorts; test calibration so predicted probabilities track observed risk.Fairness: report performance by protected subgroups; evaluate group fairness metrics (for example, demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity) where relevant to deployment; conduct disparate-impact audits.Transparency: document algorithm version, inputs/outputs, error analysis, and human–AI interaction design.6.4 Clinical integration and human oversightHuman-in-the-loop: route alerts only to licensed clinicians; require human confirmation before action; maintain override controls.Crisis protocols: immediate escalation procedures for high-risk outputs; minimize distress from false positives via confirmatory assessment and supportive communication.Monitoring: longitudinal tracking of outcomes (engagement, crisis events), model drift detection, and scheduled revalidation.6.5 Reporting standards (SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI) For interventional studies, SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI require explicit reporting of algorithm versions, settings and users, handling of input/output data, human–AI interaction, and error analysis; adherence improves transparency and reduces bias risks (Liu et al., 2020; Cruz Rivera et al., 2020; Martindale et al., 2024).Case Study: Counseling Center Implementation Setting: A university counseling center offers opt-in, consented text analysis to support early identification of suicide risk. Governance: Institutional approvals as applicable; clear privacy notices; community advisory participation. Operations: Alerts visible only to licensed counselors; clinician override; calibration checks; subgroup performance monitoring; periodic audits and updates. Evaluation: Clinical outcomes (for example, improved engagement), user trust, subgroup performance, adherence to crisis protocols, and transparency reports.Discussion: Challenges and Research PrioritiesGeneralization: Cross-cultural and multilingual adaptation remains a major challenge; external validation on diverse cohorts is essential.Temporal drift: Language and platform norms evolve; ongoing monitoring and periodic retraining are needed.Ambiguity and context: Differentiating ideation from non-risk usage requires context-sensitive models and human review.Adversarial use: Systems require abuse monitoring and resilience testing.Trials and impact: Prospective evaluations of NLP-supported interventions should follow SPIRIT-AI/CONSORT-AI to quantify patient-centered benefits and harms.Participatory design: Engaging affected communities and clinicians improves acceptability, trust, and equity.Conclusions Ethical NLP for suicide-risk support is feasible when constrained to consent-based, clinician-supervised, assistive use with robust governance. title: Ethical Proof-Carrying Causal Answers on CLadder
venue: 2025 IEEE/WIC International Conference on Web Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology (WI-IAT)
abstract: Ethical, inclusive, and human-centered AI requires not only accurate models but also methods that are reproducible, resource-conscious, and accountable to the people affected by their outputs. In causal reasoning, multi-agent collaboration has been promoted as a route to reliability; however, its ethical profile is unclear once we account for cost, transparency, and the risk of over-claiming. We revisit the CLadder [21] benchmark proposed to test whether LLMs causal reasoning capability and make two contributions aligned with the aims of EthicAI 2025 (privacy, fairness, sustainability, unlearning, and domain ethics). First, we provide a paired, cost-aware comparison of five prompting strategies-vanilla, simple Chain-of-Thought (CoT), guided CoT, Self-consistency [22], and a multi-agent system-evaluated on a test set. With phi-4, CoT reaches 78.20% (95% CI: 74.37-81.60%), while multi-agent variants achieve 76.80% (72.90-$\mathbf{8 0. 2 9 \%})$ and $\mathbf{7 7. 5 6 \%}(\mathbf{7 3. 7 4 - 8 1. 0 4 \%})$ with $\mathbf{0. 8 3} \times$ and $\mathbf{1 0. 3 5} \times$ slower latency; These results indicate that, on this task, multi-agent collaboration adds compute and latency without commensurate benefit-a sustainability and inclusivity concern for groups with limited resources. Second, we introduce Proof-Carrying Causal Answers (PCCA), a Fast/Slow scheduler that attaches verifiable certificates to answers (backdoor/frontdoor checks; minimal twin/SWIG for counterfactuals) and invokes a bounded falsifier when confidence is low. PCCA is designed to improve the Certified-Answer Rate while constraining cost, and it produces auditable evidence that supports privacy-conscious workflows and targeted unlearning: certificates and logs allow specific items to be re-run and re-certified without repeating full experiments. We discuss ethical implications for decision-making in safety-critical domains (robotics, wearables, healthcare), where unverifiable causal claims can impose real-world harms. By linking causal identification to verifiable computation, PCCA turns moral principles-sustainability, accountability, and epistemic responsibility-into measurable engineering constraints. Overall, our findings argue for responsible causal AI by default: start simple, measure cost, certify or falsify claims, and escalate orchestration only when evidence justifies the added burden.

title: Ethical and Practical Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Assistive Technologies: Challenges, Opportunities, and Inclusive Development
venue: International Journal of Engineering and Management Research
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in assistive technologies, significantly enhancing accessibility, autonomy, and quality of life for individuals with disabilities. AI-powered systems such as wearable navigation devices, speech recognition tools, smart prosthetics, and intelligent monitoring systems offer substantial benefits for visually impaired and differently-abled users. However, these advancements also introduce ethical concerns including privacy risks, algorithmic bias, transparency limitations, and accountability challenges. Practical barriers such as affordability, infrastructure limitations, and accessibility disparities further affect widespread implementation, particularly in developing nations like India. This conceptual paper critically examines the ethical and practical implications of AI in assistive technologies and emphasizes the importance of inclusive design, equitable deployment, and transparent governance frameworks. The study contributes to the broader discourse on sustainable and socially responsible AI integration.

title: Ethical considerations in digital biomarker adoption
abstract: Abstract Background Digital biomarkers (DBM) explain and/or predict health outcomes by taking advantage of the advancements in digital technologies and analytics. However, while DBMs offer promising opportunities for research by enabling frequent, remote, real‐time and objective assessments at scale they also raise ethical challenges. Despite growing recognition of these issues, practical guidelines remain scarce. To bridge this gap, we adopt a case study approach by drawing on the ethical challenges encountered in the RADAR‐AD (Remote Assessment of Disease and Relapse – Alzheimer's Disease) project. Method RADAR‐AD is a cross‐sectional observational study (N = 237) aiming to find and validate remote monitoring technologies to assess cognitive and functional decline in AD. For up to eight weeks, we employed a range of digital technologies, including smartphone apps, wearables and at‐home sensors. This case study addresses two key areas surrounding 1) the ensurance of respect for participants across the research process, and 2) feedback of results and sustainability. By reflecting on the lessons learned in RADAR‐AD, we provide practical recommendations to enhance ethical conduct in DBM research. Result The first key area suggests a participatory approach by exploring participants’ needs and concerns in focus groups and involving a patient advisory board (PAB): 1) Informed consent: Explaining the complexities of digital data collection/analysis/storage while engaging large numbers of participants; 2) Burden: Balancing privacy, burden and accessibility during long‐term data collection and offering protocol flexibility; 3) Assistance without being too controlling: Combining phone calls with remote technical checks. The second key area focuses on 1) Feedback of results: Providing consumer‐grade feedback improves adherence and sense of security and reduces risk of harm; 2) Sustainability: Increasing translation from research to clinical implications by seeking regulatory advice, taking successful results forward to explore in future projects, and sharing data to promote further research. However, contributing tangible results to the healthcare system even after research funding has ended remains a significant challenge. Conclusion The RADAR‐AD study provides an exemplary case study highlighting key challenges associated with DBM research and offering valuable insights into ethical considerations that should accompany DBM research from study conception to sustainability efforts.
