abstract: The weight-loss technique of one smartphone application (app) consisted of holding a vibrating phone against the user's body to melt away fat cells. Another app offered advice on using reflexology and hypnosis to treat prostate cancer. A third missed more than 9 of 10 melanoma cases on the basis of uploaded pictures. By 2018, according to an estimate cited by the US Food and Drug Administration, half of the world's more than 3.4 billion smartphone and tablet users will have downloaded mobile health apps. Amid the glut of new consumer options, including highly questionable ones related to cancer, oversight has extended to only a sliver. “It's a little bit of the wild, wild west when it comes to apps out there,” says Karen Basen-Engquist, PhD, MPH, professor of behavioral science and director of the MD Anderson Center for Energy Balance in Cancer Prevention and Survivorship in Houston, Texas. “It's a ‘Let the buyer beware’ sort of environment.” In its most recent guidance, issued in 2015, the FDA asserted oversight over any mobile app that meets the definition of a medical device under existing regulations and may pose a risk to patient safety “if the mobile app were to not function as intended.” The list of “mobile medical apps” aimed primarily at physicians and other providers includes those that rely on built-in features or attached sensors or electrodes to perform medical functions. The agency has exercised more limited enforcement discretion over a separate list of apps, such as those used to help diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease or condition. This sprawling category as well as another class of informational apps includes a host of free and paid options geared more toward consumers. The few independent studies to examine the evidence underlying cancerrelated apps in these latter 2 categories have found a troubling mix of good and bad. In January 2016, a group of Spanish researchers published a study in which they searched for the terms cancer and oncology in both English and Spanish in apps on the Apple iOS and Google Android smartphone platforms.1 The study concluded that only half of 166 apps marketed to cancer patients presented “sufficient scientific evidence” and that slightly more than half had upgraded their software within the preceding year. A more tightly focused 2013 study of 4 skin cancer detection apps marketed to consumers found that the 3 offering automated detection were all exceedingly inaccurate.2 “You could upload a photo and it would give you immediate feedback,” says Laura Ferris, MD, a dermatologist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in Pennsylvania and the critique's senior author. “None of them were backed up by clinical trials; none of them were backed up by data. They were just somebody's claims.” When tested on 188 moles (60 of which were cancerous according to a histologic diagnosis), the best of the automated detection apps missed 30% of the melanomas, whereas the worst missed a stunning 93% of them. For patients, a flaw of such magnitude can carry dire consequences. Melanoma can be successfully and easily removed but only if it is caught early enough. “You could miss that window of opportunity to have a curable cancer detected and treated because an app told you to wait,” Dr. Ferris says. The fourth app gave her more hope. Like its counterparts, it allowed users to upload pictures of moles, lesions, or freckles. However, instead of an instantaneous verdict via an automated system, it sent the images to a board-certified dermatologist for the final call. The result? It missed only 1 melanoma for a sensitivity of 98%. After Dr. Ferris's study appeared, offi- cials from the Federal Trade Commission asked about her research methods. Two years later, the Federal Trade Commission fined the makers of Mole Detective and Mel App for claiming to determine the relative risk of melanoma on the basis of user-uploaded pictures (the companies now say that the apps are for “educational purposes” only). In 2012, another group of researchers led by hematologist-oncologist Daniel Landau, MD, now at the UF Health Cancer Center at Orlando Health in Florida, analyzed the quality of information contained in the first 18 iPhone apps retrieved with the search terms prostate and cancer. As the researchers described in an abstract published in conjunction with the annual American Society of Clinical Oncology conference, all of the free apps provided evidence-based information. Two paid apps geared toward patients, however, offered more questionable information, including diet advice to prevent cancer and ‘alternative therapies’ including reflexology and hypnosis. “It's a little bit of the wild, wild west when it comes to apps out there. It's a ‘Let the buyer beware’ sort of environment.” —Karen Basen-Engquist, PhD, MPH A 2015 follow-up, again led by Dr. Landau, analyzed 65 iPhone apps that met the same search criteria. Only 5 of the apps studied in 2012 were even still available. Again, the researchers concluded that the free apps offered appropriate information, whereas 3 of the patientfocused paid apps lacked solid evidence for their supportive care claims. Despite the increased attention on the potential pitfalls of smartphone apps, Dr. Ferris says that a good system has yet to be put in place to vet those that fall beyond the FDA's purview. “Anybody can make an app,” she says. “I think there's a lot that needs to be done from a regulatory perspective.” “I don't believe the apps should be ‘regulated’ per se, but I do think apps that provide evidencebased data should have something attached to them that indicates they are based on said evidence with an explanation about what that means. —Daniel Landau, MD Other clinicians are more ambivalent. “I don't believe the apps should be ‘regulated’ per se,” Dr. Landau says. “But I do think apps that provide evidence-based data should have something attached to them that indicates they are based on said evidence with an explanation about what that means.” If they're not evidence-based, he says, the apps should carry a disclaimer. Who should play the sheriff? “I don't believe the FDA should be the one to enforce this,” Dr. Landau says, adding that the Apple or Android developers could perhaps do so instead. Dr. Basen- Engquist is likewise doubtful about further federal intervention. “I don't know if I would see regulation by the FDA as really the answer,” she says. On the other hand, she has been “astounded” by the audacity of the claims of some apps, including one that purported to help patients lose weight via phone vibrations. “The app store isn't screening for this at all,” she says. Instead, Dr. Basen-Engquist says, “I think it would be great if we could see some of the professional organizations get involved with providing some app reviews.” Such health and medical organizations, she suggested, might establish an endorsement or certification process for apps that meet certain criteria. In the meantime, cancer centers such as The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and the Dana- Farber Cancer Institute in Boston have curated their own lists of recommended apps. Dr. Basen-Engquist, who made some recommendations for MD Anderson's “41 Apps to Help Prevent Cancer” list, says that she looks for accurate, reliable, and accessible information as well as evidence-based techniques to help change behavior. After Dr. Ferris's study appeared, several app makers stopped making claims, whereas others published their own studies on how well they worked. Both are encouraging steps, she says. If they provide helpful and accurate information without directing a patient to take specific steps in the absence of a physician's input, she says, smartphone apps may yet prove their mettle. Letting patients take photographs of their own skin lesions or other suspicious marks and send them to medical providers, for example, can help clinicians decide who needs to be seen sooner rather than later. App-aided mole mapping can also provide a photographic checklist of whether and how a mark is changing or a skin “diary” that patients can bring to a doctor's attention. Dr. Basen-Engquist is likewise optimistic that cancer-related apps can improve and expand on their potential by tailoring feedback and information to individual users and keeping those users highly engaged. Getting to that point, though, may require closer collaborations between app developers who have the technical knowhow and health and medical researchers who have the necessary evidence. “I think that there are a lot of apps that do the things that are easy,” she says. “And we need to figure out how to get apps to do some of the things that are harder.”

title: From Accommodation to Obligation: Rethinking Menstrual Access Through Disability Law Frameworks
From Clinics to Wearables: Secure and Efficient Diabetes Prediction with Federated Ensemble Learning Across Heterogeneous Healthcare Systems (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Diabetes prediction requires accurate, privacy-preserving, and scalable solutions. Traditional machine learning models rely on centralized data, posing risks to data privacy and regulatory compliance. Moreover, healthcare settings are highly heterogeneous, with diverse participants, hospitals, clinics, and wearables, producing non-IID data and operating under varied computational constraints. Learning in isolation at individual institutions limits model generalizability and effectiveness. Collaborative federated learning enables institutions to jointly train models without sharing raw data, but current approaches often struggle with heterogeneity, security threats, and system coordination. OBJECTIVE This study aims to develop a secure, scalable, and privacy-preserving framework for diabetes prediction by integrating federated learning with ensemble modeling, blockchain-based access control, and knowledge distillation. The framework is designed to handle data heterogeneity, non-IID distributions, and varying computational capacities across diverse healthcare participants, while simultaneously enhancing data privacy, security, and trust. METHODS We propose a Federated Ensemble Learning framework, FedEnTrust, that enables decentralized healthcare participants to collaboratively train models without sharing raw data. Each participant shares soft label outputs, which are distilled and aggregated through adaptive weighted voting to form a global consensus. The framework supports heterogeneous participants by assigning model architectures based on local computational capacity. To ensure secure and transparent coordination, a blockchain-enabled smart contract governs participant registration, role assignment, and model submission with strict role-based access control. We evaluated the system on the PIMA Indians Diabetes Dataset, measuring prediction accuracy, communication efficiency, and blockchain performance. RESULTS The FedEnTrust framework achieved 84.2% accuracy, with precision, recall, and F1-score of 84.6%, 88.6%, and 86.4%, respectively, outperforming existing decentralized models and nearing centralized deep learning benchmarks. The blockchain-based smart contract ensured 100% success for authorized transactions and rejected all unauthorized attempts, including malicious submissions. Average blockchain latency was 210 milliseconds, with a gas cost of ~107,940 units, enabling secure, real-time interaction. Throughout, patient privacy was preserved by exchanging only model metadata, not raw data. CONCLUSIONS FedEnTrust offers a deployable, privacy-preserving solution for decentralized healthcare prediction by integrating federated learning, ensemble modeling, blockchain-based access control, and knowledge distillation. It balances accuracy, scalability, and ethical data use while enhancing security and trust. This work demonstrates that secure federated ensemble systems can serve as practical alternatives to centralized AI models in real-world healthcare applications.

title: From Coordinates to Context: An LLM-Bootstrapped Semantic Encoding Framework for Privacy-Preserving Mobile Sensing Stress Recognition
abstract: Psychological stress is a widespread issue that significantly impacts student well-being and academic performance. Effective remote stress recognition is crucial, yet existing methods often rely on wearable devices or GPS-based clustering techniques that pose privacy risks and lack of human understandable explanations. In this study, we introduce a novel, end-to-end privacy-enhanced framework for semantic location encoding using a self-hosted OSM engine and an LLM-bootstrapped static map for human-friendly feature extraction, and pave a pathway for privacy-aware location data transformation for dataset sharing. We rigorously quantify the privacy-utility-explainability trilemma and demonstrate (via LOSO validation) that our Privacy-Aware (PA) model achieves robust privacy protection without being statistically distinguishable in stress recognition performance from a non-private model. Model explanation analysis highlights that our extracted features, which are user-friendly features, match with psychological literature about stress. In addition, an ablation study on the GeoLife dataset also demonstrates that our privacy framework improves privacy by 2-3 times compared to a non-privacy-aware approach. This suggests that our system can be utilized for the next generation of GPS transformations in open-source datasets for future researchers.

title: From Cyberbullying to Chronic Stress: AI-Driven Approaches for Identifying Abuse and Its Consequences
abstract: The pervasive nature of digital communication has inadvertently amplified the incidence of online abuse, particularly cyberbullying, which poses significant threats to mental health. This paper provides a comprehensive review of **AI-driven approaches for identifying online abuse** and its profound **consequences on human well-being, specifically chronic stress, anxiety, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)**. We survey a diverse array of AI models, including traditional machine learning, deep learning, and large language models (LLMs), employed for abuse detection across various digital channels. Furthermore, we explore the clinical and behavioral evidence linking exposure to online abuse with adverse psychological outcomes, delving into the neurobiological mechanisms underpinning stress responses. The paper also examines contemporary **stress detection frameworks utilizing healthcare and wearable technologies**, highlighting their potential to measure abuse-related physiological and psychological strain. We critically analyze the interdisciplinary challenges inherent in this domain, encompassing **data privacy, ethical considerations, and the imperative of explainability** in AI systems. Finally, we propose **future directions for developing integrated abuse-stress monitoring systems**, advocating for a holistic approach to safeguarding digital well-being.

title: From Digital Care to Privacy Anxiety: A Communication Perspective on Human–Computer Interaction Ethics in the Xiaohongshu App
venue: Advances in information management and economic development research.
abstract: In today’s platform-driven, data-rich digital environment, women’s health apps have become central to everyday health communication and bodily tracking. Using Xiaohongshu as a case, this paper examines a key paradox: a tool promoted as “digital care” — providing scientific information, personalized services, and community support to reduce uncertainty and anxiety — can, through its specific HCI design and algorithmic operations, instead intensify women’s health anxiety and privacy concerns. In doing so, it reshapes information asymmetries, users’ control over data, and trust in platform–user relationships. Building on health communication, emotion communication, and platform studies, and engaging debates on algorithmic governance and data justice, there are two concepts which has: “algorithmic perception” and “privacy perception.” The researcher attempts to ask how women, in actual use, interpret interface cues such as data forms, notifications, consent requests, and tracking reminders, and how they imagine algorithmic influence on visibility, agenda priority, risk framing, emotional experience, and data security. Under conditions of limited algorithmic transparency and weak data control, this study examine how they respond by adjusting routines, avoiding features, or accommodating the app’s demands. Methodologically, this paper relies on semi-structured interviews with long-term users (3+ years). These interviews trace participants’ information pathways and probe their understandings of algorithms and data collection, perceived risks and fairness, and their emotional and trust-related experiences around both health and privacy. The analysis identifies three algorithmic mechanisms that jointly fuel anxiety and privacy risks: (1) personalization that creates “filter bubbles” of negative health content; (2) data-driven “ideal body” and “ideal fertility” norms that encourage comparison and self-discipline; and (3) commercial targeting coupled with medicalized narratives that turn ordinary bodily experiences into monetizable “potential risks.” This study situates women’s health apps within wider debates on digital culture, HCI ethics, and data justice.

title: From Intelligent Football to Human–Machine Collaboration: Evolution, Applications, and Governance Challenges of Football Intelligentization Systems in the World Cup Era
abstract: From Intelligent Football to Human–Machine Collaboration: Evolution, Applications, and Governance Challenges of Football Intelligentization Systems in the World Cup Era Detailed Project Description This research project is a comprehensive narrative review that systematically examines the rapid intelligentization of association football, with particular focus on technologies showcased and accelerated by major international tournaments such as the FIFA World Cup. The work addresses a critical gap in the existing literature: while numerous studies investigate isolated tools (e.g., Video Assistant Referee systems, electronic performance and tracking systems, or AI-based tactical analytics), few provide an integrated, systems-level account of how multi-source data fusion is transforming the sport from passive recording toward real-time human–AI collaboration. Purpose The primary purpose is threefold: To map the evolutionary trajectory of core intelligent football technologies—especially the transition of the match ball from a passive physical implement into a high-frequency real-time sensing node (IMU/UWB-equipped “Connected Ball”), the maturation of semi-automated offside technology, and the integration of wearable physiological monitoring with computer-vision and graph-neural-network analytics. To construct a unified conceptual framework spanning “data acquisition → intelligent analytics → decision support,” thereby clarifying the operational mechanisms that enable human–machine collaborative adjudication, athlete load management, and tactical behavior modeling. To critically interrogate the accompanying governance, ethical, and equity challenges that arise when artificial intelligence penetrates high-stakes competitive environments. By synthesizing interdisciplinary evidence from sports science, computer vision, sensor engineering, and technology ethics, the project aims to move beyond fragmented technological descriptions toward a coherent theoretical and practical understanding of intelligent football as a socio-technical system. Methods Following established narrative-review guidelines, literature was systematically searched across Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and CNKI, supplemented by authoritative technical reports, validation protocols, and regulatory documents issued by FIFA, IFAB, and leading industry vendors (e.g., Kinexon, Adidas). Search terms centered on smart football, video assistant referee, semi-automated offside technology, athlete load monitoring, and tactical intelligence analysis, with emphasis on the past decade of accelerated AI–sensor convergence. Extracted material was conceptually integrated into a multi-tiered analytical architecture covering data acquisition, algorithmic processing, decision support, and governance optimization. Key Components and Expected Outcomes The project organizes findings around three primary application domains and a cross-cutting governance analysis: Smart Football as Real-Time Sensing Node Documents the engineering realization of center-suspended IMU/UWB modules capable of 500 Hz telemetry, the generation of continuous digital twins of ball kinematics, and the residual measurement uncertainties under extreme impact conditions. Expected outcome: a clear technical baseline and validation-transparency recommendations for future independent scientific scrutiny. Human–AI Collaborative Officiating Formalizes a three-layer “ball–player–video” framework in which smart-ball timestamps serve as deterministic temporal anchors for SAOT skeletal tracking and AI-generated advisory recommendations, while human officials retain final contextual authority. Expected outcome: an operational model that reduces review latency (to ~25 s on average) while preserving the humanistic core of the game, together with explicit warnings against “spurious precision” and automation bias. Athlete Physiological Profiling and Tactical Analytics Synthesizes external/internal load monitoring, AI-driven fatigue and injury-risk modeling, graph-neural-network analysis of passing topologies, Expected Threat (xT) quantification, and reinforcement-learning counterfactual simulation. Expected outcome: evidence-based closed-loop frameworks for training titration and tactical decision support, tempered by critical appraisal of low positive-predictive values and “on-ball bias” limitations in current models. Governance Challenges Identifies three pressing systemic issues: (1) algorithmic opacity and the need to open the “black box” for explainability; (2) privacy boundaries and ownership rights over deep biometric telemetry and player digital twins; and (3) capital barriers that risk widening the global digital divide between elite and resource-scarce competitions. Expected outcome: concrete policy-oriented recommendations for standardized data certification, privacy safeguards, and technological inclusivity. Anticipated Impact Upon completion and dissemination (via open-access publication and OSF registration), the project is expected to: Provide researchers, governing bodies, and practitioners with an integrated reference architecture for intelligent football systems. Stimulate further empirical validation studies that address current proprietary opacity. Inform ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks that ensure technology enhances rather than supplants human judgment and competitive fairness. Contribute to the broader discourse on responsible AI adoption in high-stakes sports environments. The work positions intelligent football not as a trajectory toward machine substitution, but as a progressive paradigm of human–AI collaboration that prioritizes competitive integrity, athlete safety, and equitable access. All findings, conceptual diagrams, and synthesized tables will be made openly available through this OSF project to facilitate reuse, critique, and extension by the international sports-science and technology-ethics communities.

title: From Reviews to Requirements: Can LLMs Generate Human-Like User Stories?
abstract: App store reviews provide a constant flow of real user feedback that can help improve software requirements. However, these reviews are often messy, informal, and difficult to analyze manually at scale. Although automated techniques exist, many do not perform well when replicated and often fail to produce clean, backlog-ready user stories for agile projects. In this study, we evaluate how well large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3.5 Turbo, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Mistral 7B Instruct can generate usable user stories directly from raw app reviews. Using the Mini-BAR dataset of 1,000+ health app reviews, we tested zero-shot, one-shot, and two-shot prompting methods. We evaluated the generated user stories using both human judgment (via the RUST framework) and a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned on UStAI to assess their overall quality. Our results show that LLMs can match or even outperform humans in writing fluent, well-formatted user stories, especially when few-shot prompts are used. However, they still struggle to produce independent and unique user stories, which are essential for building a strong agile backlog. Overall, our findings show how LLMs can reliably turn unstructured app reviews into actionable software requirements, providing developers with clear guidance to turn user feedback into meaningful improvements.

title: From Wellness to Worrisome:Mining Online Voices on the Dark Side of Wearable Health Technologies
venue: University of Birmingham Research Portal (University of Birmingham)
abstract: As wellness technologies become increasingly embedded in consumers’ everyday lives, wearable brands are positioning themselves as partners in health and self-improvement. Yet, user-generated discourse has revealed that digital feedback can also provoke feelings of anxiety, guilt, and distrust. This study examines the darker aspects of wellness tech by analysing 3,194 Reddit posts and 126,000 comments concerning leading health-tracking devices. Using an LLM-enhanced BERTopic pipeline, we identify fourteen detrimental topics, encompassing a spectrum of concerns ranging from data reliability frustration and sleep score obsession to privacy concerns and compulsive self-monitoring. Results show how technical frictions and feedback design choices can escalate into affective strain and negative word-of-mouth. By “listening to the crowd,” this research introduces a scalable social-listening framework for detecting consumer well-being risks and emerging reputational threats. The findings highlight the importance of responsible feedback design and empathetic communication in digital marketing strategies for wearable and health-tech brands.

title: From Zero-Shot to Fine-Tuning: Classifying Privacy Policies with LLMs
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems

title: From integrated care towards DIY Health – Combining person-centered health care delivery, mobile technology and entrepreneurship
abstract: Introduction and objectives: To achieve the level of impact necessary to reverse current trends of rising incidence and costs of multimorbidity and enabling healthy ageing will require new health care policy and practices. Notwithstanding integrated care receiving worldwide attention in improving healthcare delivery, the value of data driven and mobile technology for integration of health and care services remains unclear. Nevertheless, person-centered and data driven mobile health (mHealth) has the potential to evolve integrated care from business process re-design towards a new digital health ecosystem that is truly centered around a person facing health challenges. The objective of our study was to identify the opportunities and barriers of mHealth to do this. Highlights: MHealth applications attack the underlying causes of the multimorbidity and ageing challenge in various ways. First, mHealth lifestyle apps promise to help in the prevention of chronic disease and multimorbidity by attacking high risk conditions such as obesity and diabetes. Secondly, personalised care promised by participative mHealth apps will reduce reliance on expensive, institutionalised care by augmenting the effectiveness of treatments. Finally, mHealth apps could empower patients by facilitating remote care, self-medication, independent living and more. 15th International Conference on Integrated Care, Edinburgh, UK, March 25-27, 2015 1 International Journal of Integrated Care – Volume 15, 27 May – URN:NBN:NL:UI:10-1-116961 – http://www.ijic.org/ One of the major developments in mHealth for integrated care is that (new) entrants in the mHealth market focus more on patients and consumers than on medical professionals. This development has several benefits: First the emphasis on intuitive user interfaces, usability and immediate feedback by these parties seems more effective in nudging people to change towards desired behaviors than traditional (preventive) healthcare interventions. Furthermore, mHealth applications encourage self-monitoring and self-diagnosis, potentially reducing the number of hospital visits for purposes of monitoring and simple diagnoses. However, we see certain challenges. First and foremost, attention should be paid to manage sensitivity of health information by allowing more control over data-driven solutions by end-users and other stakeholders. Secure and dedicated data platforms for the health sector should govern the secure interconnection of health data components. Secondly, to create an effective learning ecosystem, new cross-disciplinary and collaborative research and innovation approaches are needed. These will help tackle technological, behavioral and institutional challenges. Finally, to stimulate the emergence and participation of mHealth entrepreneurs, any health data exchange initiative will need to prioritize access by startups and SMEs to fast track the required fundamental innovations in a traditional health sector. Conclusions: Our analysis shows that new, consumer-focused entrants have a high potential to stimulate person-centered coordinated care. Nevertheless, research and policy should find solutions for potential ‘showstoppers’, such as challenges in privacy, accountability and security. A learning ecosystem, which has to include new research and innovation models, may facilitate this. Another important aspect is to find ways to grant new entrants, in particular start-ups and SMEs, access to core health infrastructure and key data-sets.

title: Fts App: Towards Explainable AI-Driven Adaptive Weight Tracking
venue: SeGAH ... IEEE ... International Conference on Serious Games and Applications for Health/IEEE International Conference on Serious Games and Applications for Health
abstract: We present the FTS app, an adaptive weight management tracking application that integrates an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model, specifically designed for normal weight individuals who aim to maintain their current weight status. Weight maintenance requires consistent monitoring of calories consumed from food and those expended through exercise, a challenging task with conventional apps available on Play Store or App Store. The FTS app uniquely analyzes both food logs and daily steps to predict users' current weight. A key feature is its explainable AI framework that helps users understand why certain foods might trigger weight fluctuations and offer healthier alternatives. The system integrates two complementary models: (1) a ChatGPT-4 model and (2) the proprietary FTS- XAI model, both designed to classify foods as healthy or unhealthy while calculating caloric content to estimate the user's current weight. The app includes a built-in step counting module that tracks physical activity before meals, eliminating the need for expensive wearable devices and reducing privacy concerns related to thirdparty access. By combining these calorie metrics, the app automatically calculates the user's current weight and keeps them informed. This paper presents our design framework to guide the research community in addressing the needs of this predominantly overlooked population with weight maintenance goals.

title: Future Computing Technology (3/3)
venue: CERN Document Server (European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: <!--HTML-->Computing of the future will be affected by a number of fundamental technologies in development today, many of which are already on the way to becoming commercialized. In this series of lectures, we will discuss hardware and software development that will become mainstream in the timeframe of a few years and how they will shape or change the computing landscape - commercial and personal alike. Topics range from processor and memory aspects, programming models and the limits of artificial intelligence, up to end-user interaction with wearables or e-textiles. We discuss the impact of these technologies on the art of programming, the data centres of the future and daily life. On the third day of the Future Computing Technology series, we will touch on societal aspects of the future of computing. Our perception of computers may at time seem passive, but in reality we are a vital chain of the feedback loop. Human-computer interaction, innovative forms of computers, privacy, process automation, threats and medical applications will be discussed.

title: Future Trends and Innovation
abstract: The growth in technology is transforming the healthcare sector at a high speed. The research focuses on integrating the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain in the healthcare sector. The integration of these two techniques provides many facilities, but it also presents a lot of challenges. The challenges comprise healthcare data security and privacy, collection of medical data, storage of medical data, interoperability, scalability, and cost. IoT wearable devices allow for real-time data collection, remote monitoring, telemedicine, and operational efficiency. IoT devices are often exposed to cyber-attacks in such situations blockchain provides security and data integrity. The decentralized and immutable nature of blockchain provides improved security and integrity to patient data. The analysis of current trends and inventions helps in projecting future revolution in healthcare. The chapter delivers a broad overview of how IoT and blockchain technology could transform the healthcare industry.

title: Future of Virtual Assistance in Mental Wellness Support
abstract: The global mental health crisis, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has highlighted significant gaps in access to treatment, with over 970 million people affected worldwide. Barriers to accessing treatment such as workforce shortages, financial constraints, and stigma persist, particularly in low-income areas. Virtual assistants powered by artificial intelligence (AI) presents a promising solution to these barriers due to their features of scalability, cost-effectiveness solution. This article evaluates the effectiveness of virtual assistant in mental wellness support, their roles in enhancing accessibility and reducing stigma, and their applications such as self-guided therapy, workplace wellness programs, and integration with wearables. The article also discusses the key challenges arising from the adoption of virtual assistant in mental health support such as data privacy, lack of regulation, and potential harm underscore the need for ethical development and robust oversight. The article suggest that virtual assistant applications are a critical complement to traditional care rather that a substitute.

title: GPT Attack for Adversarial Privacy Policies
venue: International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom)
abstract: While Machine Learning (ML) is widely used in many industries, one sector that is just beginning to leverage this technology is the legal field. Efforts like the construction of the OPP-115 Privacy Policy corpus make it possible to train Natural Language Processing (NLP) and ML models for legal use, and tools such as Polisis, Claudette, etc., which utilize these models can now provide users with descriptive annotations of various types of contracts, including Privacy Policies. However, these tools remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, specifically adversarial legal documents, which differ from typical text based adversarial attacks due to the necessity of preserving the continuity of a legal document. Therefore, focusing on the OPP-115 corpus and Polisis specifically, we propose a framework that consists of a Doc2Vec model and a variety of shallow and deep learning methods for classification, followed by adversarial attacks on Privacy Policy segments which utilize GPT 3.5, a state-of-the-art LLM, in order to create an adversarial Privacy Policy. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method by comparing attack results to those produced by current methods, including Bert Attack and Text Fooler. Our procedure reveals not just that an attack using GPT 3.5 is an effective means of producing an adversarial policy, but that it is surprisingly easy to prompt a widely used state-of-the-art LLM to perform such a task.

title: GRP-20194 Can Mental Health Apps Really Help Caregivers? Usability Findings from Human-in-the-Loop NLP and Sentiment-Aware Analytics
venue: DigitalCommons - Kennesaw State University (Kennesaw State University)
abstract: Caregivers face distinctive emotional and logistical burdens, yet many mental-health apps overlook their needs and show usability issues. We introduce an automated pipeline that analyzes 317K app-store reviews from 9 apps, mapping them to Nielsen’s usability components and heuristics, together with sentiment. To assess reliability, we run a human–AI agreement study (N=50) where a domain expert (A2) and a non- expert (A1) label reviews. For heuristics, the pipeline achieves 66% exact agreement and moderate κ=0.579 with the expert, outperforming human–human agreement; components remain harder, revealing a need to refine the codebook (e.g., learnability vs satisfaction). Complementary clustering and sentiment analyses highlight recurrent issues such as interface overload and inaccessible onboarding, positioning our pipeline as a pre-annotation aid for evidence-driven app evaluation.

title: General data protection regulation compliance at SMEs: guideline, incident response methodology, information security controls, and case company evaluation
abstract:
A multitude of small and middle enterprises are struggling to attain compliance with the General data protection regulation (GDPR) and it can be a challenge for companies to comprehend all the legal requirements. The purpose of the thesis was to help organizations understand the requirements of the Regulation, how data breach notification should be processed, and how to resist the incidence of data leakages caused by staff errors. The aim of the thesis was to create a GDPR guideline, GDPR personal data breach notification plan and form, to discover what are the most important information security controls regarding data leakages caused by staff errors; also, based on the research results, to evaluate the case company to encourage further development of information security system. 
 
This work used the General data protection regulation as the main source of information to build a knowledge base for the thesis. Legal literature was used to define what compliance is, what are the stages of regulatory compliance development, and how compliance can be developed in organizations. Professional literature and research articles were reviewed on 
such themes as information security management, risk management, and incident management, particularly ISO/IEC 27005 standard of 2018 and National Institute of Standards and Technology publications. InfoWatch report was examined to find information security controls that can consolidate the information security system of a company against most common data leakage types caused by staff errors. 
 
To answer the research questions a thematic analysis of theoretical framework was used to create a simple structure for a guideline, data breach notification plan and form, and to find the most important information security controls against data leakages caused by staff errors. To construct a complete picture of how the case company approaches the requirements of the law, a semi-structured interview was conducted. The interview structure was framed on the research questions and their results, so that the questionnaire had three topics based on the GDPR guideline, data breach notification form and plan, and findings on information security controls. 
 
The research results were reflected in the GDPR guideline, personal data breach notification plan and form, and additionally the research work defined the most important information security controls against data leakages caused by staff errors. The given work made an evaluation of the case company and proposed development measures towards fostering greater regulatory compliance and enhancing information security culture. The case company was presented with the development proposals and is developing its information security culture on the basis of the results of the evaluation. 
 
The given work answers all three research questions and the results can be used by SMEs to prepare for the GDPR, personal data breach notification procedures, and to protect themselves against most common data leakage types caused by staff errors.

title: Generative artificial intelligence as a confidant for youth: navigating mental support and cultural stigma in Bandung
abstract: In the unfolding age of generative artificial intelligence (GEN-AI) amidst Society 5.0, opportunity and pressure coexist within the same digital currents, shaping not only technological adoption but also the human dynamics of a generation raised in constant connectivity (Badinszky, 2025). According to the research by Chiu et al. (2023), GEN-AI has become a transformative force in reshaping human aspects of daily life especially in work, social interaction, and digital culture. Among Indonesian Generation Z (1997)(1998)(1999)(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009)(2010) and early Alpha (born in 2012), AI-driven technologies have increasingly embedded in daily activities and have become part of ordinary youth life, shaping how young people access information, carry out academic and professional tasks, communicate socially, and produce digital content (Xiao et al., 2023).However, public discourse in Indonesia often focuses on GEN-AI's utility, emphasizing efficiency, digital skills, and employability, while largely overlooking its psychosocial implications (Wiederhold, 2024). The rapid integration of GEN-AI across diverse sectors, from healthcare to creative industries, has raised expectations for younger generations to adapt to these intelligent systems to remain competitive. Yet GEN-AI's influence extends far beyond mere productivity enhancement. It also plays a significant role in shaping behavioral patterns, cognitive engagement, and psychosocial experiences, transcending formal educational environments (Panduwiyasa, 2025).GEN-AI has transformed into more than just a tool for information retrieval or task execution. It has become a conversational partner, serving as a listener and confidant, offering a safe space for sensitive inquiries, difficult conversations, and emotional expression, particularly when human interaction feels unavailable or judgmental. (Sandhya et al., 2025). This emotional engagement with AI marks a significant departure from its traditional role, raising critical questions about the evolving relationship between technology and emotional well-being (Chaniago et al., 2025).Bandung, as the capital city of West Java, provides a relevant Indonesian context for examining this transformation. The province combines a large youth population within range of 15 to 35 years old, high levels of digital exposure, and a mental health landscape that demands greater attention.According to the Indonesian Health Survey (SKI) 2023, the prevalence of depression in West Java is significantly higher than the national average-3.3% compared to 1.4% nationwide (Suprayitno et al., 2024). Within this environment, Generation Z (commonly defined as those born between 1997 and 2012) and the early Alpha (born in the early 2010s) face intense academic competition, urban pressures, socio-economic inequalities, and increasingly digital lives. These factors converge to create a fertile ground for the dual impact of AI adoption and emotional vulnerability (Panduwiyasa and Wibowo, 2025).As these young individuals face increasing emotional strain, many turn to GEN-AI as a non-judgmental and readily accessible source of support. In the absence of easily accessible formal mental health services and amidst societal stigma, GEN-AI offers an immediate, responsive, and emotionally safe space to process distress (Kamener, 2025). For some, AI is no longer merely a tool for productivity; it has become a trusted confidant that is available at any time to listen and offer perceived comfort. This transformation is crucial and reflects a broader shift in how youth experience emotional support and trust in the digital age. (Rabeyron, 2025).This reliance is especially visible in educational contexts, where young people increasingly encounter GEN-AI as part of learning, writing, problem-solving, tutoring, and academic self-regulation. Recent scholarship has shown that generative AI in education is not limited to content generation, but also includes personalized assistance, feedback, learning support, and learner engagement (Samala et al., 2025). For youth, these educational uses may gradually blur the boundary between academic assistance and emotional reliance. A student who initially uses GEN-AI to understand a difficult assignment may later use the same conversational interface to express anxiety, academic pressure, fear of failure, or uncertainty about personal capability. In this sense, pedagogical support may become emotionally meaningful because it provides immediate, private, and responsive help when human support feels unavailable or difficult to access (Crompton and Burke, 2023).A clearer understanding of large language models (LLMs) is also important for this discussion. Many GEN-AI tools used by youth are powered by LLMs that generate responses by predicting and composing language patterns from large-scale training data. This makes them highly effective in producing fluent, personalized, and conversational responses (Ouerghemmi and Ertz, 2025). However, such fluency should not be mistaken for understanding, clinical judgment, or ethical accountability. LLMs can simulate empathy and coherence, but their responses remain probabilistic, contextdependent, and vulnerable to inaccuracies. Therefore, when youth use GEN-AI as a confidant, the issue is not only that they are interacting with "AI," but that they are interacting with language systems capable of producing emotionally persuasive responses without necessarily possessing human understanding or professional responsibility (Sallam, 2023).This emerging dynamic calls for deeper reflection on the human implications of GEN-AI. As AI plays a more intimate role in youth emotional lives, it is not merely a technological phenomenon but a fundamental shift in human connection in the digital age (Wahyuni et al., 2025). The relationship between youth and GEN-AI is not only transforming digital behavior but also reshaping how emotional support is accessed and understood in an increasingly connected world. This opinion paper argues that the increasing reliance on AI as a confidant marks a pivotal turning point in the digital transformation of human emotional experiences, highlighting the need for serious consideration of its long-term implications for youth mental health and emotional well-being (Kohnke et al., 2024).According to the research by Hanif et al. (2025) both Javanese and Sundanese cultures in Bandung, there is a deeply ingrained cultural norm of "sungkan" (hesitation) and "tidak enakan" (feeling uncomfortable or uneasy, particularly when it comes to asking for favors or speaking up), which significantly shapes how youth approach their emotional struggles. The cultural emphasis on maintaining social harmony and avoiding confrontation or discomfort often discourages young people from expressing personal distress. This reluctance to discuss mental health issues openly, especially within family settings, where vulnerability is typically seen as a weakness, further complicates emotional expression. In these communities, emotional struggles are frequently kept private, either because it is considered inappropriate to burden others with personal problems or due to the fear of judgment from those closest to them (Darwanto, 2022).This cultural disposition plays a significant role in why many young people in Bandung turn to GEN-AI as a confidant (Messmer and Berkling, 2021). With GEN-AI, they can express their emotions and concerns without the fear of "sungkan" that would normally arise in human interactions. The AI provides an anonymous, judgment-free space, allowing youth to share their thoughts and feelings without the discomfort of societal expectations or the anxiety of burdening others (Wang et al., 2024).In a society where seeking help for mental health issues may still carry a stigma, GEN-AI becomes an appealing outlet (Subu et al., 2021). It offers youth a chance to "test the waters" of emotional expression, to articulate their feelings, and even to ask questions they might hesitate to pose to family members, friends, or even mental health professionals.While GEN-AI can provide immediate emotional relief in these cases, it's crucial to recognize the limitations of relying on a non-human listener. Although it can lower the barriers to emotional expression, GEN-AI should not replace the deeper, human connection necessary for meaningful mental health support. The risk lies in the possibility that, feeling more comfortable with AI, young people may avoid seeking more substantial, real-world support that can address their emotional needs comprehensively. This becomes particularly concerning when self-diagnosis is involved. AI's lack of nuanced understanding can leave youth with misguided beliefs about their emotional health, which may delay proper professional intervention and worsen existing issues.The role of GEN-AI in the lives of young people in Bandung is complex and multifaceted, acting both as a source of pressure and as a potential refuge. On one hand, GEN-AI-driven environments raise expectations of constant adaptation, speed, and high performance. As AI tools become integrated into various aspects of life, young people are exposed to higher standards of productivity, creativity, and achievement. This creates a climate of intense competition and comparison, which can contribute to rejection and technostress-an emotional strain triggered by the demands of rapidly changing digital environments (Xia, 2023). In this sense, GEN-AI is both a catalyst for innovation and a source of stress, amplifying pressures that young people already face in their academic, professional, and personal lives (Martínez-Navalón et al., 2023).This same technology that accelerates productivity also offers potential refuge. As we mentioned in the introduction, GEN-AI is not just a tool for efficiency; it is increasingly becoming a space where young people turn for emotional relief (Rabeyron, 2025). For many youths, GEN-AI functions as a non-judgmental, immediate, and private space to express emotions, ask difficult questions, or rehearse personal conversations. In environments where youth face intense pressures, this ability to offload emotional burdens into a safe, accessible space can be a crucial form of mental support (Merrill et al., 2022).The appeal of GEN-AI lies in its immediacy and privacy. It allows young users to test what they want to say before sharing it with another person and helps them articulate emotions they might otherwise avoid. GEN-AI provides a low-pressure environment where young people can organize their thoughts, identify their feelings, or ask questions they might find embarrassing, awkward or difficult to express to humans (Muldoon and Parke, 2025).Due to its conversational nature, GEN-AI may encourage young users to seek emotional answers or diagnoses that are not always grounded in professional medical knowledge. Many young people experiencing anxiety, depression, or stress may turn to AI for support. This raises the concern that they may misinterpret their symptoms or self-diagnose based on AI interactions, leading to misguided conclusions or increased anxiety. Unlike trained professionals, GEN-AI lacks the nuanced understanding needed to provide accurate mental health assessments. Without the guidance of a qualified expert, relying on AI for self-diagnosis can reinforce incorrect or harmful beliefs about their mental health. This poses a critical risk, as inaccurate self-diagnosis can delay proper treatment and exacerbate existing emotional distress (Chou et al., 2025).According to the research by Song et al. (2025) another critical risk is AI hallucination. In emotionally sensitive contexts, hallucination is not merely a technical limitation; it may become a psychosocial risk. GEN-AI systems can generate responses that sound confident, coherent, and emotionally validating, even when the information is inaccurate, clinically inappropriate, or misleading (O'brien et al., 2020). For vulnerable youth, this "confidently wrong" advice may reinforce misunderstanding, intensify anxiety, normalize distorted beliefs, or delay professional help-seeking. This risk is particularly serious when young users interpret AI-generated responses as medical, psychological, or diagnostic guidance rather than as general conversational output (Panduwiyasa and Wibowo, 2024).Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge that GEN-AI's role as a safe, private, and non-judgmental listener can be an important first step in emotional processing. For young people facing emotional challenges, AI may offer a valuable space for emotional articulation. However, the risk of misinformed emotional conclusions, such as premature self-diagnosis, must be carefully managed. It is crucial to ensure that young users understand the limitations of AI as a mental health tool and recognize the importance of seeking professional help when necessary (Ouyang and Jiao, 2021).According to the LLM research by Zhao et al. (2024) It is also important to distinguish between general-purpose LLMs and specialized mental health-oriented digital tools. General-purpose LLMs, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Microsoft Copilot, are designed to respond to a wide range of prompts across education, work, information seeking, creativity, and interpersonal communication (Chen et al., 2025). Their flexibility makes them accessible for emotional expression, but they are not designed as clinical mental health systems and should not be treated as diagnostic or therapeutic authorities. By contrast, specialized mental health-oriented tools, such as Woebot, Wysa, or Youper, are more explicitly associated with structured self-help, mood tracking, cognitive-behavioral techniques, or guided emotional reflection. Even so, these tools should be understood as supplemental support rather than substitutes for licensed counseling, psychotherapy, or crisis intervention (Qi, 2025).In Indonesia, the digital mental health ecosystem is also expanding through platforms such as Riliv, Halodoc, and Naluri. Riliv provides online counseling and meditation-based mental health support, Halodoc offers access to online mental health consultation with psychologists and psychiatrists, while Naluri provides structured health and well-being support that includes mental health programs (Diya et al., 2024). These platforms are not identical to general-purpose LLMs, but they illustrate how Indonesian users are becoming increasingly familiar with mediated, app-based, and remote forms of psychological support. This distinction matters because youth may experience both AI chatbots and digital counseling platforms as private and low-threshold spaces for emotional help, even though their clinical validation, human oversight, referral pathways, and safety mechanisms differ substantially (Boit and Patil, 2025).If the Bandung government and relevant educational institutions are serious about youth well-being, GEN-AI governance must move beyond literacy campaigns that focus only on technical competence. A human-centered agenda is needed because digital adoption may advance faster than psychosocial support systems. If this shift is ignored, young people may continue to build emotionally meaningful relationships with GEN-AI in private, without clear guidance on when such interactions are helpful, when they become misleading, and when they should be redirected toward human care.First, digital literacy for youth should explicitly include emotional literacy about GEN-AI. Young people need to understand what GEN-AI can and cannot do in moments of distress. They should be taught to distinguish between helpful reflection, persuasive simulation, general information, and situations that require immediate human support. This is important because AI-generated responses may sound empathetic and convincing, even when they are not clinically appropriate.Second, schools and higher education institutions should treat GEN-AI-mediated disclosure as a signal, not as a solution. If students increasingly turn to GEN-AI to discuss fear, shame, loneliness, academic pressure, or family-related stress, this may indicate unmet needs in their human support environment.Educational institutions should therefore strengthen counseling pathways, peer-support systems, and psychologically safe communication channels, rather than assuming that chatbot access is sufficient.Third, policymakers and platform designers should adopt a precautionary approach for youth-facing GEN-AI companions. Safety escalation, crisis signposting, privacy protection, and transparent boundaries should be treated as core design requirements, not optional features. In West Java, where psychological vulnerability and digital intensity coexist, weak safeguards should not be seen merely as technical limitations. They should be understood as public well-being concerns.In our opinion, the debate should not be framed as whether youth should or should not talk to GEN-AI. That behavior is already emerging. The more important task is to shape the conditions under which it happens. GEN-AI may help some young people begin to speak when silence feels easier. This role can be valuable, especially in culturally restrained contexts where direct emotional disclosure may feel difficult. However, youth well-being cannot be built on simulated empathy alone. The most defensible position is to view GEN-AI as a possible confidant of first resort, but never as the final holder of youth distress.Future research should therefore examine how youth use GEN-AI for emotional support, whether AImediated disclosure encourages or delays human help-seeking, and how cultural norms such as "sungkan" or "tidak enakan", emotional restraint, and mental health stigma shape this process. Further studies should also evaluate safeguards such as referral prompts, privacy notices, crisis signposting, and clear distinctions between general-purpose LLMs, specialized mental health tools, and digital counseling platforms.The author(s) wish to express their sincere gratitude to Telkom University for its generous financial support, provided under the research program with registration code RCMS/RES/Periode 1/14860/1/2026. title: Glucocare: “A Web-Based Mhealth Application with Chatbot Technology and Community Support for Enhancing Diabetes Care in Developing Countries”
venue: Zimbabwe Conference of Information and Communication Technologies (ZCICT)
abstract: Diabetes is an emerging global health threat affecting over 530 million people worldwide and posing serious problems, especially in developing nations. Traditional chronic disease management systems face problems such as a shortage of specialized personnel, poor infrastructure and overcrowded health services. Diabetic patients in particular often are deprived of timely medical care, support, and locally tailored educational tools that significantly contribute to disease management. To cover this gap, this paper presents GlucoCare, a secure web-based mobile health (mHealth) application designed to address these problems. The system incorporates multiple functional components, including an AI-powered chatbot, diabetes community chatrooms and doctor-patient communication into a single platform. GlucoCare also provides patients with real-time assistance, health education, appointment scheduling and medication tracking at the same time, ensuring data privacy and security. The Build methodology was used to guide the study, while the application was developed using an adapted version of Solo Scrum to support continuous improvement and adaptability to user needs. The GlucoCare system encourages diabetic patients to manage their condition more effectively and reduces pressure on healthcare workers. Its lightweight, low-bandwidth design makes it suitable for both urban and rural use in areas with limited resources. This innovation demonstrates how localized digital health solutions can improve chronic disease management and promote sustainable healthcare practices in developing countries.

abstract: Photo by Christian Wiediger on Unsplash INTRODUCTION Huge amounts of public data on the internet and the ease with which we regularly search it have resulted in the phenomenon called Patient-Targeted Googling (PTG). PTG occurs when a clinician conducts an online search for information about a patient through any search engine, internet database, or social media site. The practice has provoked ethical discussion and the creation of practical guidelines to ensure clinicians use PTG ethically. One common theme in PTG literature is privacy and confidentiality. However, given that the relevant information is publicly accessible, privacy and confidentiality may not be applicable or accurate. In health and medicine, correctly applying the concepts of privacy and confidentially is important because these terms have rigid legal definitions that are often confusing and misunderstood. By refraining from legitimizing claims that patients’ publicly accessible data is “private” information, we can avoid the risks of inappropriately applying privacy and confidentiality concepts and further muddying the waters. l. Privacy and Confidentiality in PTG Literature The literature on PTG consistently raises patient privacy and confidentiality concerns. For example, the article “Patient-targeted googling: The ethics of searching online for patient information” mentions the concept of privacy over a dozen times in its ethical and practical framework, designed for psychiatrists to use prior to engaging in a patient-targeted search.[1] A later work begins with a statement that “[m]any physicians would agree that seeking information about their patients via Google seems to be an invasion of privacy . . .” [2] Informal guidelines continue to address privacy and confidentiality when analyzing PTG and frame consent as necessary to respect patient privacy.[3] Research articles reporting investigations of PTG also categorize privacy violations as a risk to privacy and dignity.[4] The AMA does not have a PTG ethics policy, but an article on the AMA website about PTG by a staff writer stated that “physicians have a fundamental ethical responsibility to respect patient privacy.”[5] Ethical and practical discussions of PTG often involve concerns for privacy and confidentiality. However, the information found in PTG searches is not private or confidential. ll. The Information at Issue is Not Actually Private or Confidential The information at issue in PTG is not hidden or secured from public view and is available to anyone conducting an internet search. Thus, it cannot be said to be private or confidential. Yet, privacy and confidentiality routinely come up in analyses of PTG. Perhaps this is because the information feels private. The thought of clinicians digging through the internet to find information about the patient feels like an invasion. They are trying to access information that the patient did not share with them in an unexpected way. People commonly associate privacy and confidentiality concepts with personal data access issues, so it is not surprising that privacy and confidentiality find their way into discussions on PTG. While much of the literature focuses on privacy, some of the literature does acknowledge that this information is not really private or confidential. One article describes the patient experience as possibly a “perceived privacy” that stems from an assumption that clinicians will not conduct online searches for information about them just like they may assume “their psychiatrists would not eavesdrop on their conversations in restaurant.”[6] Another acknowledges that there is a difference between legal definitions of privacy and confidentiality and “the layperson’s notion.”[7] So, though looking up a patient’s Facebook profile does not legally violate the patient’s privacy, the patient may still consider it “private” in a layperson’s sense. It is important for clinicians to be sensitive to actions that may feel violating to a patient. Clinicians should be aware that patients may consider PTG a breach of privacy. But literature geared towards ethics in clinical practice ought not confuse lay and legal definitions because doing so risks legitimizing an incorrect position. It is also not necessary to use privacy and confidentiality concepts to justify concerns and practice guidelines concerning PTG. lll. PTG as a Potential Violation of the Clinician-Patient Relationship A better way to frame PTG is as a potential violation of the trust and respect inherent in the clinician-patient relationship. Patients understand and respect the traditional ways clinicians gather information about them. Clinicians simply ask their patients directly for most types of information, especially personal information. When done with sensitivity and patient understanding that the information is relevant to the interaction, collecting personal information does not feel inappropriately invasive (even if the process may be uncomfortable). This is partially because the questioning occurs within the confines of the clinician-patient relationship. Some information a clinician may discover in an online search can also be gathered by “legitimate” means (like by asking the patient). Yet, accessing this information via PTG can still violate the clinician-patient relationship. This shows that it is not the nature of the information that makes the clinician’s access feel like an invasion, but the method they use to gather it. If the information clinicians seek is clinically relevant, patients expect that the clinician will ask for it. During that conversation, patients can ask why and how the information is relevant to their health care. It is the act of gathering this information outside the accepted boundary of the clinician-patient relationship that makes PTG potentially violating. The use of PTG to gather information that is not clinically relevant is also problematic. Without resorting to privacy claims, the ethical analysis should identify the nature of the problem more accurately. Patients accept that clinicians ask them personal questions to serve their best interests. Once clinicians step outside that boundary by asking patients for clinically irrelevant information out of some voyeuristic or inappropriate interest, they break the trust and respect inherent in the relationship. A clinician that purposefully seeks out clinically irrelevant information is doing something problematic because the exercise does not connect to the clinician’s professional duties and patient interests. When clinicians ask for clinically irrelevant information during a patient visit, the patient has the opportunity to evaluate the questioning and respond accordingly (perhaps responding to an inquiry that seems purely conversational or designed to relieve stress or not answering an invasive, irrelevant question). With PTG, patients cannot evaluate and respond to the clinician or the inquiry, as they are unlikely to know it is occurring. Patients are not necessarily concerned that their doctor knows where they went to brunch last Sunday. Patients are concerned that clinicians are purposefully seeking out information neither connected to their health nor covered by the clinician-patient relationship and are likely doing so to satisfy their own interests. If the purpose of PTG does not serve the patient’s interests, clinicians should not conduct the search.[8] Even if it does serve the patient’s interest, PTG may not be ethical. The ethical significance does not hinge on whether the information is clinically relevant or not. What makes PTG potentially unethical is how it circumvents the methods of information gathering patients accept as appropriate in the clinician-patient relationship. Whether the information is or is not clinically relevant or in the patient’s best interests, the mode of collection is ethically problematic, nor addresses privacy. lV. Accurately Applying Concepts of Privacy and Confidentiality is Important Privacy and confidentiality are not accurate concepts to apply to PTG. This point about privacy and confidentiality is worth making, even if it does not change the way PTG should be approached in clinical practice. The concepts and legal definitions of privacy and confidentiality are extremely important in health and medicine. Thus, it is crucial that privacy not be misconstrued to protect publicly available information. One of the most important (and often misunderstood) examples is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) Privacy Rule. This Rule protects only certain statutorily defined “individually identifiable health information” and “covered entities.”[9] Violation of the Privacy Rule is grounds for statutory penalties.[10] While there is room to criticize how well the Privacy Rule protects patients today, covered entities must follow it. The Privacy Rule remains an important component in protecting both patients and healthcare entities. Despite this, misunderstandings about HIPAA abound, even among clinicians.[11] It has even been reported that some inaccurately claim that PTG violates HIPAA .[12] Other statutes also protect health data in a variety of ways.
