title: Internet of Things (IoT) and Real-Time Data Applications in the Insurance Industry
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research article examines the role of the Internet of Things (IoT) and real-time data applications in transforming the insurance industry through intelligent, connected, and data-driven operations. As digital technologies continue to reshape modern insurance services, IoT devices and real-time analytics systems are enabling insurers to improve operational efficiency, customer experience, risk management, and fraud prevention. Traditional insurance systems often rely on delayed reporting and historical data analysis, which can limit responsiveness and reduce the accuracy of operational decision-making. The study explores how IoT technologies such as telematics systems, wearable health devices, smart home sensors, and connected industrial monitoring systems generate continuous streams of real-time data that support predictive risk assessment, usage-based insurance models, personalized insurance services, and automated claims processing. It also analyzes the integration of IoT systems with cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence, and real-time analytics platforms to improve underwriting accuracy, operational monitoring, and customer engagement. In addition, the article discusses the benefits of IoT adoption in insurance, including enhanced operational efficiency, faster decision-making, improved fraud detection, proactive risk management, cost reduction, and stronger customer personalization. Key challenges and risks such as cybersecurity threats, data privacy concerns, regulatory compliance issues, device reliability, infrastructure complexity, and implementation costs are also critically examined. The research further highlights future opportunities involving AI-driven smart insurance ecosystems, expansion of connected devices and sensors, real-time insurance operations, and intelligent digital insurance infrastructures that are shaping the future of the insurance industry. This work contributes to ongoing discussions on digital transformation in insurance and demonstrates how IoT and real-time data technologies can support more responsive, scalable, and customer-centered insurance services. Keywords: Internet of Things, IoT, Real-Time Data, Insurance Technology, Telematics, Smart Insurance, Predictive Analytics, Connected Devices, Digital Transformation, Risk Assessment

title: Internet of Things: Purview, Challenges and Probability
Intra-Body Communication for the Internet of Medical Things: A Survey of Communication Modalities, Security, and Reliability
abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) enables continuous monitoring, remote management, and data-driven interventions using wearable and implantable devices. However, widespread reliance on short-range radio protocols such as Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) exposes body area networks to eavesdropping, physiological data manipulation, and Denial-of-Service (DoS), with direct implications for patient safety and privacy. Intra-Body Communication (IBC) has emerged as an alternative that uses the human body as a transmission medium. This paper reviews IBC technologies for IoMT-oriented Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs), with emphasis on security, privacy, dependability, and communication-system design. We (i) classify major IBC modalities, (ii) survey applications across implants, wearables, assistive systems, and the Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT), (iii) relate IBC to attack surfaces observed in BLE-based systems, and (iv) compare IBC with RF-based WBANs across security, reliability, throughput, and interference resilience. The comparative synthesis shows that reported IBC links span from tens of kb/s to Mbps depending on modality, with Fat-IBC reaching up to 92 Mb/s, while GC-IBC and CC/EQS-HBC offer stronger body-confined robustness and lower BER trends than BLE/SmartBAN. Overall, the review positions IBC as an enabling communication paradigm for connected medical things, highlighting its relevance to IoMT networking, system integration, and body-area communication architectures. We also identify open challenges in validation, safety assessment, multi-node coordination, and standardization.

title: Introducing Technology for Bedside Nurses: A New Department for Critical Care Practice
abstract: Critical care units in 2026 operate with significantly more technology than a decade ago. Intravenous smart pumps with integrated safety systems are standard equipment.1 Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms analyze patient parameters and generate clinical alerts.2 In some units, ambient AI systems use computer vision to monitor patient movement and detect falls before they occur.3 Smart beds equipped with contactless sensors monitor patients’ vital signs, detect changes in patient positioning, and automatically alert staff to potential safety concerns.4 However, a fundamental question remains: Do these digital tools enhance patient care delivery or do they create barriers between nurses and patients?Today, we introduce Technology for Bedside Nurses, a new recurring department in Critical Care Nurse. This department will provide practical guidance for navigating critical care technology while maintaining the clinical judgment essential to nursing practice, protecting the patient relationships that promote healing, and preserving the nursing excellence that ensures safety.Critical care nurses use technology that offers both clinical benefits and workflow challenges. Smart infusion pumps with dose error reduction systems have reduced medication administration errors. A 2022 study documented a 16% reduction in dosing errors after implementation of smart pump technology with integrated safety features.5Electronic health records enable rapid access to patient information and facilitate communication among care team members. However, these technologies create significant workflow burdens. Most critical care nurses experience alert fatigue. Studies document hundreds of electronic notifications per shift, many of which are clinically irrelevant.6 Smart pump alarms, which are designed to enhance safety, may paradoxically encourage unsafe work-arounds when activated inappropriately or excessively.7 System fragmentation requiring multiple logins and interfaces divides nursing attention between technology and direct patient care.One of the most noteworthy trends is the evolution of remote monitoring and remote staffing, often called the tele–intensive care unit (ICU) or virtual nursing model. Over the past decade, the tele-ICU has evolved from a niche service to a cornerstone of high-acuity units, with widespread adoption. Whereas historically the tele-ICU was rooted in simple audiovisual links, the modern era has seen these systems integrate real-time physiologic data streaming, AI-driven predictive analytics, and 24/7 remote expert staffing acting as a “second pair of eyes” for the bedside team. The tele-ICU model allows remote intensivists and virtual nurses to handle time-consuming tasks such as medication reconciliation and admissions procedures while maintaining continuous surveillance.8 This approach frees bedside nurses to focus on direct nursing interventions and on managing complex patient needs.9 By bridging the gap during staffing shortages and providing a safety net for less experienced clinicians, the tele-ICU has demonstrated measurable improvements in patient outcomes, including a significant reduction in ICU mortality rates, shorter critical care lengths of stay, and greater adherence to evidence-based protocols.10Several technological developments will likely affect critical care nursing practice in the coming years. Large language models and generative AI are entering clinical environments; applications range from automated documentation assistance to clinical decision support.11 Ambient listening technology, previously limited to outpatient settings, is expanding to inpatient units and may reduce manual documentation requirements.12Advanced monitoring technologies, including wearable devices and intelligent hospital beds, are becoming more sophisticated in detecting early signs of patient deterioration.4 The Internet of Medical Things promises interconnected care environments in which medical devices communicate automatically, potentially optimizing workflows and enhancing safety protocols.13These advances present implementation challenges. A 2024 American Nurses Foundation survey found that although nurses recognize the potential benefits of AI, they express concerns about accuracy, privacy, and the need to maintain human interaction in patient care.14 Rapid technological change often exceeds the capacity of health care organizations for thoughtful integration, resulting in implementation failures that may compromise efficiency and safety.15Critical care nurses occupy a unique position in health care’s digital transformation. Nurses are primary users of bedside technology and are simultaneously responsible for patient safety and therapeutic relationships. Nursing decisions regarding technology integration, adaptation, or resistance will significantly influence the evolution of critical care practice.The clinical implications are substantial. Appropriately implemented technology can enhance clinical capabilities, reduce errors, and increase time available for therapeutic nursing interventions. Poorly implemented or inappropriately adopted technology may fragment critical care nurses’ attention, increase their cognitive load, and create new opportunities for patient harm.The evolution of cardiac monitoring illustrates this principle. Early telemetry systems required nurses to manually interpret heart rhythms and calculate heart rate. Contemporary monitors provide automated analysis, trend data, and sophisticated alarm algorithms. However, research consistently demonstrates that experienced nurses often detect clinically significant changes before automated systems generate alerts,16 suggesting that outcomes are optimal when technology augments rather than replaces clinical judgment.Technology for Bedside Nurses will operate on a core principle: technology should support, rather than direct, nursing practice. The department’s mission is to equip critical care nurses with the knowledge and skills they need to evaluate emerging tools thoughtfully, implement them skillfully, and troubleshoot the digital systems increasingly embedded in critical care environments.Upcoming articles in this department will explore the realities of modern nursing practice. We will examine practical strategies for managing alert fatigue, a problem that simultaneously threatens patient safety and erodes clinician well-being. We will analyze how AI can support clinical decision-making while preserving the critical thinking skills that distinguish expert nursing practice from algorithmic response. We will investigate workflow optimization approaches that leverage technology effectively without sacrificing the therapeutic presence patients need during their most vulnerable moments.Each article in this department will connect theoretical concepts to scenarios familiar to bedside nurses: the monitor that alarms incessantly, the documentation system that fragments attention, the new device that arrives with minimal training. Content will include evidence-based integration strategies, common implementation problems with tested solutions, and frameworks for evaluating whether emerging technologies merit adoption.Technology will continue evolving rapidly, but nursing’s fundamental goals—promoting healing, preventing harm, and providing compassionate care—remain constant. Critical care nursing’s future depends not on choosing between technological capability and human connection, but on integrating both to achieve outcomes neither can accomplish alone.Technology for Bedside Nurses will provide guidance, helping nurses navigate health care’s digital transformation as active participants rather than as passive recipients. Critical care nurses can shape how technology serves practice. Through informed evaluation and skilled implementation, we can ensure that sophisticated tools amplify rather than replace the human elements that define nursing care.

title: Introduction
abstract: This edited volume reflects on the rapid digitization of health and healthcare over the last two decades, including the increasing integration of mobile health (mHealth) technologies into the everyday lives of people across the world (Hendl et al. 2023). The collection of essays aims to investigate the ongoing transformation generated and accelerated by mHealth and the power dynamics, asymmetries, ethical implications, and opportunities for health and the society involved in this process. In the context of this anthology, we conceptualize mHealth as a segment of digital health, including technologies understood as the use of mobile and wireless technologies, such as health apps and sensors, to support healthcare delivery, public health, and medical research. By now, a growing pool of research has shown that just like standard healthcare, mHealth technologies are shaped by the socio-political environment within which they are designed. Therefore, persistent forms of injustice dominant within the environment get to shape digital health technologies (DHTs), and commonly facilitate unequal health outcomes and magnify existing inequalities (Ledford 2019; Sjoding et al. 2020; Liao and Carbonell 2023). Yet these empirical findings are still not sufficiently reflected in sociological and normative research, especially not through an intersectional and global lens. Equally pressing are debates on the health potential, and more broadly, the social and ethical implications of DHTs. The idea for the book emerged during our research project “MEDA—mHealth: Ethical, Legal and Social Aspects in the Digital Age,” conducted from 2018 to 2024 and funded by Germany’s Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) under the lead of Verina Wild. The project investigated the chances, opportunities, challenges, and risks of mHealth as well as other aspects of digital transformation in healthcare on an individual, societal, and global level. One focus was on issues related to social and global health equity, such as: Where do inequalities exist in the use of mHealth, and are these inequalities unjust? What are the ethical implications of bias and discrimination? How can privacy, individual well-being and the common good be balanced with one another? Who bears responsibility for health and health equity? To answer these questions, the project combined qualitative and quantitative empirical studies with ethical analysis. In our inquiry, we integrated research from different academic disciplines: philosophy, applied ethics, sociology, science and technology studies (STS), gender studies, law, medicine, and public health. The project was first based at Ludwig-Maximilians-University (LMU) in Munich and later at the University of Augsburg, Germany. From the outset of the project, we were keen to explore the global ethical and social dimensions of mHealth technologies. During a workshop at Brocher Foundation, Switzerland, we focused on the exploration of such global concerns, and it was there that the outline for this book was initiated. We are thus immensely grateful for the funding that we received from the BMBF (Nr 01GP1791) and to the Brocher Foundation for funding our workshop “The Ethics of mHealth as a Global Phenomenon.” The workshop discussed foundational research leading to this book and involved an additional publication grant, contributing to the open-access publication of this edited volume and making this book accessible to a wide range of readers around the world. We are also thankful to fellow researchers and broader team members who supported the production of this book, including Fabian Linder, Isabel Fernandez Mayor, and Juenna Fiola for the assistance, proofreading, and formatting of the manuscript, and Verena Lippert for administrative support on the project MEDA-mHealth and the OUP team for their guidance. In this volume, we have collected the essays for an audience of students and researchers from a wide range of disciplines, readers interested in DHTs, and ethical and social issues of global health and health justice. Our book aims to provide the first global, intersectional, and interdisciplinary overview of the social and ethical issues raised by mobile health technology. Through the edited volume, we particularly seek to advance debates on structural concerns of justice and intersectionality in mobile health technology and ethics, with contributors of various positionalities and locations across the world. The book addresses gaps in research as well as in teaching about ethical and social aspects of DHTs with a global focus. As such, the book can be of particular interest to scholars and students in the following disciplines: philosophy, medicine, bioethics, public health, sociology, STS, anthropology, nursing studies, and digital health sciences. The book can further be of interest to technology developers, policy-makers, patient organizations, and the nongovernmental sector, particularly initiatives working on data safety, analysis of automated decision-making (ADM), or patient-led innovation. One of the major aims of the book is to take a closer look at mHealth technologies in different parts of the world from empirically informed perspectives and through an intersectional lens. The lens pays diligent attention to the ways through which technologies can and do replicate and magnify interlocked inequalities and dis/advantages, including those generated by the intersections of gender injustice, racialization, ableist social norms, and class/caste disparities. Through this intersectional, global, and justice-oriented analysis, materially grounded hopeful visions emerge, paving a way for more widely beneficent DHTs. As one of the first collections of this kind, and recognizing that many technologies are offered both locally and globally, this book presents a collection of essays exploring mHealth from international, cross-cultural, and global perspectives. Importantly, most essays in this book discuss so far under-researched concerns of structural justice that originate from underrepresented standpoints, centering the health and wellbeing of socio-historically oppressed and structurally marginalized populations. These essays investigate the health concerns of disability justice advocates, young mHealth users, women seeking adequate services in largely male-centric healthcare systems and tech industries, as well as global South(s) users and health experts, underserved, remote, and First Nations communities—all while imagining and codesigning future-oriented technologies that strive for health and healthcare justice. Through the implementation and advocating for an equity-based approach to health benefits, more robust regulation of DHTs, equitable, just, and cross-cultural mHealth design, community outreach, and related initiatives, the approaches put forth in this book can inspire and foster intersectionally beneficent DHTs and their meaningful adoption and integration into people’s everyday lives. In any case, the essays in this book reveal that participatory, codesigned, and community-led processes are fundamental to building healthcare justice in the digital age. As readers will observe along the journey through this book, digital health explored in context, in line with debates that do not take a technocentric approach, taps into the tensions between the global and the local, raising a richness of complex social, ethical, and legal implications. Within such contextualized discussion, we approach mHealth tools as embedded within larger politics and policies of healthcare systems and lived experiences of people with technologies that influence how they build trust with and within such systems. It is worth reconsidering these debates due to their contemporary nature with newly emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools and cross-cultural contextual character. This applies to, for example, data localization policies on sensitive data flows and data sharing; Indigenous health platforms within a largely privatized digital health economy shaped by legacies of (data) colonialism and commercial interests; health problems that are oftentimes looked upon through the prism of universalized norms, e.g. normative whiteness and maleness, yet come with intersectional and social angles based on nationality, gender, socio-economic status, racialization/ethnicity, etc. This implies that there are biases and inequalities replicated in healthcare datasets that feed into digital health systems and influence how we imagine healthcare concerns and their broader contexts (Gilbert 2019; Mihelcic 2022; Arora and Huang 2025). As such, questions arise as to which health concerns, treatments, needs, and wants the making of mHealth tools are oriented toward and to whose benefit? Further, it is worth speculating on internal variations within nations and other internal variables such as rural-urban, class, caste, settler/Indigenous, and those implications within national healthcare contexts. The essays in this book are organized in three sections: transformations, power, and ethics, focusing on major shifts and transformations introduced and magnified by mHealth; power imbalances and structural inequalities in mHealth; and ethical approaches addressing the shifts and inequalities and proposing effective responses and solutions to major social and ethical problems raised by mHealth—but of course, these are largely interconnected issues. Most contributions in this book are academic essays from scholars in a range of disciplines, some are interviews with scholars and experts on different aspects of health and digitization, and some texts are also contributions from nonacademics who work in the field of digital health or have lived experiences in living with chronic illness while using DHTs. abstract: The "Security and Privacy Challenges in Healthcare" minitrack explores the critical issues surrounding data protection and privacy in healthcare systems.With the increasing digitization of healthcare, including the widespread use of electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, and wearable health devices, sensitive patient information is more vulnerable to cyber threats.This minitrack addresses key challenges such as ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of healthcare data, while complying with regulations like HIPAA.Topics include advanced encryption methods, secure data sharing, threat detection, and privacy-preserving technologies.Additionally, it considers the ethical implications of data usage in healthcare research and personalized medicine.By examining current trends, threats, and emerging technologies, this minitrack aims to highlight solutions that balance innovation with robust security and privacy measures, ensuring trust and safety in healthcare environments.

title: Introduction to the Special Issue on Role of Scalable Computing and Data Analytics in Evolution of Internet of Things
abstract:
The evolution of Internet of Things has given way to a Smart World where there is an improved integration of devices, systems and processes in humans through all pervasive connectivity. Anytime, anywhere connection and transaction is the motto of the Internet of things which brings comfort to the users and sweeps the problem of physical boundary out of the way. Once it has come into the purview of developers, new areas have been identified and new applications have been introduced. Small wearables which can track your health to big automated vehicles which can move from one place to another self navigating without human intervention are the order of the day. This has also brought into existence a new technology called cloud, since with IoT comes a large number of devices connected to the internet continuously pumping data into the cloud for storage and processing. Another area benefited from the evolution of IoT is the wireless and wired connectivity through a wide range of connectivity standards. 
As with any technology, it has also created a lot of concerns regarding the security, privacy and ethics. 
  
Data protection issues created by new technologies are a threat which has been recognized by developers, public and also the governing body long back. The complexity of the system arises because of the various sensors and technologies which clearly tell the pattern of the activities of the individual as well an organization making us threat prone. Moreover, the volume of the data in the cloud makes it too difficult to recognize the privacy requirement of the data or to segregate open data from private data. Data analytics is another technology which supposedly increases the opportunity of increasing business by studying this private data collected from IoT and exploring ways to monetize them. It also helps the individual by recognizing their priorities and narrowing their search. But the data collected are real world data and aggregation of this data in the cloud is an open invitation to the hackers to study about the behaviors of the individuals. 
  
The special issues of Scalable Computing has attract related to the Role of Scalable Computing and Data Analytics in Evolution of Internet of Things has attracted 28 submissions from which were selected 12.

title: Introduction: The Convergence of AI Wearables and the Metaverse
abstract: The ongoing advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and wearable sensors coupled with the metaverse touch every field of study, as they intertwine the physical, digital, and cognitive realms in an unprecedented way. In this work, we establish an initial AI, wearables, and metaverse interconnection point in the field. We focus on the possible collaborations, socio-ethical considerations, and challenges in the field of research. We present the arguments that AI-powered inference, which can run on wearable devices, is capable of real-time, situational awareness, and adaptive real-time granularity. Concurrently, metaverse applications deliver real-time profiles for social collaboration and teleportation, significantly extending the physical. We assist with adaptive health surveillance, augmented human work, and new modes of work and education that span the monolithic physical and virtual realms. We discuss the health and social applications of real-time, edge, and federated learning, and the privacy framework for digital systems. Finally, we determine the most critical social and technological needs in the field: real-time privacy systems, human-centred interoperability, and social/secondary real-time systems. This chapter also analyses the social threats of surveillance, the erosion of bias, and the loss of consent, and proposes future investigations aimed at addressing this surveillance and bias erosion through auditing models with transparency, preserving architectures with privacy, and guiding governance models with regulation. Identifying the potential of technology and proposing balanced innovations, this chapter aims to assist responsible researchers and professionals in the construction of integrated systems that provide high technical quality, ethical values, and social quality.

title: Investigating The Role of Trust and Behavioral Barriers in Shaping Investor’s Decision to Delegate Portfolio Management to AI-Driven Robo-Advisors
venue: Nolegein - Journal of Organizational Behavior and Management
abstract: AI-based Robo-advisors have emerged at a striking pace across the Indian financial landscape, with disciplined, low-cost investment management options increasingly becoming accessible to a diverse retail investor market. Yet the decision to relinquish portfolio management to these algorithms is one substantial psychological hurdle that many still face. This paper aims to assess the role of trust dimensions and behavioral obstacles in adopting Robo-advisory services among Indian investors. Using secondary data from market research reports, academic papers, and fintech analyses, this paper outlines an important distinction in how trust dimensions impact adoption among the Indian investor population. Many factors become significant – three trust dimensions of algorithmic performance assessment, privacy reassurance and communication dissimilarity stand out, as well as three behavioral biases of algorithm aversion, loss aversion, and socio-emotional attachment. In this instance, algorithmic aversion refers to a distaste for Robo-advisor services despite evidence supporting the potential advantages of algorithmic performance over human-driven performance. Additionally, loss aversion means the risks of making financial sacrifices to an algorithm are more tangible than making sacrifices to a human endeavor. Finally, socio-emotional attachment refers to India’s reliance on interpersonal investment services and the challenge of overcoming such in-built historical behavior. Ultimately, this paper argues that potential Robo-advisory providers must adopt strategies that build trust to reach the average Indian investor beyond efficiency concerns. They must be demystified, privacy policies made more robust, and a hybrid approach that combines all benefits with easy-to-access human support might be best for a cultural image. Ultimately, this paper sets the foundation for understanding new markets regarding adoption and provides valuable insights for fintech startups and stakeholders seeking meaningful implementation to bridge the trust gap.

title: Investigating the Cross-app Data Sharing Implications of Using Android Health Connect
venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare
abstract: Mobile health and fitness (mHealth) apps are widely used, and they process sensitive user data. To improve the interoperability among them and enable fine-grained permission controls for users, Google strategically introduced an on-device centralized mHealth data sharing platform, Android Health Connect (AHC), in 2022. However, we argue that the current AHC design may exacerbate privacy risks because it enables broad but implicit mHealth data sharing across apps. In this article, we first conduct a cross-app data sharing study on 41 AHC-compatible apps; by analyzing their declared AHC-related permissions and privacy practice disclosures, we reveal that they can broadly and intensively share different types of mHealth data with each other but do not adequately disclose AHC-related practices. We further conduct an online user study for 105 participants to interact with our simulated AHC permission management interfaces for two apps; by quantitatively and qualitatively analyzing participants’ interactions and their responses to the follow-up questions, we demonstrate that most participants have a flawed understanding of AHC’s permission model and its implicit cross-app data sharing implications. Our findings highlight the pressing need to improve the design of this new and pivotal AHC platform to better protect mHealth app users’ privacy.

title: Investigation of Scientific Studies on Wearable Technologies in terms of Security and Privacy
venue: The Eurasia Proceedings of Educational and Social Sciences
abstract: This research aims to present the general situation of scientific publications in the WoS database dealing with wearable technologies in terms of security and privacy from a comprehensive and holistic perspective. A total of 71 publications were reached within the scope of the research by going through various screening processes. Document analysis method was used to collect the data, and content analysis method was used for the analysis. The results of the research show that there has been a steady increase in the number of publications on this subject since 2015. In particular, it has been observed that 86.8% of the publications have been published in the last five years. In addition, it has been revealed that the most publications on the subject are in the fields of "Computer Science", "Engineering", "Telecommunications" and "Science Technology". On the other hand, it has been seen that the concept of Security is used more than the concept of Privacy in the fields of Computer Science, Telecommunications and Engineering. In addition, when the keywords of the publications are mapped, it has been seen that the words "Wearable Technologies", "Security", "Privacy", "Internet of Things", "Authentication" and "Attack" are used more frequently.

IoT Enabled Mental Health Monitoring and AI Driven Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Systems for Personalized Treatment
abstract: The integration of Internet of Things (IoT) devices with artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced blockchain technologies is redefining the landscape of mental health care delivery. This book chapter explores the design and deployment of IoT-enabled mental health monitoring systems and AI-driven Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) interventions, emphasizing their potential to deliver personalized, scalable, and privacy-preserving treatment solutions. Continuous data streams from wearable sensors and mobile platforms provide real-time insights into behavioral patterns and emotional states, enabling adaptive therapeutic responses based on dynamic user conditions. The chapter investigates secure data transmission mechanisms, identity authentication protocols, privacy risk modeling strategies, and regulatory compliance measures essential for the ethical handling of psychological data. By introducing blockchain and federated learning frameworks, the text highlights a decentralized approach to AI-based therapy that ensures data sovereignty, transparency, and trustworthiness. Through a multidisciplinary lens, the chapter presents architectural models, trust frameworks, and interoperability solutions that form the backbone of secure and intelligent mental health ecosystems. The fusion of emerging technologies in this context promises not only enhanced treatment accessibility but also a paradigm shift in patient empowerment and care outcomes.

title: IoT Security Challenges and Solutions: Threats, Standards and Layered Protection
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has become an important part of modern life. Smart homes, wearable devices, healthcare systems, industrial machines, and smart agriculture use connected devices to collect and exchange information. Although IoT makes many activities easier, it also introduces security and privacy risks. Weak passwords, insecure communication, outdated firmware, unauthorized access, and data leakage can expose devices and users to cyberattacks. This paper examines major security challenges faced by IoT systems and discusses practical solutions based on established cybersecurity guidance. It synthesizes three complementary perspectives: academic survey research on IoT security, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) IoT security baseline, and the OWASP Internet of Things security guidance. The study explains common threats, reviews relevant standards, and proposes a layered protection model covering devices, networks, applications, data, and system management. It concludes that IoT security should be considered throughout the device lifecycle rather than added only after a problem occurs

title: IoT and Machine Learning Based Attacks Detection Model on Wearable Health Care Devices
venue: South Eastern European Journal of Public Health
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) in healthcare is becoming more and more popular in the field of research aimed at improving the effectiveness of intelligent healthcare networks and applications. Nonetheless, distinct risks affect the security and privacy of data in smart health (S-Health). IoT enables healthcare professionals to engage with patients more proactively and with greater vigilance. Smart gadgets with tiny sensors attached to them that communicate with one another to track each other's performance are part of the Internet of Things. To defend S-Health from MITM attacks. The suggested method employs two layers of machine learning algorithms for attack detection and security mechanisms, including low-cost access policies for SHRs (Smart Health Records), lightweight IoT detection schemes, and timely detection of to lessen their impact on the network. According to simulation data, the suggested Hybrid ML performs better than current methods and has a higher attack detection rate overall. The main goal of this research article is to develop an attack detection technique.

title: IoT based cardiovascular health monitoring: Ensuring security with machine learning and AI techniques
IoT forensics
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has transformed the digital world, linking billions of devices in healthcare, smart homes, transportation, and agriculture. While increased connectivity improves convenience and productivity, it has also created humongous security threats and forensic challenges. The nature of IoT devices is such that they produce enormous amounts of data, offering potential for forensic analysis but making the processes of data acquisition, preservation, and analysis challenging due to their heterogeneity and resource constraint. This review gives an overall assessment of the state of the art of IoT forensics with a special focus on the specific challenges that arise from the IoT environment. The primary challenges are the lack of standardization of forensic tools, the difficulty in extracting evidence from complex ecosystems of IoT devices, privacy, and the risk of tampering with the information. Application of non-forensic and commercial tools has been promising but consequently has created the need for specialized frameworks and approaches specifically designed for IoT-specific cases. Recent techniques—like electromagnetic side-channel analysis and machine learning—promise to potentially improve forensic investigations; however, in practice, applications are very few due to technical and logistic barriers. This would also ensure integrity and immutability in the data by blockchain integration on one side and, on the other, developing extensible plug-ins for diverse IoT devices; artificial intelligence will also be essential in analyzing complex datasets. Case studies depict how traces left behind by IoT devices, from wearables to smart home systems, have been instrumental in providing crucial evidence in investigations. However, this remains theoretical and has seen no practical large-scale implementation—the gap that needs bridging with frameworks. We have also identified open research directions, such as the requirement for interoperable forensic tools, scalable frameworks for analyzing IoT-generated data, and privacy-preserving mechanisms. Addressing these challenges will make IoT forensics a strong discipline that can rise to the current and future demands of supporting law enforcement and cybersecurity efforts in an increasingly interconnected world.

title: IoT in Healthcare
abstract: The fields of computer science and electronics have merged to result into one of the most notable technological advances in the form of realization of the Internet of Things. The market for healthcare services has increased exponentially at the same time security flaws could pose serious threats to the health and safety of patients using wearable technologies and RFID. The volume and sensitivity of data traversing the IoT environment makes dangerous to messages and data could be intercepted and manipulated while in transit. This scenario must absolutely respect the confidentiality and privacy of patient's medical information. Therefore, this chapter presents various security issues or vulnerabilities with respect to attacks and various situations how information will be attacked by the attacker in healthcare IoT. The working principle of healthcare IoT also discussed. The chapter concludes the performance of various attacks based on the past work. In the future this work can be extended to introduce a novel mechanism to resolve various security issues in healthcare IoT.

title: IoT in healthcare ecosystem
abstract: In recent years, IoT has been revolutionizing the technology landscape, leading to explosive growth in fields like automated manufacturing, asset management, and wearable consumer healthcare products. IoT’s presence can be seen in all domains. Ever since IoT gained its entry into the medical field, there has been a magnificent transformation in the healthcare domain. Personal healthcare is now made a reality with IoT offering solutions in several dimensions like remote healthcare;smart clothing such as smartwatches, smart bands, and smart pants;and telemedicine like smart pills and personal care robots. This chapter gives a comprehensive walkthrough of IoT in the healthcare ecosystem, addressing the different applications of IoT in healthcare, the architecture models, challenges faced by IoT in healthcare, security practices and issues, and the future of IoT in the domain. In the first section, IoT applications in healthcare are discussed, which include patient-centric applications like remote health monitoring and critical care monitoring;and hospital-centric IoT applications such as the deployment of the staff, reducing charting times, and real-time location of medical equipment, subsequently followed by a discussion on how the data collected from the patient-centric and hospital-centric applications contribute to the ease of other domains like health insurance;and then, IoT’s support toward the pharmaceutical industry to restrict counterfeit medicine is discussed. Secondly, the implementation designs of healthcare IoT are discussed. Apart from the traditional cloud services, new offerings like fog and edge computing have seen a spike in recent years. Fog and edge computing are considered intelligent and flexible architectures. The subsequent section deals with architecture designs and the advantages and challenges of the two computing models. The next section demonstrates the actual implementation methodologies of the two applications in the following domains in detail: (1) Heart disease prediction and (2) healthcare IoT-based affective state mining using deep convolutional neural networks. The following section discusses the challenges faced by IoT in the healthcare domain. In general, the challenges can be categorized into technological challenges;people-oriented challenges like the acceptance of IoT in the healthcare domain;and finally, security bottlenecks. The data generated and maintained by the IoT platforms serves as a gold mine for different healthcare professionals for future research and development in the medical field and the health insurance providers and pharmaceutical industries for their benefits. Hence, more emphasis is given to the security and privacy aspects of how the domain handles sensitive data of the patients. The next section provides insights into the security issues along with the cyber threats and attacks faced by healthcare IoT and the defensive mechanisms. Furthermore, this chapter deals with the IoT’s role in combatting the novel coronavirus that has caused an unprecedented global pandemic. Finally, the future of IoT is talked about. With the advent of 5G and an upsurge in artificial intelligence, the different dimensions of the IoT that are expected to see an outburst of growth are discussed. © 2022 Elsevier Inc. title: IoT security and privacy assessment using software-defined radios
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has seen exceptional adoption in recent years, resulting in an unprecedented level of connectivity in personal and industrial domains. In parallel, software-defined radio (SDR) technology has become increasingly powerful, making it a compelling tool for wireless security research across multiple communication protocols. Specifically, SDRs are capable of manipulating the physical layer of protocols in software, which would otherwise be implemented statically in hardware. This flexibility enables research that goes beyond the boundaries of protocol specifications. This dissertation pursues four research directions that are either enabled by software-defined radio technology, or advance its utility for security research. First, we investigate the anti-tracking mechanisms defined by the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) wireless protocol. This protocol, present in virtually all wearable smart devices, implements address randomization in order to prevent unwanted tracking of its users. By analyzing raw advertising data from BLE devices using SDRs, we identify a vulnerability that allows an attacker to track a BLE device beyond the address randomization defined by the protocol. Second, we implement a compact, SDR-based testbed for physical layer benchmarking of wireless devices. The testbed is capable of emulating multiple data transmissions and produce intentional signal corruption in very precisely defined ways in order to investigate receiver robustness and undefined device behavior in the presence of malformed packets. We subject a range of Wi-Fi and Zigbee devices to specifically crafted packet collisions and "truncated packets" as a way to fingerprinting wireless device chipsets. Third, we introduce a middleware framework, coined "Snout", to improves accessibility and usability of SDRs. The architecture provides standardized data pipelines as well as an abstraction layer to GNU Radio flowgraphs which power SDR signal processing. This abstraction layer improves usability and maintainability by providing a declarative experiment configuration format instead of requiring constant manipulation of the signal processing code during experimentation. We show that Snout does not result in significant computational overhead, and maintains a predictable and modest memory footprint. Finally, we address the visibility problem arising from the growing number of IoT protocols across large bands of radio spectrum. We model an SDR-based IoT monitor which is capable of scanning multiple channels (including across multiple protocols), and employs channel switching policies to maximize freshness of information obtained by transmitting devices. We present multiple policies and compare their performance against an optimal Markov Decision Process (MDP) model, as well as through event-based simulation using real-world device traffic. The results of this work demonstrate the use of SDR technology in privacy and security research of IoT device communication, and open up opportunities for further low-layer protocol discoveries that require the use of software-defined radio as a research tool.

title: IoT-Based Healthcare: Assessing Its Actualities, Possibilities, and Concerns
abstract: The healthcare industry is transforming by the emergence of IoT-enabled devices and systems including wearable fitness trackers, connected blood pressure monitors, remote patient monitoring systems, smart pill dispensers, telemedicine and robotic surgery. These innovations improve patient engagement, emergency response, preventive care, resource management, continuous monitoring, clinical research etc. Major companies like Verily by Alphabet, Amazon Web Services IoT, Microsoft Azure IoT, Philips Healthcare, GE Healthcare, Medtronic, Cisco Systems, IBM Watson Health, Qualcomm Life, Honeywell Lifecare Solutions are investing heavily in this domain. Innovative start-ups are also contributing such as BioIntellisens’ biosensing patches, Huma Therapeutics’ chronic disease management wearables, Nura&s;s earbuds for stress management, Sonde Health&s;s AI-powered portable ultrasound devices, and Termdrop&s;s ovulation-tracking sensors. Despite its potential, IoT healthcare raises ethical concerns, including privacy, data security, accuracy, bias, autonomy, equity, and psychological impacts. Legal challenges such as data ownership, liability, regulatory gaps, cybersecurity threats, and risks of misdiagnosis and malpractice further complicate its adoption. Adequate regulations are crucial to address these 380 challenges, ensuring user trust and enabling the safe and effective integration of IoT technologies into healthcare systems. IoT healthcare holds great promise for advancing medicine but must overcome significant ethical and legal hurdles to fulfill its potential.

title: IoT-Based Smart Healthcare Monitoring Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Technologies, Challenges, and Innovations
venue: IEEE International Conference on Computing, Applications and Systems (COMPAS)
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has transformed the healthcare space with efficient, constant management of vital health measures using wearables, ambient or embedded systems, and mobile platform applications. The concept of these systems has great utility for chronic disease patients and those coming from low resource settings and rural areas. This paper provides a systematic review of IoT systems applied in healthcare, emphasizing on healthcare monitoring technologies through wearable devices, ambient systems, implantable devices, mobile applications, and cloud edge computing frameworks. The contributions of each category are presented along with barriers and key applications in healthcare settings for the respective subcategories, with particular consideration for the issue of the value to the patient and the extent of health system resource use provision. IoT systems for healthcare also have barriers for a system such as challenges of integration, security of data, safety of devices, battery consumption, and legislation policies.Before the healthcare sector can realize the full prospect of the IoT, issues like these will have to be resolved. Furthermore, an objective of this review is to identify areas where additional research is needed to create a resilient, adaptable, and inclusive IoT architecture for use in the healthcare sector facilitating efficiency and fairness.

title: Is there an app for that? A Systematic Search and Analysis of mHealth apps in the digital marketplace for pediatric cancer patients (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND The significant increase in smart phone ownership has led to a rise in mobile health (mHealth) app use. This type of app aims to improve patient outcomes by reducing barriers to recovery through various features. Developing tailored features through mHealth apps creates a pathway to address healthcare needs of pediatric cancer patients and their families who have complex care needs. However, few apps are designed specifically to integrate with pediatric cancer care. OBJECTIVE This study reports a systematic search and analysis findings of mHealth apps available on the Apple App and Google Play Store, designed for managing pediatric cancer through a list of features that serve patients, caregivers, or both audiences. METHODS Following the PRISMA guidelines, we reviewed apps for pediatric cancer patients and caregivers that were available as of January 2024. We searched the Apple App and Google Play Stores with a list of keyword combinations focusing on pediatric cancer care. Inclusion criteria were (a) specifically targeted apps on pediatric oncology patients, their families, or both; (b) available in either app store, and (c) available in English (not exclusively). Once identified, apps were assessed by reviewing their features, user ratings, and app store information with descriptive analysis. RESULTS In total, 22 apps were identified, and 17 of those apps were available on both platforms. The most popular features (n=12) amongst the selection in order were resource sharing, symptom tracking, reminders, care team connections, journaling, community support, medication tracking, data visualizations, appointment tracking, health activity data, data sharing, and integration with other health apps. These platforms designed their features and interface for caregivers (n=9) more frequently than the patients (n=7) while a subset of apps created options for both users (n=6). Out of 18 apps with publicly available reviews, 16 of them were rated highly (M=4.4, Min=3.1, Max=5.0, SD=0.59). A small subset (n=3) achieved over 5000 downloads while the remaining 19 apps had fewer than 500. Despite the growing inclusivity of multilingual platforms, more than half of the apps (n=12) were not publicly available in languages other than English. Apps that required extra hardware or software requested access to a range of device functionalities (M=2.72, Min=0, Max=10, SD=3.13). CONCLUSIONS Our review highlights the promising yet underdeveloped potential of mHealth apps in pediatric oncology care, underscoring the urgent need for more inclusive, comprehensive, and integrative digital health solutions. Future developments should actively involve key stakeholders from the pediatric oncology community, including patients, families, and healthcare professionals, to ensure the apps meet specific needs while addressing linguistic and cultural barriers. Our findings could guide developers, patients and caregivers, and healthcare providers towards understanding the state of pediatric oncology mHealth and approaches to enhancing existing platforms.

title: LLM-Orchestrated Clinical Decision Platforms Integrating HL7-FHIR Interoperability with Homomorphic Encryption for Distributed Healthcare Analytics Security
venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
abstract: Healthcare systems are undergoing rapid digital transformation driven by the increasing adoption of electronic health records, telemedicine platforms, wearable medical devices, cloud-native infrastructures, and artificial intelligence-enabled clinical support systems.While these technologies improve healthcare accessibility and precision-driven treatment delivery, they simultaneously introduce significant challenges associated with fragmented data ecosystems, interoperability barriers, privacy preservation, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and secure multi-institutional analytics.Conventional centralized healthcare architectures remain inadequate for supporting real-time, privacy-preserving clinical intelligence across geographically distributed healthcare networks.In response to these limitations, emerging large language model (LLM)-driven orchestration frameworks provide advanced capabilities for contextual reasoning, semantic workflow automation, intelligent clinical interpretation, and adaptive decision support within complex healthcare environments.This study presents a secure LLM-orchestrated clinical decision platform that integrates HL7-FHIR interoperability standards with homomorphic encryption to enable protected distributed healthcare analytics without compromising sensitive patient information.The proposed architecture facilitates standardized healthcare data exchange, encrypted computation across decentralized systems, privacy-preserving federated intelligence, and secure clinical collaboration among hospitals, laboratories, insurers, and public health agencies.Furthermore, the framework strengthens regulatory compliance, semantic interoperability, and resilience against cyber threats while supporting scalable AI-driven healthcare analytics.The study concludes by examining implementation challenges, computational trade-offs, governance requirements, and future directions for secure intelligent healthcare ecosystems.

title: LOCATION SHARING: PRIVACY THREATS AND PROTECTION
venue: Archivio Istituzionale della Ricerca (Universita Degli Studi Di Milano)
abstract: In recent years there has been a growing increase in the number of users that use smartphones,tablets, wearable technologies and other devices that users have with them constantly. The capability of these latest generation mobile devices to detect the position of the users has led to the emergence of ad-hoc services as well as geo-aware social networks (GeoSN). Even if the sharing of our locations can enhance many useful services, there are several practical cases that unveil the danger of sharing location indiscriminately. For instance, let?s suppose that a user has just told everyone that he is on vacation (and not at his house): if he adds how long his trip is, then thieves know exactly how much time they have to rob him. Many contributions in the scientific literature have shown how through the location information it is possible to infer several information about the user. It has been shown that it is possible to identify user?s identity, if he is anonymous in the LBS, and, if the user is not anonymous, it is feasible to infer user?s home location, habits and also politic preferences and sexual orientation. The scientific literature reflects this concerns, proposing many contributions that deal with privacy, in general, and location privacy, specifically. This dissertation deals with location privacy in Location Based Services and Geo-Social Networks. The goal is two-fold: on one hand we want to motivate the importance of the location privacy topic by identifying the privacy threats of sharing locations. In particular we study a new privacy threat, the co-location threat, and we further study an already known threat stemming from the use of distance preserving transformations.On the other hand, we want to propose privacy preserving techniques and tools: we propose a novel privacy preserving technique as well as presenting three (spatial and/or temporal) cloaking techniques, specifically designed for privacy techniques in which the privacy is granted by the use of a location?s generalisation.

title: Labbi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Complete summary The document develops Labbi, a personalised AI and augmented-reality laboratory assistant built around an independent, low-voltage safety-training system. The design evolves from LabShield, a simulated hazard-detection and evacuation platform, into a chibi-style fairy companion that supports laboratory safety, research, office work, learning, wellbeing reminders, and incident recording. The central rule remains that the AI must be advisory and user-facing, while deterministic safety functions remain under a separate controller. 1. Safety concept and design limits The document rejects the idea of building a device intended to absorb or withstand an explosion. Instead, it proposes an explosion early-warning and evacuation system based on: Hazard-specific gas, heat, smoke, or pressure detection Fail-safe control with battery backup Audible and visual alarms Remote notification Professional emergency-shutdown and ventilation interfaces Clearly marked escape routes An outdoor assembly point Manual emergency activation Procedures that prevent re-entry until the area is authorised as safe Testing must use simulated signals or safe calibration methods. Explosives, flammable mixtures, hazardous gases, pressure vessels, and live emergency equipment must never be used for testing. For a chemistry or teaching laboratory, the proposed operating model is detect, warn, isolate, and evacuate. The system is intended to reduce harm from accidental vapour releases, fires, and pressure events, not to withstand a deliberate explosion. Any real deployment would require review by an environmental health and safety officer, a fire-protection engineer, and the relevant building or fire-code authority. 2. LabShield Trainer v1 The first practical build is LabShield Trainer v1, a low-voltage tabletop simulator. It is designed to teach hazard detection, alarm response, simulated shutdown, evacuation, and event recording without connecting to real laboratory infrastructure. The proposed hardware includes: Arduino Uno or ESP32 Breadboard and jumper wires Push buttons or toggle switches to simulate hazards A potentiometer to simulate changing sensor values Red, yellow, and green LEDs LED resistors A 5 V piezo buzzer Small OLED or LCD display Large emergency-alarm button USB power bank or regulated 5 V supply Fuse or resettable fuse Enclosure and secure connectors Optional real-time clock and microSD logging modules Optional low-voltage warning beacon The switches simulate vapor hazards, heat hazards, ventilation failure, and completed evacuation. The prototype must not include flammable gases, chemical vapours, gas cylinders, solenoid valves, heaters, ignition sources, pressure vessels, suppression agents, explosives, or connections to real ventilation, gas, or emergency systems. The intended behaviour is: Normal state: green indicator and “System normal” Simulated hazard: red indicator, buzzer, and hazard identification Ventilation failure: yellow fault indicator, warning tone, and simulated-shutdown indication Emergency button: immediate alarm Evacuation button: stops the evacuation timer and records response time Sensor or wiring fault: yellow fault indicator and a separate fault message Reset: permitted only after the simulated emergency has been acknowledged The shutdown output must be a clearly labelled LED such as SIMULATED SHUTDOWN. It must not be a relay controlling real equipment. The recommended build sequence is to install the indicators and buzzer first, then hazard inputs, emergency controls, display, alarm-state programming, evacuation timing, and finally event logging. 3. Simulated suppression sequence The document adds a simulated fire-suppression module, not a real discharge system. The module uses a suppression-status LED, pre-discharge warning LED, separate warning tone, test button, protected reset button, display messages, and optional event logging. The proposed sequence is: A simulated heat or fire input activates. The red alarm and evacuation buzzer start. The display shows EVACUATE. A short simulated pre-discharge warning begins. A blue indicator shows SIMULATED SUPPRESSION ACTIVE. The evacuation timer continues. The system remains locked until the reset procedure is completed. The event records the alarm, evacuation, simulated suppression, and reset stages. The output must be an LED or display only. It must not connect to pressurised cylinders, water lines, chemical agents, aerosol cartridges, valves, or real fire-control equipment. The educational purpose is to demonstrate decision sequencing and human response, not to discharge an extinguishing agent. 4. Separation between the safety controller and AI The document requires two independent systems. Safety controller The Arduino or ESP32 handles all immediate and predictable functions: Alarm activation Evacuation timing Simulated suppression Sensor-fault detection Manual emergency activation Reset lockout These functions must continue working if the AI, computer, internet connection, or display fails. AI assistant layer The AI receives simulated sensor data from the controller through a laptop or Raspberry Pi. It may: Identify the most likely simulated hazard Detect unusual sensor patterns Flag disconnected or failing sensors Explain why an alarm activated Recommend evacuation or later inspection steps Score evacuation response time Generate training reports Predict maintenance needs from logged faults The AI may say that a possible heat event and ventilation fault were detected and advise evacuation, but it must not activate real suppression, operate chemical or gas valves, override or delay an alarm, or declare an area safe for re-entry. The proposed AI test scenarios include normal operation, heat events, vapour warnings, ventilation failure, disconnected sensors, simultaneous faults, power interruption, and false alarms. Evaluation should measure detection accuracy, false-alarm rate, explanation time, evacuation response time, and safe failure when the AI is disconnected. 5. Office and learning companion The AI is also designed as an office companion, separate from the safety controller. Smart glasses may show the assistant, but a projector is unnecessary for the glasses themselves. A projector is relevant only when a shared wall or desk display is desired. Homemade laser projection aimed at the eyes is explicitly excluded. In office mode, the companion can provide: Time, reminders, timers, and checklists Calendar and task summaries Document drafting and organisation Email or message drafting, with human approval before sending File search Meeting-note preparation In theory mode, it can explain chemistry, create flashcards and quizzes, check formulas and units, provide step-by-step conceptual explanations, summarise uploaded material, and distinguish established information from uncertainty. In safety mode, it displays the alarm state, shows EVACUATE, reads the warning aloud, stops distracting office functions, and remains unable to reset alarms, activate suppression, or authorise re-entry. The AI receives information from the safety controller but must never send commands back to it. 6. Privacy and wellbeing The proposed privacy controls include: Microphone and camera off by default Physical microphone mute switch Push-to-talk operation Visible recording indicator No recording unless explicitly enabled No face recognition Local processing where practical Human approval before sending messages, deleting files, or changing appointments Wellbeing functions are optional and non-medical. They include break, hydration, stretching, posture, work-hour, focus-session, mood-check-in, breathing, and excessive-work reminders. The assistant must not infer that someone is stressed, depressed, or otherwise mentally unwell from their face, voice, typing, or work speed. It should ask whether the user wants a break rather than make a diagnosis or claim. 7. Accident and incident recording The document defines “measuring accidents” as detecting, recording, and analysing incidents rather than diagnosing injuries. The system may record: Time and location Triggering sensor event Incident, near miss, or equipment fault classification Alarm-to-evacuation response time Whether the simulated suppression sequence started Injuries entered by an authorised person Corrective actions and completion status Repeated hazards and trends Possible inputs include a manual incident button, a voice command such as “log a near miss,” read-only safety-controller data, and an optional wearable accelerometer for a possible fall signal. A human must confirm an incident before it is finalised. The design excludes facial recognition, automatic injury diagnosis, camera-only accident detection, and AI-generated blame. During an emergency, Labbi must stop normal tasks, change to a clear warning appearance, display and speak evacuation instructions, show the configured assembly-point direction, log the event and response time, and remain silent about ordinary office or theory tasks until an authorised person clears the emergency. 8. Labbi’s character and procedural personality The final assistant is called Labbi. She is envisioned as a small, expressive, fairy-like laboratory companion who is curious about science, gentle, encouraging, organised, honest about uncertainty, protective without being dramatic, and personalised to the user’s name, subjects, schedule, learning level, and communication style. Her personality is procedural, meaning it is expressed through defined rules rather than unpredictable improvisation: Normal operation: calm and cheerful Learning mode: curious and patient Task mode: focused and concise Unusual sensor pattern: observant and cautious System fault: clear and technical Emergency: serious, direct, and repetitive Recover

title: Last Lecture: Tips for Lawyers Who Want to Get Good Results for Clients and Make Money
venue: University of Missouri School of Law Scholarship Repository (University of Missouri)
abstract: Lawyers often assume that they know what their clients want-to get as much money or pay as little money as possible. While clients usually are very concerned about their bottom line, they often have additional interests. In virtually any kind of case, parties may have an interest in being treated respectfully and fairly, minimizing the cost and length of the process, freeing time to focus on matters other than the dispute, reducing the emotional wear and tear caused by continued disputing, and protecting privacy and reputations. Plaintiffs may have interests such as obtaining favorable tax consequences, getting nonmonetary opportunities, and receiving explanations or apologies. Defendants may have interests such as receiving acknowledgments about the lack of merit of the charges, making payments in kind, stretching payments over time, sharing liability with other defendants, preventing ancillary harm (such as loss of credit rating or business opportunities), receiving favorable tax consequences, obtaining nondisclosure agreements, and avoiding future lawsuits. If you satisfy your clients' interests, they are more likely to pay your bills, hire you again, and refer other clients to you.

title: Laws for COVID-19 Containment and Human Rights Consideration
venue: Medical Journal of Dr D Y Patil Vidyapeeth
abstract: Dear Sir, COVID-19 is still the public health problem around our world. For containing this new infection, it requires good collaboration from everyone. A good policies making is required to derive a good public measure for COVID-19 containment.[1] In order to implement a preventive measure, it sometimes requires laws. In many countries, there are many kinds of laws regarding COVID-19 containments. Example of commonly used laws is “facemask laws.” In brief, one who does not wear facemask and expose to the community might be fined.[2] Many countries implement specific laws for mandatory facemask wearing during COVID-19 outbreak. In some situation, a strict legal control such as curfew implementation might be used. Nevertheless, an important issue is on the appropriateness of legal control. Some legal measure might violate human rights. For example, in a setting with a dictator leadership, the local people might not be permitted to have COVID-19 and one who get the disease will be seriously punished. Some might impose strange laws to force local people to buy modern smartphone and have some internet apps for identification during COVID-19 outbreak. Ones who do not follow the laws might be fined or jailed. The aims of those laws are good, focusing on strict disease control. However, the important question is whether it is appropriate or not. Some too sophisticate legal control might be hard to follow and many low educated poor persons might not possible to follow. Indeed, for public health control, it requires exact public health expert for generating policies. The poor policies might be from nonexpert. Sometimes, the military style laws are can implement and it might cause problem rather than a successful disease control. Last but not least, any legal enforcement can affect individual privacy. It is an interest dilemma issue for discussing regarding strict legal control versus human rights. A pandemic can do harm to general people but inappropriate public health policies might sometimes do more harm. Ethical consideration is required before implementation of any public health measure for COVID-19 containment.[3] Financial support and sponsorship Nil.
