Privacy-Aware Access Governance: Aligning Access Decisions with Organizational Privacy Commitments
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
abstract: Modern organizations make data-access decisions through complex information systems, while the privacy commitments that constrain those decisions are documented separately in privacy notices, internal policies, and compliance guidelines. This separation creates a governance gap: a runtime access decision may be technically permitted by the organization’s access-control policy yet difficult to justify against its stated privacy commitments. For compliance, audit, and IT governance functions, the central question is no longer only who can access what, but also why this access is justified, under which privacy commitment, and who can explain it? This research proposes Privacy-Aware Access Governance as an organizational capability for aligning runtime access decisions with documented privacy commitments. The proposed framework would represent privacy primitives, including purpose, consent, obligation, and retention, as governance-relevant attributes within attribute-based access control, and use graph-based traceability to connect runtime access decisions, the rules that authorized them, and the privacy commitments that constrain them. Organizations could then ask end-to-end questions such as: Which rule authorized this access? Which privacy commitment constrains this data use? Does the access exceed the stated purpose or consent boundary? Realizing this capability requires integrating three pieces that have so far been studied in isolation: graph-based representation and analysis of access policies, LLM-assisted translation of natural-language policies into machine-enforceable rules, and LLM-assisted analysis of natural-language privacy policies (Yang et al., 2024, 2025a, 2025b). Several open questions motivate the desire for AMCIS audience feedback: How should privacy-aware access governance be evaluated from the perspective of compliance, auditability, and decision quality? What level of traceability do privacy officers and auditors need to trust LLM-assisted policy analysis? How should organizations divide responsibility between automated extraction and human review when access-control rules are derived from natural-language policies?

title: Privacy-Aware Federated Learning for Intelligent XR Systems at the Wireless Edge
venue: International Conference on Smart Applications, Communications and Networking (SmartNets)
abstract: Mixed Reality (XR) systems increasingly integrate artificial intelligence to enable real-time perception, classification, and interaction across healthcare, education, and industrial domains. However, these systems often require transmitting highly sensitive data, such as body movements, biometric signals, and spatial environments, to centralized servers for training, raising serious privacy and bandwidth concerns. In this paper, we present a novel federated learning (FL) framework for intelligent XR systems that performs on-device training and model aggregation at the wireless edge. Our architecture enables multi-user XR devices, including headsets, wearables, and IoT sensors, to collaboratively learn user behavior patterns without exposing raw data. We evaluate our system across simulated XR datasets involving gesture recognition and avatar personalization, comparing centralized and federated configurations in terms of model accuracy, communication cost, latency, and privacy leakage. Results show that our FL framework achieves comparable performance to centralized training while significantly reducing bandwidth consumption and exposure to inference attacks. We also present a detailed analysis of inference time and convergence behavior in edge environments. This work demonstrates the feasibility and necessity of privacy-preserving learning for next-generation XR networks and lays the foundation for future deployment in sensitive domains such as telehealth, rehabilitation, and smart training.

title: Privacy-Aware Modeling of Healthcare IoT With Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Networked medical devices have revolutionized modern healthcare by offering round-the-clock patient monitoring, distant diagnosis, and real-time data transmission. The benefits are, however, overshadowed by catastrophic cybersecurity and privacy concerns. Pacemakers, insulin pumps, and wearable monitors, for example, are vulnerable to wireless network use and are vulnerable to hacker attacks, data breaches, and unauthorized access. Weak authentication methods, unsecured data transmission, and obsolete software are susceptible to attack by patients and medical professionals alike, ranging from compromised patient health data to patient safety risk. The problem in this research is solved by developing a robust prediction model via bi-stacked artificial neural networks (ANNs) for cyber attack detection and classification against medical device network security. A large dataset was collected, preprocessed, and boosted with particle swarm optimization (PSO) for feature extraction.

title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies for Mobile Applications and Services
abstract: Over a third of the world 's population owns a smartphone. As generic computing devices that support a large and heterogeneous collection of mobile applications (apps), smartphones provide a plethora of functionalities and services to billions of users. But the use of these mobile apps and services often introduces privacy risks for users. First, app developers often fail to take into account the fact that as smartphones are generic computing devices, they do not provide adequate privacy and security guarantees for certain types of apps (e.g., those that collect and process sensitive data). As a result, new security and privacy threats are introduced by such apps. Second, due to the lack of privacy by design, apps often over-collect information about users, and can misuse the collected data. Our goal in this thesis is to identify privacy risks in mobile apps and services, and to design privacy-enhancing technologies to mitigate the identified threats. To broaden the impact of our research efforts, we focus on popular apps and services that are currently used by millions of users, and potentially by billions in the future. These include three use-cases: (mobile-health) mHealth apps, ride-hailing services, and activity-tracking services. First, in the case of mHealth apps, we find that the Android operating system allows apps to easily fingerprint and identify other apps installed on the same phone. This causes privacy problems for mHealth apps, because the presence of an mHealth app can already reveal the medical conditions of its users. We investigate the apps' ability to fingerprint other apps and present HideMyApp, a practical system for hiding the presence of sensitive apps on Android. HideMyApp works on stock Android, and no firmware modification or root privilege is required. Second, in ride-hailing services (e.g., Uber), to use the services, riders have to share their pick-up and drop-off locations with service providers. Consequently, the service providers can infer sensitive information about riders' activities (e.g., their visits to health clinics). Therefore, we propose ORide, a privacy-preserving ride-hailing service that efficiently supports the anonymous matching of riders and drivers. Also, ORide still supports functionalities that are often considered as important as privacy, including accountability, payment and reputation-rating operations. Third, in activity-tracking services (e.g., RunKeeper), users report their location-based activities to service providers and obtain rewards based on their performance. However, from the location traces, the service providers can infer sensitive information about the users, e.g., their home/work addresses. Also, to obtain better rewards, the users might try to falsely report their activities to the service providers. Therefore, we propose SecureRun, a solution that enables service providers to compute accurate activity summaries of the users, while guaranteeing the users' location privacy vis-a-vis the service providers. In short, in this thesis, we identify privacy risks in popular mobile apps and services. We show that it is possible to provide them with added privacy, while preserving their rich functionality and usability. We are confident that the contributions presented in this thesis will inspire more future work on protecting users' privacy, not only in the context of mobile apps and services, but also in many other contexts brought about by new technological advances.

title: Privacy-Preserving Boosting with Random Linear Classifiers for Learning from User-Generated Data
Privacy-Preserving Covert Communication Using Encrypted Wearable Gesture Recognition
abstract: Secure communication is essential in covert and safety-critical settings where verbal interactions may expose user intent or operational context. Wearable gesture-based communication enables low-effort, nonverbal interaction, but existing systems leak motion data, intermediate representations, or inference outputs to untrusted infrastructure, enabling intent inference, behavioral biometric leakage, and insider attacks. This work proposes a privacy-preserving gesture-based covert communication system that ensures, no raw sensor signals, learned features, or classification outputs are exposed to any third-party. The system employs a multi-party homomorphic learning pipeline for gesture recognition directly over encrypted motion data, preventing adversaries from inferring gesture semantics, replaying sensor traces, or accessing intermediate representations. To our knowledge, this work is the first to apply encrypted gesture recognition in a wearable-based covert communication setting. We design and evaluate haptic and visual feedback mechanisms for covert signal delivery and evaluate the system using 600 gesture samples from a commodity smartwatch, achieving over 94.44% classification accuracy and demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed system with practical deployability from high-performance systems to resource-constrained edge devices.

title: Privacy-Preserving Feature Extraction with Differentially Private Contrastive Objectives for Time Series
abstract: The proliferation of ubiquitous sensing technologies has resulted in an explosion of time series data generation, ranging from personal health metrics collected by wearable devices to complex industrial telemetry in smart infrastructures. While Deep Learning has demonstrated remarkable utility in extracting latent representations from such high-dimensional temporal data, the deployment of these models raises severe privacy concerns. In particular, the inversion of feature embeddings can inadvertently reveal sensitive attributes of the underlying subjects. This paper introduces a novel framework for Privacy-Preserving Feature Extraction using Differentially Private Contrastive Learning (DP-CL). We propose a rigorous methodology that integrates gradient perturbation mechanisms directly into the optimization of a normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss (NT-Xent) adapted for temporal data. By enforcing Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees during the pre-training phase, we ensure that the resulting encoder yields representations that are robust against membership inference and reconstruction attacks while maintaining high downstream utility. Our approach addresses the specific challenges of applying DP to contrastive objectives, such as the sensitivity of gradient magnitudes in projection heads and the impact of noise on alignment and uniformity metrics. Extensive experiments on standard multivariate time series benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves a superior trade-off between privacy budgets and classification accuracy compared to traditional auto-encoding baselines and supervised differentially private training.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Models for Telehealth: Architecture, Implementation, and Performance Analysis
venue: Digital health & telemonitoring advances E: 3117-6461 | P: 3117-647X
abstract: Telehealth systems generate vast amounts of sensitive patient data, requiring secure, scalable, and privacy-preserving computational frameworks. Federated Learning (FL), a decentralized machine-learning paradigm, allows multiple telehealth nodes to collaboratively train predictive models without sharing raw data, thus reducing privacy risks and data transfer burdens. This research investigates privacy-preserving FL models tailored for telehealth applications and evaluates their architectural design, implementation feasibility, and performance efficiency. A multi-site experimental framework involving remote clinics, wearable devices, and hospital servers was designed to assess the impacts of data heterogeneity, communication latency, encryption overhead, and model accuracy. The study incorporates secure aggregation protocols, homomorphic encryption layers, differential privacy (DP) noise calibration, and optimized communication compression to ensure user data confidentiality. Quantitative results show that privacy-preserving FL achieves nearly comparable accuracy to centralized models while significantly improving resilience against data breaches. The architectural and performance analysis demonstrates that an integrated pipeline of FL + DP + secure aggregation offers a robust solution for sensitive telehealth environments such as chronic disease monitoring, medical imaging, and remote diagnostics. The findings contribute to advancing secure digital health infrastructures and provide actionable design guidelines for healthcare institutions and telehealth vendors.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for EEG-Based Biometric Recognition in AI-Enabled Epilepsy Detection
abstract: The convergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence and biometric recognition is reshaping modern healthcare. It enables more adaptive and intelligent human–machine interactions. Epilepsy, a common neurological disorder affecting millions worldwide, relies heavily on electroencephalography (EEG) signals for diagnosis and monitoring. Wearable consumer devices with EEG sensors support continuous physiological data collection. However, transmitting sensitive biometric data to centralized servers introduces serious privacy and security risks. Federated learning (FL) provides a distributed training framework that keeps raw data on local devices. Despite this advantage, existing FL methods remain vulnerable to gradient leakage attacks, where adversaries may infer private biometric information from shared model updates. To address this issue, we propose PFED, a privacy-preserving federated learning protocol that combines randomized group interaction with volunteer-assisted secure aggregation. The proposed method effectively obfuscates gradient information while maintaining model utility. Experiments on the public CHB-MIT EEG dataset show that PFED achieves reliable epilepsy detection performance and strong privacy protection. These results demonstrate its potential for secure AI-enabled biometric healthcare applications in consumer device environments.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Transfer Learning for Secure Cross-Domain Knowledge Sharing in Healthcare
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Systems and Embedded Design (ISED)
abstract: The rate of expansion of medical data of every field, such as electronic health records, medical imaging, and wearable sensors has brought extensive scope of opportunities to help enhance diagnostics and treatment yet, have raised arising vital challenges of privacy, security, and interoperability. The proposal of this work suggests a Federated and with the Protection of Privacy. Transfer Learning (PPFTL) System of knowledge transfer across domains in healthcare which combines advanced cryptographic and deep learning algorithms. The framework uses Snowflake-based Miller Digital Rabin Signature Algorithm (MDRSA) to verify identity of a client and to manage keys effectively and Differential Viennet Privacy (DVP) as protection against model inversion attacks on sensitive patient data. To minimize data imbalance, overfitting, synthetic data generation through SMOTE and GANs is implemented and a new Jacobian Bidirectional ExpExpish GRU (JBiEEGRU) is created to improve prediction accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, Three-Hump SHapley Camel Additive Explanations (THSHCAP) guarantee the clarity of the model and confidence in the making of clinical decisions. The suggested system is tested on the dataset of coronary artery disease, kidney disease, and a brain stroke, and the performance is assessed with the measures of security, privacy, classification, clustering, and explainability. The strategy will allow delivering safe, precise and understandable AI-mediated healthcare-related solutions and guarantee the maintenance of patient confidentiality to the letter.

title: Privacy-Preserving Lightweight Federated Learning For IOMT
abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has transformed modern healthcare byenabling continuous patient monitoring, real-time diagnostics, and personalized treatment. However, thesensitive nature of medical data raises significant privacy, security, and regulatory concerns, particularlyin distributed healthcare environments. Traditional centralized machine learning approaches require dataaggregation, increasing the risk of data breaches and violating privacy norms such as those outlined inframeworks like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). To address thesechallenges, this study proposes a privacy-preserving lightweight federated learning (FL) framework for IoMTsystems. The proposed model enables decentralized training of machine learning models across resource-constrained IoMT devices while ensuring that raw patient data never leaves local nodes. A lightweightarchitecture is designed to minimize computational overhead, communication cost, and energyconsumption, making it suitable for wearable devices and edge-based healthcare systems. Furthermore,the framework integrates privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy and secure aggregationto protect sensitive information from inference attacks and model inversion threats. Optimizationstrategies, including model compression and adaptive communication protocols, are incorporated toenhance efficiency without compromising model accuracy. Our method reduces communication by 80% andoffers strong privacy assurances while nonetheless attaining 95% of the accuracy of centralized learning.This paper offers a useful federated learning method to provide effective distributed machine learning withrespect for privacy for next-generation IoMT systems.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Mental Health Risk Prediction
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Machine learning can support earlier identification of mental-health risk from electronic health records, speech, social-media text, wearable sensors, and other digital traces, but centralized data collection creates substantial privacy and governance concerns. This paper presents a literature-grounded analysis of privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) for anxiety and depression risk prediction, focusing on federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, and trusted execution environments. The study compares the privacy guarantees, utility implications, computational requirements, and deployment constraints of these approaches and examines recent evidence from mental-health applications. Particular attention is given to federated depression detection from multilingual social-media text, privacy-preserving speech-based depression diagnosis, and federated classification of major depressive disorder from EEG. The analysis shows that federated learning can reduce the need to centralize raw sensitive data, but it does not eliminate privacy risks: model updates may still leak information and can be exposed to poisoning or inference attacks. Differential privacy provides formal protection but introduces a measurable privacy–utility trade-off. The paper proposes a layered deployment framework combining local training, secure aggregation, differential privacy, robustness checks, and human-centred governance. The study concludes that privacy protection should be evaluated jointly with predictive performance, calibration, fairness, robustness, communication cost, and clinical utility rather than treated as an independent feature.

title: Privacy-Preserving Protocols for Health Data Transmission in IoT-Based Wearable Ecosystems
venue: International Conference on Information and Communication Technology for the Muslim World (ICT4M)
abstract: The use of Internet of Things (IoT)-supported wearable health devices has revamped the capture, monitoring, and transmission of personal health data. From fitness monitors to sophisticated medical wearables, these units produce streams of sensitive biometric information on a real-time basis, enabling real-time patient monitoring, early detection, and tailored treatment. The widespread nature of data capture and transmission across the ecosystems, however, raises important privacy issues. Unauthorized intrusions, data breaches, and abuse of health data pose tremendous threats to patient privacy and trust within digital health systems. This work discusses the privacy-preserving protocols particularly for the transmission of health data in IoT-based wearable systems. It first conducts a systematic review of the current methods, ranging from cryptographic solutions, anonymization, decentralized systems, to secure machine learning. Drawing from the security risks and shortcomings of existing solutions, we introduce a lightweight, privacy-preserving protocol for use on resource-limited wearable devices. Our protocol combines end-to-end encryption, secure key agreement, and edge-supported privacy-preserving computation, promoting strong security without sacrificing usability or performance. For comparison purposes, we compare our suggested method against cutting-edge protocols and consider them based on privacy assurances, computational complexity, and communication effectiveness. The outcome shows that our protocol attains an optimal trade-off between security and resource usage, which makes it scalable for real-world implementation on health care IoT systems. We close the paper by discussing practical implementation issues and avenues for further research. A theoretical validation and comparative analytical assessment were performed to evaluate the protocol’s energy efficiency, latency, and privacy strength against existing frameworks. The results indicate conceptual feasibility for real-world deployment within healthcare IoT ecosystems.

title: Privacy-aware Security Applications in the Era of Internet of Things
abstract: In this dissertation, we introduce several novel privacy-aware security applications. We split these contributions into three main categories: First, to strengthen the current authentication mechanisms, we designed two novel privacy-aware alternative complementary authentication mechanisms, Continuous Authentication (CA) and Multi-factor Authentication (MFA). Our first system is Wearable-assisted Continuous Authentication (WACA), where we used the sensor data collected from a wrist-worn device to authenticate users continuously. Then, we improved WACA by integrating a noise-tolerant template matching technique called NTT-Sec to make it privacy-aware as the collected data can be sensitive. We also designed a novel, lightweight, Privacy-aware Continuous Authentication (PACA) protocol. PACA is easily applicable to other biometric authentication mechanisms when feature vectors are represented as fixed-length real-valued vectors. In addition to CA, we also introduced a privacy-aware multi-factor authentication method, called PINTA. In PINTA, we used fuzzy hashing and homomorphic encryption mechanisms to protect the users' sensitive profiles while providing privacy-preserving authentication. For the second privacy-aware contribution, we designed a multi-stage privacy attack to smart home users using the wireless network traffic generated during the communication of the devices. The attack works even on the encrypted data as it is only using the metadata of the network traffic. Moreover, we also designed a novel solution based on the generation of spoofed traffic. Finally, we introduced two privacy-aware secure data exchange mechanisms, which allow sharing the data between multiple parties (e.g., companies, hospitals) while preserving the privacy of the individual in the dataset. These mechanisms were realized with the combination of Secure Multiparty Computation (SMC) and Differential Privacy (DP) techniques. In addition, we designed a policy language, called Curie Policy Language (CPL), to handle the conflicting relationships among parties. The novel methods, attacks, and countermeasures in this dissertation were verified with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments with real devices and users. We believe that the research in this dissertation has far-reaching implications on privacy-aware alternative complementary authentication methods, smart home user privacy research, as well as the privacy-aware and secure data exchange methods.

title: Privacy-preserving collaborative seizure detection from wearable EEG, ECG and EMG: analysis code and results for the SeizeIT2 validation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Analysis code and results for “Privacy-preserving collaborative seizure detection from wearable EEG, ECG and EMG: a large-scale validation on SeizeIT2” (Ramakrishnan S and Arokia Renjit J, 2026, submitted to Physiological Measurement). The archive contains the complete pipeline — quality control, feature extraction, per-recording normalisation, gradient-boosting and MLP baselines, simulated federated training (FedAvg, FedProx), differentially private training (DP-SGD via Opacus with Rényi accounting), membership-inference attacks with real non-members, and figure generation — together with every result table and figure in the paper. Data: SeizeIT2, OpenNeuro ds005873 (not included; download instructions in README.md). Licence: MIT.

title: PrivacyLens: AI-Powered Privacy Policy Analyzer
Private Fitness Tracking from Wearable Sensors with Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning
abstract: Fitness apps help users track their exercises and health. Wearable sensors provide increasing amounts of data, bringing motivation but also challenges to privacy. Data shared by users’ devices may exceed what they want to share for the desired results. Health insurers, corporate wellness programs, and gamified apps all want proof of exercise, but current systems require users to disclose raw activity logs, heart rate, and location data. This paper presents a system that lets users prove they met exercise goals without revealing raw sensor data. We embed a Decision Tree classifier inside a zero-knowledge proof circuit using the Groth16 protocol. The classifier distinguishes rest, moderate, and vigorous activity from accelerometer and gyroscope readings. The model reaches 97.19% holdout accuracy on the MHEALTH dataset, validated through $\mathbf{1 0}$-fold crossvalidation. The circuit uses 10,447 constraints, small enough for smartphones and wearables. Proofs take about 500 ms on desktop and 1.1 seconds on mobile, with only 800 bytes each. Unlike systems where classification runs outside the proof, our approach makes the classification itself verifiable, so label injection attacks become computationally infeasible. We tested 30 cases covering all intensity classes and boundary conditions, and all proofs were generated and verified correctly. The system provides cryptographic guarantees while remaining practical for real-world deployment.

title: Privy: From Fine Print to Fair Practice in Privacy Rights Exercise
abstract: Privacy regulations such as the CCPA and GDPR grant individuals rights over their personal data, yet it remains challenging for most users to exercise them in practice due to vague policy interpretation and unapproachable settings on web interfaces. We introduce Privy, an LLM-powered browser assistant that guides users through exercising their privacy rights on websites. Privy automatically analyzes a website's privacy policy and surfaces the specific rights available as action labels in a side panel. When a user selects a right, Privy provides step-by-step guidance and navigation, presenting direct links, generating email templates, or guiding form completion. Users can also request on-demand policy evidence and rights education to enhance their literacy. A technical evaluation across 14 websites shows that Privy extracts rights with high precision (0.979) and completes 96.3\% of privacy tasks in an average of 3.2 steps. A user study (N=15) also demonstrates the overall high-level of perceived helpfulness among users. Our findings suggest that comprehension and usability are not two separate challenges but a single interaction problem, and that effective privacy support requires integration of policy understanding and privacy actions. We offer design suggestions for future privacy assistants.

title: Proactive Execution in LLM-based Agent Systems: A Survey of Triggers, Mechanisms, and Challenges
abstract: Most LLM-based agent systems operate reactively, taking action only after receiving explicit user instructions. Yet many real-world settings demand that agents anticipate user needs, detect environmental changes, and correct their own reasoning before problems surface---capabilities we collectively term proactive execution. These capabilities are particularly relevant to consumer technologies and electronics, where proactive LLM-based agents can support smartphones, smart homes, wearables, personal robots, and IoT devices. However, related research remains scattered across proactive dialogue, embodied perception, feedback-driven adaptation, and self-reflection, with no unified framework connecting them. This survey bridges that gap. We propose a trigger-source taxonomy that organizes proactive execution into three paradigms: (i) user behavior-driven, encompassing need inference from interaction history, task-driven clarification, and assistance under intent shifts; (ii) external event-driven, covering environmental, behavioral, and informational event perception as well as feedback-driven closed-loop adaptation; and (iii) internal uncertainty-driven, addressing confidence-aware verification and self-reflection-based correction. For each paradigm, we analyze representative methods, compare their mechanisms and limitations, and identify the conditions under which they are most effective. We further extend the discussion to the Internet of Agents (IoA) setting, examining how proactive coordination scales across heterogeneous, networked agent infrastructures. Finally, we outline open challenges, including the trade-off between proactive intervention and user disruption, security and privacy risks, and the lack of evaluation standards for proactive behavior, and propose concrete directions for future research.

title: Proactive Federated Anomaly Detection in Consumer Electronic Ecosystems via Adaptive Learning and Lightweight Auditability
abstract: Consumer electronic ecosystems, such as smart vehicles, wearable devices, connected homes, and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled transportation systems, face increasing cyber threats, privacy risks, and reliability challenges. Although federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative training, its deployment in such environments is still hindered by statistical heterogeneity, hyperparameter sensitivity, and limited training auditability. This paper proposes SABFL, a federated intrusion detection framework for consumer electronic ecosystems. It combines FedProx-based local training, online simulated annealing for adaptive hyperparameter tuning, and lightweight blockchain-assisted audit logging. The framework improves convergence stability under heterogeneous data and provides traceable training records with low additional overhead. Experimental results on the CICIDS2017 dataset show that SABFL achieves performance comparable to existing methods under IID conditions, while yielding significantly stronger robustness under non-IID scenarios. In highly heterogeneous settings, SABFL improves the Macro-F1 score by up to 20.58% compared with standard federated baselines, and outperforms the advanced FedNova approach by 16.43%. These results demonstrate the practicality of SABFL for proactive intrusion detection in distributed consumer electronic environments.

title: Proceedings from a multidisciplinary workshop defining the scope of Resilience Informatics in Public Health (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND In recent years, public health has confronted two formidable challenges: the devastating COVID-19 pandemic and the enduring threat of climate change. The convergence of these crises underscores the urgent need for resilient solutions. Resilience Informatics (RI), an emerging discipline at the intersection of informatics and public health, offers promising avenues for mitigating and adapting to these challenges. Addressing critical questions regarding target audiences, privacy concerns, and scalability is paramount to fostering resilience in the face of evolving health threats. OBJECTIVE The University of Arizona's workshop on Resilience Informatics in Public Health was held in November 2023 to serve as a pivotal forum for advancing these discussions and catalyzing collaborative efforts within the field. METHODS A purposive sampling strategy was employed to invite 40 experts by email from diverse fields including public health, medicine, weather, informatics, environmental science, and resilience to participate in the workshop. The event featured presentations from key experts followed by group discussions facilitated by experts to ensure diversity in backgrounds. Attendees engaged in collaborative reflection and discussion on predetermined questions. Discussions were systematically recorded by University of Arizona students, and qualitative analysis was conducted. A rapid analysis of workshop notes was initially performed, followed by a more comprehensive qualitative thematic analysis. A codebook was developed iteratively, all transcripts and notes used from the workshop were coded twice using MAXQDA software. Discrepancies in coding were resolved through discussion, leading to a narrative synthesis of findings. RESULTS The workshop hosted 27 attendees at the University of Arizona, predominantly from academia, with 21 participants from public health-related fields and 8 experts in resilience. Additionally, participants from governmental agencies, Native American groups, weather services, and mHealth organizations attended. Qualitative analysis identified major themes, including the potential of resilience informatics (RI) tools, threats to resilience (e.g., healthcare access, infrastructure, climate change), challenges with RI tools (e.g., usability, funding, real-time response), and standards for RI tools (e.g., technological, logistical, sociological). Attendees emphasized the importance of equitable access, community engagement, and iterative development in RI projects. CONCLUSIONS The RI workshop emphasized the necessity for accessible, user-friendly tools bridging technical knowledge and community needs. Future directions include focused discussions to yield concrete outputs like implementation guidelines and tool designs, prioritizing community engagement, cultural sensitivity, and ongoing learning. title: Process Evaluation And Uptake Of The Incentive-based Caterpillar Mhealth App
abstract: PURPOSE: The cost of delivering financial incentive (FI) based mHealth apps can be prohibitive. The main objective was to evaluate uptake of an mHealth app offering very small financial incentives during an exclusive 3-month launch period in Leeds, UK. METHODS: A 12-week single cohort process evaluation was conducted. Adults downloaded the app between September 12 and December 12, 2022 and provided informed consent. Users were rewarded for achieving personalized daily step goals and completing two short educational health quizzes per week (worth about $0.10 USD per day for step goal reached, and $0.25 per quiz completed, respectively). FIs were provided in the form of “points” that could be redeemed for movie passes and gym discounts. Aligning with dimensions of the RE-AIM framework (i.e., Reach and Implementation), information regarding uptake, sociodemographic and health characteristics, as well as engagement and acceptability (Mobile Application Rating Scale (MARS)) were collected. Data are presented descriptively. RESULTS: The app was promoted via email campaign (~25,000 sent by app partners to Leeds residents, e.g., Leeds gym members, Leeds City Council), paid social media advertisements (27 advertisements with 3484 impressions (number of app views on platform)) and posts via the app’s social media accounts (28 across three platforms i.e., 341 followers). A total of 204 app store “visits” (viewed store listing) were recorded, leading to 106 app downloads (52.2% iOS users). Forty-six provided consent (36.4 ± 13.5 years; 69.6% female; 18.9% classified as lower income). Most users indicated living with at least one chronic disease (70.7%). On average, users accumulated 5003 ± 3329 steps per day at baseline. Among those using the app for 30+ days (n = 22), 47.1% opened the app at least once per week (8.2 app opens per week). Participants completing the MARS (n = 28) provided a high overall app rating (3.7/5) with most likely to recommend the app to others (68.8%). CONCLUSION: Early results suggest more must be done to promote app downloads (e.g., optimizing email campaigns). The app was downloaded by younger females especially, with lower income adults well represented. Last, it appears that very small incentives contributed to high early engagement in a field where attrition is the norm. (Sponsored by MF Mottola FACSM)

title: Process Model-guided Post-filtering for Wearable Activity Recognition in Ergonomic Work Processes
abstract: Ergonomic assessment of manual work processes requires continuous recognition of workers' physical activities – a task complicated by privacy constraints, sensor complexity, and noisy movement data. This paper proposes a process model-guided post-filtering approach that leverages existing process knowledge to refine the output of wearable activity classifiers, regardless of the underlying recognition method. Evaluated across two industry-derived use cases using body area networks with 3, 5, and 7 sensors, the approach yields dramatic accuracy improvements – from below 50 % unfiltered to over 82 % with as few as three sensors. Results demonstrate that explicit process model knowledge can substantially compensate for reduced sensor setups, lowering hardware costs and privacy risks without sacrificing recognition quality. This proof-of-concept establishes process model filtering as a promising component in ergonomic monitoring pipelines for structured manual work.

title: Products of Interest
abstract: British company Blackstar Amplification has long been known for its guitar amplifiers but it has more recently branched out into a range of portable instruments through its Carry-on series. The Folding Controller 49 is a wireless 49-key MIDI controller keyboard that can be folded in half for easy transport and storage. It offers a range of options for transmitting MIDI, including USB, wireless Bluetooth, and a mini-jack MIDI output. It has a built-in rechargeable battery which can be charged by USB-C for up to eight hours of playing time.Along with the 49 velocity sensitive piano keys, the controller also has two assignable control knobs for control or parameter values, octave shift and transpose functions, transport controls for use with a Digital Audio Workstation (DAW), a built-in arpeggiator, and a touch pad. When used in Pitch/Mod mode, the left half of the touchpad controls pitch and the right side controls modulation. Alternately, the touchpad can be used as an x-y pad, with a control change number assigned to each axis.The velocity curve of the keys can be changed by the user to predetermined settings: Off, Default, Soft, or Hard, or to a custom curve created using an accompanying software editor, the Carry-on Control App. It can also be used to control MIDI mappings, and to save and recall custom settings. The application is compatible with macOS and Windows.The controller weighs 1 kg. It measures 755 × 126 × 21 mm when unfolded and 390 × 126 × 48 mm when folded up. It comes with a USB-C charging cable and purchase also includes Cubase LE and Cubasis LE.The Folding Controller 49 is listed for approximately US$ 125. Contact: Blackstar Amplification Ltd, Suite 2, Hawes Business Centre, Sandfield Cl, Moulton Park, Northampton, UK; e-mail enquiries@blackstaramps.com, Web www.carryonplaying.com.UK company ROLI has released a new portable, wireless, accessibly priced addition to their Seaboard family of MIDI keyboard controllers. Like its predecessors, the Block M features a soft, tactile, continuous silicon surface, MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE), and 5D Touch technology (see Figure 1). It can be used to create expressive performances with more nuanced control of instrument than traditional MIDI keyboard controllers.This instrument is a 24-keywave model which measures 11 × 5.5 × 1 in and weighs 650 g. Users can shape the sounds created using five different kinds of touch: Strike, Press, Glide, Slide, and Lift. Strike can be used to determine the velocity of a note. Press can be used to deepen the sound. Slide is an up-and-down movement that can be used to add brightness, texture, or depth. Glide is a side-to-side movement on the keys to bend the pitch and create vibratos. The speed of the users lifting their Figure 1.The Seaboard Block M controller from ROLI. fingers from the keys can be used to affect the resonance of the sound. Octave shift buttons are also provided to increase the range from two to seven octaves. Parameters and MIDI settings can be adjusted with ROLI Dashboard software, which has visualizers to help tweak settings, including customizing the velocity curve.The MPE capabilities of the Seaboard M works with most DAWs. It has a MIDI output on a mini-jack TRS connector and comes with an adapter for connecting it to MIDI hardware synthesizers. There is also a USB-C port for connection and charging and the instrument has Bluetooth capability for wireless use. It is class-compliant for MIDI over both USB and Bluetooth. An internal rechargeable battery gives 10 hours of operating time. DNA connectors, which easily snap together, can be used to expand the instrument by connecting it to other ROLI products including the larger ROLI Seaboards Rise 2, LUMI Keys, or additional Block Ms.Purchase includes ROLI Studio, which is a set of two plug-ins for music and audio production: ROLI Studio Player and ROLI Studio Drums. These can be integrated into a DAW or used as standalone applications. They include 400 sounds and presets and production tools such as Smart Chords, arpeggios, effects, and macros. ROLI Studio Drums is an MPE plug-in with 15 drum kits, each of which has 16 controllable parts.The Seaboard M and its software are compatible with macOS 12 and 13, and with Windows 10 or higher (64-bit). 16 GB RAM is recommended. The instrument bundle also includes a USB-C to USB-A cable, and a mini-jack to MIDI output adapter.The Seaboard M is listed for US$ 349. Contact: Luminary HQ, Railway Arch 326, Stean Street, London E8 4ED, UK; Web www.roli.com.French company Viper Synths has developed a high-quality MIDI controller for use with synthesizers, virtual instruments, and effects. The Robotron is designed to look and feel like a vintage analog synthesizer (see Figure 2). The controller is hand-made with a top panel made from anodized brushed aluminum, a powder-coated steel bottom, and side panels made from sapele wood. It has 26 potentiometers and 6 momentary switches, which can be assigned to any control change message. Six assign knobs are made from aluminum and are similar to those found on sequential circuit synthesizers. The remaining knobs are constructed from Bakelite, similar to those used on Moog synths. Figure 2.Viper Synths’ Robotron MIDI Controller.The controls are organized into sections that correspond to common synthesizer functions, including oscillators, LFOs, amplitude, mixer, filter, two envelopes, MIDI channel selector with OLED screen, and six knobs that are free to assign. However, the user can choose to change these to any control change messages. A Max for Live plug-in is included for mapping the controller to virtual synthesizer in real-time. Users can re-name control knobs to suit their custom mappings, record automations, and save the entire synthesizer settings for recall. A VST plug-in is in development.The Robotron measures 39.5 × 25 × 7.5 cm and weighs 2.5 kg. It is USB MIDI plug and play compliant. It has a USB-C port and comes with a USB-C to USB-A cable.The Robotron is listed for approximately US$ 526. Contact: Viper Synths; Web www.vipersynths.com.The Mezzz is a portable handheld haptic wireless MIDI controller that fits in the palm of your hand (see Figure 3). It can be used to control parameters in a range of audio software, DAW, or video applications. The controller also comes with a carabiner and wrist strap for wearable use. Figure 3.The Mezzz haptic wireless MIDI controller.The Mezzz unit features eight haptic rotary encoders arranged in a hexagon enclosure, which can send over 1,000 control change message via Bluetooth MIDI. The controller is a class-compliant Bluetooth MIDI device. The haptic-enabled encoders buzz when a valid MIDI value is entered and stop buzzing if the user reaches the lower or upper boundary of a control. There are eight banks of parameters with eight control change messages in each, giving 1,024 parameters in all. At the center of the encoders is an LED display section. An outer ring of LEDs indicates which bank of parameters is currently active/selected. A short press of an encoder will open up the associated bank and light up the LED nearest to it. An inner circle of LEDs displays a visual representation of the last parameter value. At the very center of this LED section, and the unit itself, is a context sensitive button. It has a corresponding LED that displays the level of battery power by default.Buttons are provided on the side of the controller for selecting the MIDI channel, randomizing control change messages, and resetting parameters. title: Promoting Weight Management Using Technology
abstract: Q: ARE THERE ANY BENEFITS OF USING TECHNOLOGY TO HELP WITH WEIGHT LOSS? A: Computers, tablets, smart phones — these devices are ubiquitous in society. From accessing the Internet to using short messaging service (SMS or text messaging), people have come to rely on technology in day-to-day activities. In 2015, nearly two thirds of Americans report owning a smartphone, an increase from 35% in 2011 (18). To give some insight on how smartphones are being used, during a 1-week sample period, 97% of smartphone owners used text messaging, 89% accessed the Internet, and 88% accessed email (18). In addition, smartphone apps are available in a staggering variety of categories and the number keeps growing (see Box 1 for insights on the number of apps available) (2,6). Although the prevalence of technology often is bemoaned as a “cause” for inactivity, and associated weight gain, interventions incorporating technology have potential to promote adherence to exercise and dietary changes. BOX 1. Growing Number of Apps The number of apps in all categories in the Apple App Store increased from 800 in 2008 to 1.3 million in 2014 (6) and, as of April 2015, the number of Android apps available on Google Play surpassed 1.5 million (2). Health and fitness apps are widely available (e.g., App Store: https://itunes.apple.com/us/genre/ios-health-fitness/id6013?mt=8 and Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/category/HEALTH_AND_FITNESS). Healthy lifestyle choices are made daily and are impacted by many, many factors. Six key strategies, from an individual perspective, for long-term weight loss success have been detected from the National Weight Control Registry data (see Box 2 for the six strategies) (21). Consider how these strategies might be supported with technology (e.g., tracking physical activity, monitoring body weight). From a program standpoint, common characteristics found in clinical weight loss/management trials have been identified and also include aspects of monitoring (see Box 3 for common features) (10). Researchers have identified three behavioral components of effective weight management interventions, including 1) addressing behavior change, 2) encouraging self-monitoring of individual data (e.g., weight, steps), and 3) providing personalized recommendations and feedback (10). The question is if technology can be used effectively by individuals, and within weight management interventions, to promote behavior change, support self-monitoring, and provide feedback.BOX 2. National Weight Control Registry: Key Strategies of Individuals Successful at Long-Term Weight Loss (21) Since 1994, the National Weight Control Registry has been tracking individuals who have lost weight and maintained that weight loss for at least 1 year. Based on questionnaires, individuals with effective maintenance after weight loss tend to: 1) engage in high levels of physical activity 2) eat a diet that is low in calories and fat 3) eat breakfast 4) regularly self-monitor weight 5) maintain a consistent eating pattern 6) prevent small regains from turning into larger regains BOX 3. Features of Weight Loss and Weight Management Studies (10) Clinical trials for weight loss management in obese individuals appear to have similar features, including: individualized weight loss goals contact with individuals (one-on-one or group settings) body weight, activity, and food intake monitoring structured behavioral modification program delivered by trained professionals individual adherence monitoring and use of strategies to overcome barriers Various evidence-based content and theory-based strategies have been studied related to effective behavior change. In one study, apps were assessed for knowledge (general information), cognitive strategies (e.g., perceived benefits and barriers, self-efficiency, perceived social norms), behavior strategies (e.g., self-monitoring, goal setting, time management, stimulus control, social support, relapse prevention), emotion-focused strategies (e.g., stress management), and therapeutic interventions (e.g., skill building, increasing knowledge, motivational readiness) (3). In this review of 23 apps, inclusion of theoretical content or strategies to guide behavior change was low (3). In another study focused on 127 apps targeting physical activity, theoretical content was found to be lacking (7). Of the theories included in the physical activity apps, the health belief model was the most common (32%) (7) (The health belief model suggests that one’s belief regarding personal susceptibility to disease and perceptions of benefits regarding avoiding disease influences readiness to act (1)). Opportunities may therefore exist for collaboration between behavior change professionals and app developers to optimize integration of theory along with user-friendly programming (7). Given the lack of studies actually comparing the impact of weight management apps (e.g., does using the app change behavior and result in weight loss), researchers point out that the effectiveness of an app may rest in the app’s ability to engage individuals across time, thus supporting long-term behavior change maintenance (3). According to a Pew Research Center survey in 2012, 60% of U.S. adults report tracking weight, diet, or exercise (9). For individuals who report tracking behaviors, approximately half keep track “in their heads”; about one third track on paper (e.g., notebook, journal); and one in five use technology, including 8% who use a medical device (e.g., glucose monitor), 7% who use a mobile app, 5% who use a spreadsheet, and 1% who use a Web site or online tool (9). To examine this from a different perspective, when considering smartphone owners, 19% of this group have downloaded an app intended to track or manage health. In particular, health app users focus on tracking exercise (38%), diet (31%), and weight management (12%) (9). Although record keeping is an effective strategy, the Pew survey found that only about half of individuals who track behaviors update on a regular basis (9). Thus, having an app is not the same as using the app. Actively monitoring behavior is key. Consistent self-monitoring (paper-based tracking) was found to be associated with weight maintenance across a 1-year period after an initial weight loss period (13). In particular, those who both frequently and consistently monitored dietary intake were more likely to reduce weight regain than those who did not frequently self-monitor (13). Unfortunately, self-monitoring tends to decline across time. Recognizing the value of self-monitoring as an effective strategy to increase awareness of desired behaviors and circumstances surrounding those behaviors, the potential value of making the process easier with technology is appealing (4). The value of a given tool will depend on the quality of the content (e.g., accuracy of information found in an app) and must be considered carefully before adopting or recommending. In addition, see Box 4 for some cautions related to privacy and the use of technology (14). BOX 4. Privacy Issues Related to USE of Apps (14) With thousands of apps available related to health and fitness, one area often overlooked is privacy. Many apps collect personal information (e.g., age, height, weight) as well as other information (e.g., exercise habits, food consumption, search terms). Such information may be made available for advertising or data analysis, potentially unencrypted on insecure network connections. Any app user should reflect on what personal information is being given and seek to find how that information is being used. Additional consumer tips from the Privacy Rights Clearinghouse include limiting input of personal data, being cautious of sharing options (e.g., divulging walking route including location and time with others), checking permissions and turning off any unnecessary options, investigating the app developer credibility, and deleting apps no longer used (as well as personal profiles and data archive of any apps no longer used). Having access to food databases to look up nutrient values or storing and retrieving commonly consumed meals is possible using technology (4). Weight management apps focusing on dietary calorie intake may include bar code scanners for packaged products and manual entry options for favorite food in addition to large food databases (10). Most apps rely on self-report, but more objective methods to assess dietary intake include food photography programs in which before and after photos are used to estimate portion size and the amount consumed (10). Some apps focus exclusively on calorie counting (e.g., Fooducate), whereas others include physical activity tracking as well (e.g., MyFitnessPal) (10). As with diet-related apps, physical activity apps have databases of activities that help track energy expenditure (10). In addition, to move beyond self-report, use of the GPS capacity of smartphones allows for more objective tracking of movement (10). The pivotal question remains if apps actually are an effective tool in weight management. One pilot study compared weight loss when using a smartphone app (My Meal Mate), Web site, or paper-based diary (5). Adherence to dietary self-monitoring was higher for the smartphone app group compared with the Web site and paper diary groups, although self-monitoring declined across time (16% of the smartphone app group recorded dietary intake every day during the 6-month duration of the study compared with 0% in the other two groups) (5). Weight loss was significantly greater in the smartphone app group after 6 months (5). This study provides support for the use of apps within a weight management program both in terms of sticking with a program as well as effectiveness in promoting weight loss. Many different methods of “interaction” are possible — thanks to available technology. The Mobile Pounds Off Digitally (Mobile POD) intervention examined if mobile delivery of behavioral intervention sessions, using a combination of podcasting, mobile support communication, and mobile diet monitoring, would promote weight loss (19). The 6-month study included two groups: 1) Podcast group that received only podcasts (2 per week for 3 months and then 2 minipodcasts per week for the next 3 months) and monitored diet any way the participants desired, and 2) Podcast Plus group that received the podcasts plus used a diet- and physical activity-monitoring app (FatSecret’s Calorie Counter app, FatSecret.com) and used a Twitter account through which the study coordinator sent out daily messages and participants could interact with one another. Weight loss did not differ between the two groups (∼2.6 kg) (19). Both groups monitored diet (the Podcast group used the Web or paper, whereas the Podcast Plus group was more likely to use an app) and felt supported in their weight loss efforts (the Podcast group relied on real-life friends, whereas the Podcast Plus group turned to Internet-based sources of support) (19). Thus, the similarity in outcomes between the two groups may be because both groups found ways to self-monitor and receive social support, even if these ways differed. Future studies will be helpful to determine optimal approaches and how to tailor support systems to individuals. Another interesting consideration is the impact of human contact in addition to technology. In a recent study, coaching was added to a Web-based weight management program (Positive Online Weight Reduction that included weekly online sessions); the coaching element was added via short coaching phone calls (8). There appeared to be some benefit, but the telephone coaching group also had more dropouts from the study (8). The impact of coaching may vary; some individuals may respond positively, but others may find the prospect of coaching undesirable. In another study that involved regular in-person group intervention meetings, telephone contact with participants was found to be predictive of weight loss, along with adoption of healthy eating behaviors and physical activity (20). Recognizing the difference in study designs — online versus in-person interaction — the impact of subsequent phone contact differed. The question remains if, or what, types of contacts may be beneficial (e.g., email contacts, online chat rooms, social networking sites) and how this may interact with other aspects of the weight management intervention. Text messaging (SMS) is an intervention that seems to hold promise for promoting weight loss. SMS provides messages of up to 160 characters (15). Text messaging is the most widely used and the most frequently used smartphone feature, exceeding email use and Internet use on smartphones (18). A recent review found body weight changes to be greater in those receiving text messages compared with controls (noted in five of six studies using text messaging to promote weight loss) (11). Another review noted that 79% of studies reviewed (11 of 14) reported positive effects on weight, physical activity, and/or diet (15). Use of SMS as an intervention tool is still relatively new, and additional studies are needed to examine effectiveness. Potential benefits include direct contact independent of location, real-time assessments, recording date/time linked data, and personalization of information (15). Aspects of SMS that will need to be considered in future studies include the text message frequency, level of interactivity, duration of the intervention, and analysis of content and outcomes (15, 17). When looking at long-term use of any intervention, “stickiness” and participant follow-through must be considered (16). With any weight management program, adherence is a challenge and technology is not immune. What was once a new and novel app may become less engaging across time, and text message fatigue may result in ignoring contacts made using this method (16). Long-term interventions will need to be prepared to adapt to address loss of interest or relapse (16). New technologies continue to appear and become more advanced (e.g., on-body activity sensing systems to chart physical activity); the rapid pace of technology development will continue to create challenges for researchers who seek to establish best practices (12). The use of technology to promote healthy behaviors provides intriguing opportunities. Realizing that no approach is a one-size-fits-all method, health and fitness professionals may want to consider how various technologies (e.g., apps, SMS) may be incorporated within individualized weight management plans. Using technology as a tool within the framework of behavior change theories and strategies is an exciting area of future research considering the promising initial findings.

title: Protecting Your IoT Devices
abstract: This chapter points out common dangers to Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Bad actors taking control of an Internet-connected vehicle is just a single example of an IoT cyberattack. The additional dangers to IoT devices are botnets, ransomware, and spyware. The chapter discusses IoT privacy holes and how a fitness app leaked top-secret military base location information. It provides a deeper insight into what our smart home IoT devices are doing behind the scenes. IoT devices have benefits in helping with daily tasks, enhancing home security, and monitoring our health. However, there are some innate security and privacy risks with many manufacturers. The chapter also discusses how to protect our privacy when it comes to reviewing IoT devices before making a purchase, check how much data our IoT devices are tracking about us, and evaluate how the device is publicizing our information on the Internet.

title: Protection Against Person-Identification from EEG Patterns: A Blockchain-based Approach
venue: 2024 Conference on Building a Secure & Empowered Cyberspace (BuildSEC)
abstract: Monitoring brain cognition functions with the help of wearables like Electroencephalography (EEG) sensors has recently become a popular assistive technology for the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). EEG is popularly established as a safe, practical, and portable IoMT device. From monitoring stimuli responses to facilitating critical diagnosis, EEG is highly effective in clinical, research, and home settings. Nonetheless, the brain patterns of EEG linked with a person can be easily verifiable through backtracking and is a threat to the person’s identity. Hence, privacy preservation of EEG data is critical, implying we need to keep it confidential and free from susceptibility. We propose a Blockchain-based access control mechanism for users to manage their EEG data and share it imperatively. We consider a fully homomorphic encryption method for the dynamic data exchange between authorized users and doctors within a private Blockchain network. The decentralized application (DApp) uses lightweight smart contracts to process data at the source and optimize the on-chain storage. Moreover, our proposed methodology adequately tackles privacy preservation by enabling users to control their personal information directly, building trust, and promoting more extensive acceptance.

title: Publisher's Note
Push and pull factors shaping hormonal contraceptive decision-making: A scoping review of global qualitative research
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Decisions to use, avoid, switch, or discontinue hormonal contraception are shaped by a range of social, cultural, relational, and embodied factors. Our objective was to review global qualitative evidence on the push and pull factors influencing individuals' decisions regarding hormonal contraception, and to synthesize these influences across diverse global contexts. STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a scoping review following JBI guidance and report it according to preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses extension for scoping reviews. We searched six databases for English-language qualitative studies published between 2014 and 2024. Fifty studies met the inclusion criteria. We extracted data using a structured form and synthesized it using a thematic analytic approach to identify cross-cutting push and pull factors. RESULTS: We developed five interrelated themes relating to different dimensions of contraceptive decision-making: embodied experiences; relational and social influences; cultural and symbolic meanings; concerns about fertility and reproductive futures; practical, structural and system-level factors. Multiple factors operated simultaneously as discouraging and enabling influences - experiences of side effects, menstrual changes, concerns about "naturalness," partner dynamics, community norms, provider interactions, access barriers, and the need for privacy. Decisions reflected ongoing negotiation between anticipated harms, perceived benefits, and broader desires for autonomy, well-being, and reproductive control. CONCLUSIONS: Decision-making about hormonal contraception is dynamic, contextually situated, and shaped by interrelated embodied, relational, cultural, and structural factors. While researchers and clinicians often attribute concerns about hormonal contraception to misinformation, our findings suggest that such concerns often reflect experiential and contextual realities. Person-centered counseling, engagement with users' experiences, and policies and practices that address cost, access, and method choice are essential to support contraceptive autonomy.

title: P–469 Period Tracker Applications – are they giving women accurate menstrual cycle information?
abstract: Abstract Study question Are period trackers giving women accurate information about their periods and ovulation? Summary answer The top 10 period trackers gave conflicting information on period dates, ovulation day and the fertile window. What is known already Period tracking applications allow women to track their menstrual cycles and receive a prediction for their periods. The majority of applications also provide predictions of day of ovulation and the fertile window. Previous research indicates applications are basing predictions on assuming women undergo a textbook 28-day cycle with ovulation occurring on day 14 and a fertile window between days 10 and 17. Study design, size, duration An audit of menstrual cycle apps was conducted on the Apple app store using menstrual cycle tracker/period tracker as the search terms. The top ten apps that followed the inclusion and exclusion criteria were analysed and used for this study. All apps had the ability to allow retrospective data entry giving future cycle predictions and fertile window, and nine of the apps predicted a day of ovulation. Participants/materials, setting, methods Five women’s profiles for 6 menstrual cycles were created and entered into each app. Cycle length (CL) and ovulation day (OD) for the 6th cycle were; Woman 1 – Constant 28 day CL, 0D 16, Woman 2 – Average 23 day CL, OD 13, Woman 3 – Average 28 day CL, OD 17, Woman 4 – Average 33 day CL, OD 20 and Woman 5 – Irregular, average 31 day CL, OD 14. Main results and the role of chance For cycle length, the apps all predicted woman 1’s cycles correctly but for women 2–5, the apps predicted 0 to 8 days shorter or longer than expected. For day of ovulation; for woman 1, no apps predicted this correctly; the apps ranged from day 13–15. For woman 2, 1 app was correct and overall the apps showed a lot of variation from day 8 to 13. For woman 3, no apps got it right, with a range of day 13–16. For woman 4, 2 apps got it right, but the apps ranged from day 13–20. For woman 5, no apps got right; the apps ranged from day 13–21. Irrespective of cycle length, 7 apps predicted a fertile window of 7 days in almost all cases; except 1 app that predicted 6 days for woman 2 and a different app which predicted 8 days for woman 4. For the remaining 3 apps, one always predicted a 10 day fertile window. One app predicted an 11 day fertile window in 4/5 women. One app predicted a 12 day fertile window in 4/5 women. Limitations, reasons for caution The five profiles created spanned a range of observed cycle characteristics, but many permutations are possible. A Monte Carlo type analysis could be conducted to examine these possibilities to provide more precise assessment of app performance, but as data had to be added manually into apps, this was not possible. Wider implications of the findings: The apps do not use the same algorithm and show variation. The information given by these apps is not 100% accurate, especially for the day of ovulation and the fertile window which can only be predicted if using a marker of ovulation, such as basal body temperature or ovulation sticks. Trial registration number Not applicable

title: QRELHE-X: Extended Quantum-Resistant Edge Learning with Homomorphic Encryption for Next-Generation Distributed Intelligence Systems
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Recent proliferation of edge intelligence systems, including Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, self-driving vehicles, wearable medical devices and industrial control platforms—requires privacy-preserving computation subject to availability constraints on resources. At the same time, the recent arrival of large-scale quantum computers can break all classical cryptographic protocols with Shor's algorithm in a short time. State-of-the-art post-quantum homomorphic encryption systems incur computational overhead orders of magnitude larger than the energy and memory budgets of resource-constrained microcontrollers, giving rise to a disparity between security and deployability that remains unaddressed. We introduce QRELHE-X in this paper, a comprehensive framework building on post-quantum edge learning with four novel contributions: (1) a tri-family hybrid cryptography architecture leveraging Algebraic Geometry (AG) codes, Hidden Field Equations minus (HFE-) and eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS), which guards against cryptanalytic attacks targeting any single family using defend-in-depth approach; (2) our Deep Reinforcement Learning Parameter Orchestration (DRL-PO) engine that dynamically tunes cryptographic parameters based on real-time device telemetry via PPO-trained policy network yielding 23.4% efficiency optimization compared against static configurations; (3) our Structured Noise Calculus framework providing Lyapunov-stable guarantees of the noise growth within deep level homomorphic neural circuits enabling T*=47 operations between bootstrapping — 3.9x fewer than prior art implementations of state-of-the-art systems; and finally, we present BREFL, the first Byzantine Resilient Encrypted Federated Learning protocol capable of detecting malicious gradient submissions completely within encrypted domain at detection rate 98.7%. Over six hardware platforms, we establish a 5.1x latency improvement over CRYSTALS-KyberHE, while reducing energy by 4.7x, and successfully deploy on,256 KB RAM microcontrollers—the lowest memory footprint ever reported of any post-quantum homomorphic inference solution.

title: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT Safety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMITSafety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli How much continuous molecular observability should a health civilization build, and when does measurement burden exceed health benefit? QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT is a large-scale research monograph exploring what happens when quantum-enabled measurement moves beyond isolated devices and becomes longitudinal health infrastructure. Its flagship Three-Coupling is: Longitudinal Insight x Human Rights x Life-Centered Utility The Quantum Health Civilization Index (QHCI) is introduced as a book-defined research heuristic linking longitudinal insight, rights integrity, health gain, and continuity/trust while explicitly accounting for privacy risk, overdiagnosis, and measurement overreach. QHCI is not a natural law, clinical score, diagnostic threshold, regulatory standard, or policy mandate. Across 82 chapters, the volume develops research architectures for exposure safety, nanomaterial fate, molecular privacy, high-dimensional consent, equitable access, nanomedicine, AI-interpreted health, wearables, portable sensing, home calibration, autonomous and remote care, cybersecurity, human override, molecular observatories, personal baselines, longitudinal molecular information, digital twins, missingness, overdiagnosis, incidental findings, intervention thresholds, watchful waiting, measurement restraint, data minimization, health infrastructure, standards, manufacturing readiness, interoperability, health economics, dual-use risk, environmental lifecycle, hype resistance, responsible communication, trust, intergenerational governance, failure science, and successor handoff. Every chapter begins with a Three-Coupling System, a named Core Relation, and an artistic geometric research model. The geometric research grammar includes the Longitudinal Molecular Observatory Helix, Health-Rights Corridor, Personal Molecular-State Manifold, Intervention Threshold Boundary Surface, Wearable-Home-Hospital Lattice, Autonomous Care Oversight Torus, Civilization Health Constellation, and Measurement-Burden Basin. The volume contains 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos. The Research Gates are designed as falsifiable entrances for safety studies, molecular-rights research, longitudinal validation, threshold experiments, wearable and autonomous-care stress tests, molecular-observatory infrastructure, standards work, governance, negative-result programs, measurement-restraint research, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain deliberately provisional. Each provides a working answer structure, evidence that could strengthen it, evidence that could weaken or falsify it, a design consequence, and a question for the next research hand. The central distinction is simple: More measurement does not automatically produce more health. A civilization capable of measuring nearly everything still needs a rigorous science of what not to measure, when not to alert, when not to intervene, how to preserve the right to refuse observation, and how to hand unresolved uncertainty to the next research generation. Better measurement becomes better life only when technical capability remains subordinate to health gain, dignity, access, trust, proportionality, and human agency.

title: QUANTUM INFRASTRUCTURE & CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT From Laboratory Quantum Advantage to Planetary Scientific Infrastructure
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: QUANTUM INFRASTRUCTURE & CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMITFrom Laboratory Quantum Advantage to Planetary Scientific Infrastructure Feng Cheng-en (33) × Starli What must exist for quantum technology to become dependable infrastructure for a civilization? QUANTUM INFRASTRUCTURE & CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT is a large-scale research monograph examining what lies beyond laboratory-scale quantum performance. Rather than asking only how powerful a quantum device can become, this book asks how quantum capabilities can move through manufacturing, calibration, standards, networks, governance, economics, deployment, and public trust until they become durable scientific infrastructure. The central civilizational pathway is: Laboratory→ Manufacturing→ Standards→ Networks→ Infrastructure→ Civilization→ Handoff The volume develops research programs across: quantum sensor manufacturing,production yield,calibration systems,reference materials,interlaboratory reproducibility,portable quantum devices,wearable quantum sensing,quantum sensor networks,distributed observatories,molecular observatories,cybersecurity,privacy,regulation,economics,equitable access,autonomous medicine,planetary sensing,off-world sensing,scientific memory,technology succession,and civilization-scale continuity. A central framework introduced in the book is the Quantum Readiness Index (QRI): QRI =(Scientific Utility × Reliability × Deployability × Accessibility)/(1 + Infrastructure Burden + Cost + Governance Risk) The purpose of the QRI is not to declare a technology “civilization-ready” through a single score. It is a research heuristic for testing whether useful quantum capability survives the full transition from laboratory performance to reliable deployment. The book therefore asks whether quantum systems can remain: scientifically useful,manufacturable,calibratable,reproducible,maintainable,economically viable,secure,governable,accessible,and transferable across institutions and generations.
