title: Wearing Your Heart (Monitor) on Your Sleeve: Will Data Be the New Doctor?
abstract: Imagine wearing a shirt or a wristband that tells you how hard you are exercising or warns you if you are getting sick. These are simple examples of wearable medical devices that could transform healthcare—either by helping people to manage serious diseases that they already have, or by spotting the early signs of a disease so that it can be treated before the person even feels sick. This article will focus on two examples of wearables: one for the management of diabetes and another that may be able to prevent heart attacks. Wearables like these and many others that are being developed could greatly improve human health. However, these technologies come with some big challenges, because they collect a lot of personal data. We need to find ways to protect people’s privacy by keeping that sensitive data safe. In the future, wearables will certainly help doctors do their jobs… but might they even replace doctors altogether?

title: Weight training mobile application for ipad based on Ti BLE sensor tag
abstract: Bluetooth low energy, also known as BLE, is an upgraded version of Bluetooth 3.0, which consumes less power compared to the older version but with more amazing features such as healthcare, pedometer, intelligent instrument and sensors etc. BLE significantly expands the markets of Bluetooth, making it increasingly popular among people. In this dissertation project, the core peripheral is called TI BLE sensor tag, which can be considered as a new generation of wearable device that allows developers to measure different kinds of parameters. There are 6 low-power sensors on one sensor tag that can detect temperature, humidity, pressure, acceleration, gyration and magnetism in real time. So far there are only a few mobile applications available on App Store that make use of sensor tag. Furthermore, people are paying more attention on the fitness, but the existing fitness apps on the App Store just teach users the methodology and use the gyroscope and GPS in the mobile devices itself to make things happen. None of them can connect to a peripheral to make the fitness more effective and more precise. Based on the current situation, the author decided to combine the peripheral and some reasonable methodologies together by developing a weight training mobile application for iPad. This mobile application fully utilizes the TI BLE sensor tag that allows users to calculate calorie consumption precisely and exercise more effectively. Additionally, it also involves health care including temperature and humidity alert. It also allows motion control and recognition that enables user to control the application based on the motions.

title: What She Signs They Mine: Quantifying the Gaps in FemTech Privacy Policies
venue: International Conference on Data Analytics for Business and Industry (ICDABI)
abstract: Femtech applications have revolutionized women’s healthcare, yet transparency failures are inevitable in their data privacy practices. While recent investigations highlight privacy violations in reproductive health applications, existing automated assessment frameworks lack domain-specific adaptations to evaluate femtech privacy practices. This study explores privacy policy transparency in femtech applications through domainspecific risk weighting and an XLNet-based multidimensional evaluation. The methodology compares Data Safety Section declarations with privacy policy content across 68 femtech applications listed on the Google Play Store. The comparison is supported with a custom-defined three-tier transparency assessment framework encompassing Information Coherence Analysis, Privacy Disclosure Assessment, and Privacy Protection Evaluation across comparable features. The XLNet-based classification system achieves substantial performance improvements with F1score ranging from 0.792 to 0.845 across pre-defined privacy dimensions. The transparency assessment reveals discrepancies where privacy policies disclose a higher health data monetization compared to Data Safety Section declarations (8.8% versus 2.9 %), while 17.6 % of applications exhibit critical security gaps through inadequate encryption and deletion capabilities. This research advances femtech privacy assessment through domainspecific risk weighting and multi-dimensional evaluation, establishing a foundation for ethical data handling, fostering trust and accountability.

title: What do we assess when we assess mHealth app privacy and security? A rapid scoping review of mHealth app privacy instruments
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
abstract:
OBJECTIVES
While there are numerous mobile health (mHealth) apps on the market, previous research has highlighted their risks to privacy and security. Therefore, an instrument to assess the privacy and security of these apps may be helpful for ensuring consumers' data safety. We therefore conducted this rapid scoping review with the objective of surveying the landscape for instruments used to measure and quantify privacy and/or security of mHealth apps in the past 10 years.


MATERIALS AND METHODS
Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched the relevant literature in 4 electronic databases between May 2015 and May 2025. The characteristics of the papers and/or instruments were analyzed and reported descriptively. The instruments' content was analyzed using content analysis.


RESULTS
We identified 66 papers describing 42 distinct instruments. We found that the number of items and rating methods varied significantly across the instruments. Five topics were identified from content analysis: data practice, security measures, risk and incident management, regulatory compliance and users' rights, and privacy policy and terms and conditions.


DISCUSSION
While the nature of the instruments is diverse, it is currently unknown how many items, which topics, or how responses should be structured is optimal. Additionally, the majority of identified instruments cannot comprehensively measure the proposed 5 topics. Moreover, questions on security measures may not be easily rated by users without specific domain knowledge.


CONCLUSION
This review can serve as a guide for future mHealth app privacy and security evaluation.

title: What do you fear?: A study on user generated health data and privacy behavior
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
abstract: Health tracking wearables used outside the clinical settings to monitor an individual’s health are widely used recently despite the information privacy concerns these devices evoke. Academic research addressing the effect of fear appeals on information privacy in the context of user-generated health data is scarce. It is important to understand what is an individual’s perspective on health data privacy and the influence of fear appeals on privacy behavior. The present exploratory qualitative study captures an individual’s perspective of information privacy on health data from 27 respondents using an adapted extended parallel process model. The study reveals what individuals perceive as threats and their extent of efficacy to handle the concerns over information privacy. It is observed, fear appeals influenced the respondents to choose between danger control or fear control behavior. This study provides an insight into the importance of an individual’s privacy and their behavioral change, which could prove useful for manufacturers and regulators.

title: What's on Your Mind? Exploring Privacy of Mental Health Apps
abstract: Therapy and life-coaching apps have grown rapidly in number, variety, and popularity. At the same time, their users often share highly sensitive and personal information, including mental health issues, trauma experiences, fantasies, desires, and relationship difficulties. This prompts the need to examine privacy practices across the ecosystem. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of a corpus of 25 popular Android mental health and life-coaching apps, such as Replika and Headspace. It builds on static analysis and dynamic network traffic analysis, coupled with identifying gaps between each app's observed behavior and its privacy policies. Our analysis highlights serious concerns and substantial transparency gaps. First, every app in our corpus embeds at least one tracker SDK not named in its privacy policy, and 85\% of the apps we instrument fail to disclose at least half of the trackers detected in their APKs. Second, more than half of the apps declare several dangerous permissions without corresponding privacy-policy disclosures, including camera or microphone permissions. Third, nearly half the apps disclose third-party AI processing (e.g., via OpenAI, Anthropic, and Groq) in their privacy policies, while several use only generic language (e.g., "AI services"), failing to identify which company receives user data. Overall, our results show that current disclosure practices fall short of the transparency needed for meaningful informed consent. We argue for a significantly updated regulatory framework for therapy apps that more closely aligns with the professional and ethical standards that bind licensed human therapists.

title: What’s Wrong with Lookism? Personal Appearance, Discrimination, and Disadvantage
abstract: Lookism is a topic that philosophers have been eerily silent about. Some notable exceptions notwithstanding, it seems that some philosophers either have personal looks as a blind spot in their thinking or simply do not deem it a relevant topic for systematic philosophical inquiry. But given that race and gender receive so much attention in social philosophy, it is an increasingly notable omission that looks are so underappreciated, given that looks, like race and gender, arguably determine one’s social life in significant ways. In this relatively sparse landscape, Andrew Mason has now published what is one of the first monograph-length philosophical reflections on looks and lookism. Part 1 deals with the nature of what makes discrimination wrong, part 2 considers three different contexts of lookism, and part 3 addresses possible strategies for ameliorating the negative societal effects of lookism.Part 1 espouses Mason’s preferred (meta)ethical framework of what makes something wrong. Mason opts for a pluralist account that allows for something to be wrong for either contingent or noncontingent reasons. Discrimination is noncontingently wrong iff it is wrong irrespective of its causal consequences. Discrimination is contingently wrong iff it is wrong in virtue of its causal consequences (i.e., it has unjust effects). Mason suggests that lookism can be wrong for either type of reason in what he calls a pluralist account. The two main noncontingent features that make discrimination wrong lie in its constituting disrespect and deliberative unfairness. The main contingent wrong associated with discrimination lies in “contributing to lowering the perceived moral standing of members of a group” (70). Mason’s approach then consists in teasing out the wrongness of lookism by finding noncontingent and contingent wrongs it incurs.Part 2 applies the views developed in part 1 about the wrongness of discrimination to three different contexts of lookism: the workplace, personal relationships, and everyday lookism. Mason suggests that appearance discrimination—at least in the workplace—is like racial discrimination in certain respects. In particular, since many parts of our appearance are as immutable as our race, “some of what is classed as racial discrimination is a distinctive kind of discrimination on the basis of appearance” (73). But racial discrimination and appearance discrimination are unlike one another insofar as not all cases of appearance discrimination seem to deny the fundamental moral equality of people. As for personal relationships, Mason argues that the wrongness of appearance discrimination lies in the following aspects: in reducing other people to their appearance if one deems their looks below a certain threshold, and that being the only factor in one’s partner selection; in denying someone access to goods that figure as the result of a personal relationship; and inflicting negative consequences on someone by lowering their moral status. Regarding everyday lookism, the relevant wrongs are in the victims being demeaned; in the added costs for people having to adjust their looks to meet certain standards; and in instances of psychological suffering of the victims (e.g., poor self-image).Part 3 suggests possible interventions to appearance discrimination—namely, legal means (e.g., outlawing appearance discrimination in some contexts) and interpersonal forms of amends (outside of the legal system). Unsurprisingly, Mason argues that there ought to be relatively thorough legal influence on employment discrimination based on appearance. Legal methods may consist in prevention and compensation. Mason argues that, in general, compensation is an inadequate response to appearance discrimination, such that our societal focus ought to be on prophylaxis through legislation. He suggests that such legislation can be reasonably modeled after existing legislation that prohibits discrimination in terms of disability. Mason, however, acknowledges that legislation against lookism in personal relationships is likely equally as futile as attempting to legislate, say, rules for friendship with others in terms of race and gender, which would most likely encroach on one’s right to privacy (197). However, Mason also suggests a Dworkin-type hypothetical insurance model that can be used to compensate individuals who suffer from appearance discrimination—for example, by funding plastic surgery, perhaps.Mason’s overall account of lookism is tightly argued and comprehensive, an achievement that is amplified considering the relative dearth of already existing scholarly debate on the topic that one could usually use to structure one’s account. But these are areas that I would have wanted Mason to explore more. These are not ‘knock-down’ arguments against his views but rather suggestions for future clarification.The Private as Political? I wonder whether the principled distinction between private and professional spheres really exists in the way that Mason seems to assume throughout the book. Work life and social life can often not neatly be distinguished. By the same token, looks work as a social ‘lubricant’ in professional settings just as much as in private settings. Hard-skill-related competence is not the only thing that is relevant in an office job; charisma—which usually cannot be fully distinguished from looks—is often just as important in many professions.When Looks Are the Point. In some work environments, looks are the point of employment, not just a side phenomenon. For example, while many would agree race plays virtually no role, by itself, in work performance, the point of being a professional model usually lies in the looks of the person. As far as I can tell, Mason is not overly concerned with such cases. But it may be the case that his account implies duties for either corporations or private customers hiring models. Even if Mason’s account holds up for the cases he envisions (employment and private interaction), it does not seem to apply to cases where having certain looks is the point. Mason may likely rebut that such cases would not constitute wrongs because they do not involve disrespect or unfairness. One possible problem here is that granting model agencies the right to discriminate in terms of looks also opens the door for other forms of discrimination. The people selecting models for the agency may have implicit bias that makes them judge Black people on average as less attractive, resulting in them hiring few or no Black people. Overall, it seems that circumstances where looks are the point include a degree of subjectivity of selection that makes it at least difficult to determine whether disrespect or deliberative unfairness is involved. It is at least difficult to see why models agencies being free to hire based on standards of beauty that are largely opaque does not create unjust effects as a result of deliberative unfairness. Analogously, we are often more inclined to grant that companies hiring for a position based on similarly opaque standards at least potentially involves unjust effects.Which Cases Are Relevant? Some of Mason’s core cases (106) and key cases (107–109) may prove to be inapt insofar as it is questionable whether they are really related to appearance. Most notably, some of the cases may be cases not of appearance discrimination but rather of sex or religious preferences. The case in which a female patient prefers a female doctor is rather a case of sex discrimination (or a benign preference). In some hiring scenarios involving a woman who wears a hijab, the decision to hire (or not hire) her might not hinge specifically on the fact that she wears a headscarf. The relevant people may have an issue with certain religions (for example, the three Abrahamic religions) themselves. This would not meet the criteria for unjust discrimination regarding appearance although appearance is involved. Mason goes on to sort such core and key cases into legitimate and illegitimate, but my point here is that whether such cases are legitimate discrimination is sometimes not a matter of appearance at all. Because people are embodied, their appearances signal visible features aside from their looks—for instance, their race, sex, or religion. And so a Hijabi woman could suffer religious discrimination because of her (visible) headscarf without suffering lookism per se.Alternative Approaches. Mason mainly seems to assume a consequentialist framework in his considerations. This is not necessarily a limitation, but the book would have benefited from some further justification as to why consequentialist approaches are (presumably) more fruitful than deontological or virtue theorist approaches. In particular, remedies or future prophylaxis against appearance discrimination could prominently feature virtue ethical considerations about duties to foster attitudes of not caring about other people’s looks.Extreme Ugliness. The most common form of lookism is directed upon what we may call conventionally unattractive people: people who are just not good looking, but nothing out of the ordinary. The most extreme case Mason considers is about a hard-to-look-at lawyer with facial scarring. There are, however, certain hard cases that Mason’s account may not cover. One sort of case is extreme facial disfigurement. Some survivors of horrific accidents or attacks, or people with rare genetic disorders, are often so difficult to look at—no matter how much one tries to be nondiscriminatory—that we cannot help but prefer others. If ought implies can, then there cannot be a duty to not discriminate against people with extreme facial disfigurement, at least in cases such as dating, romance, or close personal friendship. In such cases, the subjectively felt horror at their appearance may win out against one’s good-natured attitude toward others. But it is an interesting and important question to consider what, if anything, we ought to do in such cases.Difficult Cases. Mason discussion includes relatively ‘mundane’ instances of appearance discrimination regarding tattoos and piercings. But there are also related difficult cases. For example, think about someone with extremely ‘problematic’ tattoos: someone who has a visible swastika tattoo or someone who has genitals tattooed on their forehead. Suppose further that they are by miles the most qualified worker for a certain position. Is it still acceptable to exclude them from this opportunity? Similarly, in some cases of extreme body modification, people cut off their noses or implant or put subdermal implants into their foreheads to mimic the appearance of horns. Body modifications of this kind are sometimes executed with the goal of scaring or intimidating others. In some cases, it may be necessary for one’s own well-being to avoid people with certain extreme body modifications. To be sure, I am not blaming Mason for not having considered these cases extensively; they just pose a different kind of problem his views can be tested against.Mason’s book is an enormous step into the right direction and is sure to provide the foundation for future works on normative aspects pertaining to human looks and looks-based discrimination. It is rigorous, clear, and principled in the best way possible. I recommend this book as an important resource for anyone working in normative ethics, political philosophy, or aesthetics.

title: When Your Therapist Is an Algorithm: Understanding the Role of AI in Mental Health Mobile Applications
venue: International Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
abstract: Mental health applications offer accessible alternatives to traditional care, with many now integrating AI features like chatbots and personalized recommendations. However, little is known about how AI is actually implemented or how users experience these features. Our study examines both developer positioning and user perceptions of AI in mental health applications. We systematically analyzed 244 mental health apps from the Apple App Store, identifying 12 distinct AI roles (e.g., coach, tracker, companion) and four interface types. We then conducted thematic and sentiment analysis of 996 user reviews from 27 AI-enabled apps to understand user experiences. Our analysis revealed recurring tensions around AI replacing human roles, trust, and augmentation. Our findings contribute a structured understanding of AI’s current roles in digital mental health and offer design recommendations for more effective and empathetic implementation.

title: Who's Wearing? Ear Canal Biometric Key Extraction for User Authentication on Wireless Earbuds
abstract: Ear canal scanning/sensing (ECS) has emerged as a novel biometric authentication method for mobile devices paired with wireless earbuds. Existing studies have demonstrated the uniqueness of ear canals by training and testing machine learning classifiers on ECS data. However, implementing practical ECS-based authentication requires preventing raw biometric data leakage and designing computationally efficient protocols suitable for resource-constrained earbuds. To address these challenges, we propose an ear canal key extraction protocol, \textbf{EarID}. Without relying on classifiers, EarID extracts unique binary keys directly on the earbuds during authentication. These keys further allow the use of privacy-preserving fuzzy commitment scheme that verifies the wearer's key on mobile devices. Our evaluation results demonstrate that EarID achieves a 98.7\% authentication accuracy, comparable to machine learning classifiers. The mobile enrollment time (160~ms) and earbuds processing time (226~ms) are negligible in terms of wearer's experience. Moreover, our approach is robust and attack-resistant, maintaining a false acceptance rate below 1\% across all adversarial scenarios. We believe the proposed EarID offers a practical and secure solution for next-generation wireless earbuds.

title: Why We Need to Consider Patient-Centered Care in Online Records
abstract: Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social NetworkingAhead of Print Free AccessWhy We Need to Consider Patient-Centered Care in Online RecordsBrenda K. WiederholdBrenda K. WiederholdSearch for more papers by this authorPublished Online:23 Jan 2024https://doi.org/10.1089/cyber.2023.29306.editorialAboutSectionsPDF/EPUB Permissions & CitationsDownload CitationsTrack CitationsAdd to favorites Back To Publication ShareShare onFacebookXLinked InRedditEmail Your phone dings as you wait for an Uber: new medical test results are available. You've been dealing with back pain for months, and you're eager to see the report from your recent MRI. Seated in the back seat of the car, you access your medical records from your phone. You log on to your patient portal, click the notification—and are presented with several long, confusing paragraphs of medical jargon.What does it all mean? It depends. Your doctor will need to explain the results and come up with a treatment plan, but that won't happen until your next appointment. In the meantime, all you can do—other than Google your results over and over again—is wait. You have information, but you haven't been given the knowledge to read it.Patients often receive their test results long before their scheduled follow-up with their physician. What can (or should) a patient do with this information while they wait? In many cases, nothing. Yet, there is a big push, especially in the digital age, to ensure that patients receive their test results and appointment notes as soon as possible, sometimes even before their doctors review them.This presents a dilemma. While the Digital Age creates opportunities for easier access to information, it also opens up problems ranging from misinterpretation to breakdowns in communication. As such, patient portals should focus more on patient-centered care, creating opportunities that complement the patient's treatment—not confuse them.The Rush of Instant GratificationTechnological advancements, in both devices and software, have allowed medical offices to embrace digital systems for record management and patients to review their medical information directly from their devices. Additionally, the passage of the 21st Century Cures Act facilitated greater patient control over their health information. Effective in 2020, the Act aims to empower patients by mandating transparency in electronic health records.1 It includes a provision that requires that patients receive their health information without delay, with violations triggering penalties of up to $1 million for technology developers and networks.2 The aim of this policy is to ensure that patients have easy, immediate access to their health records, satisfying the compelling moral argument that medical information rightly belongs to the patient.3 The Act also allows providers to choose the software that allows them to provide better care. Similar regulations are under consideration globally.Enabling patients to access the results of their actions in near real time and to review the changes in their test values as they progress can be extremely motivating. In diabetes management, patients who are able to monitor how their blood sugar numbers are affected by lifestyle changes, both at home and on official lab tests, have increased success at managing their treatment. Similar self-management programs include anticoagulation therapy with Coumadin, migraine and tension headache treatment, and heart failure monitoring. In these cases, laboratory values can guide the patient to determine effective dosages of their maintenance medications. For these programs to be effective, patients need access to their lab results as soon as possible, without the delay of waiting for their doctor to review them first. This increase in access corresponds with changes in patient behavior during and after the COVID-19 pandemic: as telehealth usage rose, so did the proportion of U.S. adults accessing their medical records online.The Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT reports that from 2020 to 2022, the percentage of adults who were offered access to their medical records and used it surged by 50%, from 38% to 57%.4 However, greater access to information also requires patient support, particularly in light of disparities among those who do not have a way to access online medical records easily.Primum Non Nocere: First, Do No HarmAs with any new technology, there are issues around electronic medical records that must be addressed. In addition to privacy and equity of access concerns, there is the very real possibility that patients may receive immediate access to medical information that makes them feel confused and anxious—particularly without the interpretation and explanation that medical professionals can provide.First, the timing of receiving medical news is crucial. In a clinical appointment, patients typically receive news in a controlled environment with minimal distractions, allowing them to process information immediately and seek guidance from their healthcare provider. However, accessing test results as soon as they become available outside the clinical setting can leave patients alone to deal with potentially distressing news. Often, results are uploaded at times when the doctor isn't available to provide immediate explanations, leading to hours or even days of anxious waiting for the patient. This delay can impact the doctor–patient relationship. Patients rely on their doctors for clarity on health concerns and treatment options, and the anxiety of waiting can undermine their trust.Moreover, imaging or pathology reports are usually written in medical jargon unfamiliar to patients, potentially leading to anxiety and misinterpretation. Without a medical professional's insight, patients might make health decisions based on incomplete or misunderstood information. Not all abnormal results are necessarily alarming, but it requires a trained medical professional, sometimes more than one, to interpret medical data accurately and decide on an appropriate course of action for the patient's specific condition.Although these systems and laws were designed to help patients take control of their health while at the same time increasing efficiency of care and reducing workload, immediate release of results can, at times, negatively impact both patients and healthcare providers. Clinicians have voiced that these policies have increased their workload, stress, and potential burnout for several reasons.3 In some cases, increased patient anxiety has led to an uptick in messages from patients outside of regularly scheduled appointments. Policies also state that it is the doctor's responsibility to coordinate the release of data for each patient—even if their software does not support that capability, leading to added administrative work.5Additionally, equitable access is a significant concern. Patients with Medicaid, those without a college degree, males, Hispanics, or those without Internet access are less likely to use an online patient portal.6 In certain instances, patients prefer direct communication with a provider or may not have a regular healthcare provider. Other times, concerns about privacy or discomfort with technology can be barriers. While patient portals facilitate access to medical information, they don't address the fundamental challenges that restrict access. Consequently, a portion of the patient population remains unable to access essential health information.From Patient Portals to Patient-Centered PortalsDespite the potential pitfalls, almost all patients (96%) claim to want access to their information as soon as it is available.7 However, most draw a line between speed and care. Sixty-five percent of patients would prefer to speak with their physician before getting results that might be “life-changing.”5 So, how do we strike a balance between empowering patients to be active participants in their own recovery, which we aim to do, and avoiding causing them undue anxiety or trauma, which we certainly want to avoid? The solution lies in what this technology promotes: personalizing healthcare and allowing individual patients to make informed decisions.Medical staff can assist patients by asking how they would like to receive their results and suggesting they set their devices accordingly. For example, if a particular patient is prone to anxiety, especially over health issues, they can consider turning off portal notifications and wait for appointments to receive test results. Pre-counseling about possible outcomes and being clear about what various test results may mean can also help reduce patient worry, both before and after results are posted. Providing the patient with information and resources ahead of time may help them interpret data if they receive medical test results before their provider has a chance to speak with them.Furthermore, patient portal designers can mitigate anxiety and misinterpretation of results by giving them instructions on how to customize their user experience, prompting patients to set notification settings and alerts. Ideally, portals are designed with the ability to adjust to the patient's preferred language seamlessly. Portals can also provide access to medically backed resources to help patients interpret their data until they are able to speak with their doctor, or to encourage providers to provide a layperson explanation when test results are delivered. For patients who are concerned about privacy and cybersecurity, patient portals should clearly communicate how patient information is stored and protected, with added security measures such as two-factor authentication when appropriate.Finally, policymakers need to enact laws that maintain a free flow of information, while at the same time allowing flexibility for addressing the health needs and preferences of individual patients and the complexities of patient–physician relationships. As we work toward an ideal electronic medical information system, ensuring that the portals themselves are as customizable as the medical data contained within, we must keep in mind the goal of patient-centered care.References1. 21st Century Cures Act.
